sections.note:
Full Title: Serve the People: Asian/Black American Anti-Colonial Struggle

In the structure of American racial hierarchies, a durable legacy of colonialism, Asian Americans and African Americans have long been pitted against one another—in education, labor, social standing, political objectives, and, always, in their perceived relation to whiteness. Yet, for at least a century, strong Black and Asian/American inter-influences and alliances have existed in political movements, intellectual thought, and cultural productions: from Ho Chi Minh’s anti-lynching writings; Paul Robeson’s and W.E.B. Du Bois’ visits to China; the 1955 Bandung Conference; through to the influence of Maoist thought on the Black Panthers; Black Power and Yellow Power movements; Bruce Lee as global masculine (non-white) icon; coalitions against the Vietnam War; and up to current alliances in various anti-racist and anti-imperialist endeavors (George Floyd, Gaza), Black and Asian/Asian diasporic peoples have refused Western colonial strategies of divide-and-conquer and have repeatedly challenged white supremacy and racial capitalism through acts of political solidarity and ideas and movements whose praxis was (and is) rooted in making concrete material change “for the people,” in this country and abroad. We will examine political and theoretical writings, literature, film, and music by Du Bois, Hughes, Richard Wright, Ho Chi Minh, Mao Tse-tung, Martin Luther King, Malcolm X, Bruce Lee, Huey Newton, Fred Hampton, George Jackson, Yuri Kochiyama, Fred Ho, Grace Lee Boggs, and Jackie Wang, among others.

courses.title: Faculty Seminars - Close Looking
courses.desc: A special seminar for first-year students taught by faculty who serve as their pre-major advisers.

sections.note: This course is designed to develop the skill of close and slow looking in order to deepen and strengthen thinking, learning, and understanding. Close and slow looking involves developing the capacity to explore the world closely in a variety of settings and taking the time to observe details, move beyond one’s first impression and be open to different perspectives. The ability to look slowly and closely can be learned and developed, and offers transferrable skills across disciplines; in fact, these tools are frequently used by doctors, scientists, and criminologists. This course will introduce students to Visual Thinking Strategies, Artful Thinking Routines, and other observational methods to help guide and facilitate the slow and close looking processes and to help deepen and strengthen thinking. Field trips to area museums and galleries are planned.

courses.title: Faculty Seminars - Financial Literacy
courses.desc: A special seminar for first-year students taught by faculty who serve as their pre-major advisers.

sections.note: Ever thought “Why doesn’t someone teach a class about how to handle all that adult financial stuff?” well you are in luck. Paychecks, budgets, taxes, savings, credit cards, loans, and more…what does it all mean and where to begin? In this course we will discuss all the pieces that make up a personal financial life and how they interact with one another and how policy and laws (pulled from the headlines) can have an impact on individuals and families. The goal of this class is not to make you a financial expert, but to provide a basic toolkit in order to set you up to make thoughtful and informed decisions as you move forward.

courses.title: Faculty Seminars - Gender and American Politics
courses.desc: A special seminar for first-year students taught by faculty who serve as their pre-major advisers.

sections.note: In 2021, Kamala Harris became the first woman to hold the office of Vice President. Women now register and turn out to vote at higher rates than men. Yet women comprise less than one third of Congress and statewide elected officials and govern in only 14 states (a record high). What explains these phenomena? In this course we will examine the role of gender in American politics, covering women and men as political participants, office-seekers, and members of the various levels and branches of government. We will also analyze how sex and gender-based issues intersect with other politically relevant categories and identities such as race, class, age, ideology, and partisanship. Finally, we will take advantage of the 2026 electoral contests in discussions and assignments throughout the course so students should be prepared to keep up with those events and analyze them through a gendered lens.

courses.title: Special Topics - Kenya, Britain, & Mau Mau
courses.desc: Please see departmental website for detailed course description.

sections.note: The Mau Mau War in 1950s Kenya was one of the bloodiest chapters in the history of the British Empire after World War Two. This foundation seminar examines the different theoretical and methodological approaches that historians have employed to study the war, including feminism, Marxism, and peasant studies. It also explores the wide variety of sources that exist for the war, such as films, novels, news reports, colonial records, and the memoirs of Mau Mau guerrillas, government troops, and European settlers. The seminar thus introduces students to the historian’s craft by teaching them how to critically analyze primary and secondary sources, how to assess the validity of competing historical narratives, and how to develop new avenues of research on a widely studied topic.

courses.title: Special Topics - Intro to Carceral Studies
courses.desc: Please see departmental website for detailed course description.

sections.note: This course critically engages the political, economic, and social histories of the contemporary criminal legal system. Together, we will historicize and theorize the advent of the US prison in a genealogy of surveillance, captivity, and punishment constitutive of racial slavery. Thematics including abolition, resistance and revolt, state repression, borders, gendered violence, and Black radicalism will be at the heart of the coursework. Students can expect to gain a better understanding of the key terms of the developing disciplines of Carceral Studies and Prison Studies using primary and secondary source material, film, poetry, and other new media.

courses.title: Special Topics - History of transAtlantic Slavery
courses.desc: Please see departmental website for detailed course description.

sections.note: This course broadly considers Atlantic slavery through its multiple geographies, temporalities, and institutions of emergence. Through an engagement with canonical and contemporary historiographic texts of slavery that consider themes and problematics like political economy, gendering, and intellectual history, students will encounter a range of perspectives on Atlantic Slavery, not as an historical event of the ‘past,’ but as a condition of possibility for our modern world. Using primary archival sources to supplement vital secondary literature, the course offers access to resources that are held in hard-to-access libraries and archives to prompt curiosity regarding the nature of historiographic evidence, the predicament of experience, and the complexity of ‘official records.

courses.title: Introduction to Africana Studies
courses.desc: A wide-ranging survey of the history, culture, and politics of people of African descent on the African continent and in the diaspora. Issues of colonialism, migration, slavery, revolution will be emphasized. The formation and growth of black communities in the New World and in the former colonial capitals.

courses.title: Special Topics - W.E.B Du Bois
courses.desc: Please see departmental website for detailed course description.

sections.note:
7 seats reserved for CAP advising 

W.E.B. Du Bois and the Problem of the Color Line 

In 1903, W.E.B. Du Bois wrote that "the problem of the twentieth century is the color line." By that time, Du Bois had already published multiple works examining the lived experiences and political struggles of Black people in the United States. He continued to write on these topics for the nearly sixty years. This course examines the interdisciplinary scholarship of W.E.B. Du Bois. Reading across his sociological, historical, and literary works, we will study how he employed multiple research methods and genres of writing to explore how Black people in the United States understood, experienced, and sought to redress "the color line." Readings will include fiction and non-fiction books, essays, poems, and newspaper articles written by Du Bois

courses.title: Gender in World Cultures
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as WGSS 12) Introduces anthropological approaches to gender in diverse contexts, and to theories of gender and culture, focusing on how individuals and societies create, reproduce, and navigate systems of sex and gender. Asks how gender is defined and contested, and how it is subject to systems of power as well as creative reimagining. Takes a cross-cultural and transnational perspective.

courses.title: Anthropology of the Environment
courses.desc: Key issues and frameworks of environmental anthropology across the 20th and 21st centuries. Provides students with an introduction to both the discipline of anthropology and changing forms of environmental thought. Introduces students to anthropological concepts including culture, nature, ethnography, adaptation, and human exceptionalism using cross-cultural materials and case studies.

courses.title: Introduction to the Anthropology of Science and Technology
courses.desc: (Cross listed w/ STS 32) An anthropological approach to the social and cultural studies of science and technology. Asks how and whether sociocultural forces shape the content of science, how to define “technology,” and how science and technology impact culture and society. Covers anthropological methods and research findings on topics such as algorithms, genetics, theoretical physics, classification, cyborgs, facts, infrastructure, and magic.

courses.title: Biological Anthropology
courses.desc: Human biological diversity and introduction to problems of biological diversity in living populations. Variation in genetic makeup: our size, shape, and color; our bodily responses to heat, cold, and workload; our neural responses to the world. Basic evolutionary principles applied to explain origins, mechanisms, and trends of human diversity. Topics include the interplay of biology and culture; adaptation to environmental stresses including cold, high altitude, and megacities; co-evolution of infectious disease, including STDs, smallpox, and malaria; basic Mendelian, molecular, and population genetics; primate biology and behavior; human growth; and the selective significance of contemporary behaviors such as using social media, reshaping the natural environment, taking risks in extreme sports, and online dating that meld genetic predispositions with new cultural frames. Includes a weekly lab..

courses.title: North American Archaeology
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ARCH 31) Introduction to North American archaeology—primarily focused on pre-colonial Indigenous histories and cultures. Examines history of the field, basics of archaeological method and theory, key insights and controversies associated with North American archaeology. Includes ancient population movements, Ice Age transformations, hunter-gather-fisher societies, moundbuilders, Indigenous-colonial interactions,with special emphasis on decolonization and Indigenous archaeologies.

courses.title: Internship In Anthropology
courses.desc:
Supervised internship in wide range of community organizations, health organizations, museums, governmental and non-governmental organizations. Twelve to fifteen hours work per week. Written assignments, with supporting readings, to place internship in critical analytical frame.
Recommendations: Anthropology majors only.

instructors: Alex Blanchette, Amahl Bishara, Cathy Stanton, Craig N. Cipolla, Nick Seaver, Tatiana Chudakova, Zarin P. Machanda

courses.title: Culture and Disability
courses.desc: Examines disability from an anthropological perspective. Focuses on how embodied differences are defined, experienced, and governed across cultures and historical periods. Topics include social constructions of normalcy; intersections of disability with race, gender, class, and nationality; and the influence of medical, technological, and political systems on the experience of disability. Readings draw from anthropology and disability studies in the US and international contexts.

courses.title: Food, Nutrition And Culture
courses.desc: Biological perspectives on human and non-human primate food systems, diet, and nutrition. Particular focus placed on the evolutionary processes and interactions between biology and culture that shape and are shaped by food. Topics include food webs, the evolution of cooking, the development of human social and foraging systems, physical and behavioral adaptations to diet, the science of nutrition, relationships between food and disease, and food sharing.

sections.note: Recommendation = ANTH 40

courses.title: Mesoamerican Archaeology
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ARCH 128 and LAS 128.) An introduction to the archaeology of pre-Columbian cultures of Belize, Guatemala, Honduras, and Mexico. Focus is on the origins of village life, the development of social complexity, emergence of states, ritual, religion, and culture collapse. Cultures studied include the Olmec, the Maya, the Zapotec, and the Aztec through artifacts, architecture, murals, inscribed monuments, hieroglyphs, and codices.

courses.title: Selected Topics - Queer Nightlife
courses.desc: Current Topics in Anthropology. Please see departmental website for specific details.

sections.note:
FULL COURSE TITLE: Queer Nightlife: Pleasure, Politics, Place

This class takes up a variety of nightlife spaces and contexts in which queer and trans people perform their pleasures and politics. Queer nightlife has been the center or political action. We have witnessed state sanctioned raids on Compton’s Cafeteria in San Francisco in 1966, Stonewall in NYC in 1969, the White Party in Bombay in 1999, the Queen Boat in Cairo in 2001, amongst many others. Additionally, in the wake of the massacre at Pulse Nightclub in Orlando in 2016, scholars have connected overlapping projects of imperialism that made queer life so precarious at Pulse. From these key moments have erupted important moments of activism that shifted common understandings of queer and trans life; nightlife has been a politically salient ground for shaping queer and trans cultures. In this class, we explore how and why queer nightlife become so threatening to the state, and the ways that nightlife offers a place of refuge from the mundane violence of everyday life. The class explores ball, drag, BDSM, disco, and rent party cultures, amongst many other forms of queer nightlife, and will include visits to local nightlife venues and class guests working in various nightlife worlds.

courses.title: Fieldwork Lab
courses.desc:
A hands-on field course in ethnographic methods, the signature toolkit of
cultural anthropology. Individual and collaborative small-scale projects. Students develop skills and experience in key strategies of "participant-observation"; research design; spatial, visual, and discourse analysis; formal and informal interviewing; fieldnote writing and coding; ethnographic writing. Fieldwork ethics, including IRB applications. Questions arising from the politics of difference, encounter, experience, and representation in relation to scholarly, community, and industry/client interests. Intensive but suitable for students at all levels.

courses.title: Chimpanzee Behavioral Ecology
courses.desc: (Cross-listed with Bio 182) Advanced seminar on current topics in behavioral research of chimpanzees and bonobos. Topics may include foraging, dominance, cooperation, adolescence, reproduction, culture, ranging, cognition, molecular ecology, and social relationships. Discuss behavioral flexibility of chimpanzees among different communities across Africa. Learn to collect and analyze behavioral data. Compare the behavior of chimpanzees and bonobos with that of humans and examine how these species might serve as models for human evolution. Prerequisite: ANTH 0044/BIO 0044 or consent.

sections.note: Graduate students may join the waitlist and will be able to move into the class as space allows starting 4/15/2026.

courses.title: Archaeologies of the Contemporary
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ARCH 184) Seminar in contemporary archaeology, using an archaeological lens to examine our world. Archaeologies of and for the contemporary world with special emphasis on method and theory. Themes covered may include campus archaeology, migration, settler colonialism, utopian communities, homelessness, nuclear waste, and the Anthropocene. Design your own contemporary archaeology project focused on the Tufts campus. No prerequisites.

courses.title: Ethnography for Policy and Planning
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as UEP 204) Introduction to ethnography and how qualitative, embedded, and socially committed research can critically and constructively contribute to addressing urban spaces and lead to just policymaking. Reading of ethnographic texts on urban and environmental issues. Practicing ethnographic and other qualitative research methods (for example participant observation, in-depth interviewing, material culture analysis, and archival, discourse, and media analysis). Students design and execute original research projects. Enrollment preference is given to UEP graduate students. Instructor permission required for Undergraduate students.

courses.title: How to Pay Attention
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as STS 189 & FMS 109) Collective investigation of attention as a sociocultural phenomenon. Reading-, writing-, and discussion-intensive seminar, supplemented by experimental exercises in and out of class. Topics include information overload, distraction, boredom, enchantment, expertise, social media, attention economies and ecologies, attention deficits and surpluses, and ideologies of attention in politics, education, and ethnographic fieldwork. Recommendations: Junior standing and one sociocultural anthropology course, or permission of instructor.

courses.title: Arab And Middle Eastern Cinemas
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ILVS 87, FMS 76 and ILCS 82). courses.title: Modern Arabic Literature
courses.desc: The Modern Arabic Literature course offers an introductory survey of major Arabic literary works of the modern period: the short story, the novel and poetry (with a look at other experimental forms). The literature selected represents many of the major figures of Arabic writing, from across the Arab world, spanning from the nineteenth century through the present day. A variety of cultural and social themes will be highlighted, including the way by which colonialism, nationalism, gender, sexuality, and political resistance have been reflected in Arabic literature. Readings will be supplemented with secondary texts and lectures, so as to offer thematic frameworks through which the literary readings will be discussed. In English.

courses.title: Ancient Egypt - Civ of The Nile & Near East
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as HIST 76, CLS 26, and ILVS 26) Survey of roughly 4,000 years of ancient Egyptian and Near Eastern civilization spanning c. 3,200 BCE to 651 CE. Analysis of the interrelations between art, architecture, history, and ideology, as preserved in material culture, inscriptions, and literary texts: pyramids, temples, tombs, settlements and cities, exceptional masterpieces and artifacts of daily life. Multiple excursions into religion, diplomacy, hieroglyphic writing, and artistic technique. Examination of the internal and external relations of Egypt in the context of a world system that included the kingdoms and empires of the Near East and the Mediterranean: from the Sumerians, Assyrians, Hittites, and Babylonians, to the Achaemenid Persian Empire, Alexander the Great, and the Imperium Romanum. Includes a field trip to the collections of the Museum of Fine Arts.

courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CHEM 6 and BIO 6). courses.title: Wanderers In Space
courses.desc: Space-age exploration of the planets and their moons; human landings on the moon; robot landings on Venus and Mars; liquid hydrogen and helium rain; planetary rings; asteroids and comets; thermonuclear reactions in the Sun; solar oscillations; the million-degree solar corona; the solar wind; solar effects; the greenhouse effect; ozone depletion and global warming.

May be used to satisfy the concentration requirements for major and minors in the Department of Physics and Astronomy. Prerequisites: Physics 11 and 12, or by instructor consent.

courses.title: Plants And Humanity
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ENV 10.) Principles of botany accenting economic aspects and multicultural implications of plants, their medicinal products, crop potential, and biodiversity. Emphasis placed on global aspects of this dynamic science, with selected topics on acid rain, deforestation, biotechnology, and other applications. Also covered are medicinal, poisonous, and psychoactive species, as well as nutritional sources from seaweeds and mushrooms to mangos and durians. Three lectures.

courses.title: Evolution In Our World
courses.desc: Designed for non-biology majors, explores the diversity of life on our planet, how that diversity came about, and how human actions are causing changes for the future. The evidence for evolutionary change; the mechanisms through which such changes occur; and the ways in which pollution, ocean acidification, and climate change are subjecting all organisms to a new range of selective pressures. Applications of evolutionary thinking to biomedical research.

courses.title: Cells And Organisms
courses.desc: An introductory course primarily for prospective biology majors. General biological principles and widely used methods related to current advances in cell and molecular biology, genetics, immunology, plant and biomedical sciences. A&S students, BSCHE, BSEvE, and BSE-EH majors enrolling in BIO 13 must concurrently enroll in BIO 15, Cells and Organisms Lab. SOE students who are planning a second major in Biology or to apply for medical school should concurrently enroll in BIO 15. Credit cannot be received for both BIO 13 and BME 33. Prerequisites: first-year standing in the school of Arts and Sciences, or sophomore standing in the School of Engineering. Recommendations: Advanced high-school chemistry and biology.

courses.title: Computational Biology
courses.desc: Quantitative and computational methods are central components of contemporary evolutionary, ecological, and biomedical research. Examines the process of biological inquiry through a computational lens with special attention to current areas of biological research, such as the genetic basis of complex traits and the predictability of evolution. Topics include introductory Python programming, evolutionary genetics, molecular genetics, simulation, and data analysis. No programming skills are assumed. Prerequisites: BIO 013 and BIO 014 or permission of instructor.

sections.req: Completion of Bio 13 and Bio 14 or equivalents.

courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ECS 38) Introduction to the origin, evolution, morphology, and paleoecology of life forms throughout the history of the earth. Laboratory emphasis on description, classification, and recognition of the most important groups of invertebrate fossils. Prerequisite: ECS 1 or ECS 2 or BIO 14 or permission of instructor.

Classes will concentrate on several biological concepts and emphasize appropriate experimental design, data collection, data analysis and presentation. One laboratory session per week plus one discussion period.
Requires completion of BIO 0014 or equivalent.

courses.desc: Concepts and techniques in microbiome science through independent research projects. Designing and conducting experiments to characterize microbiome diversity, identify processes that control microbiome composition, and quantify functional roles of microbiomes. Principles of experimental design, microbial genomics and metagenomics, microbiome data management and analysis, in vitro microbiome reconstruction, experimental evolution, microbial trait analysis, and microbial genetic screens.

courses.title: Research in Biology
courses.desc: Academic credit for students participating in biology research. Students must find their own research positions and may seek opportunities within or outside of Tufts. Students should speak with potential faculty supervisors prior to enrollment; see department website for project eligibility criteria and information on finding research opportunities. At least 150 hours (roughly 10 hours/week in the academic semester) of guided research involvement, including reading primary literature, data collection/analysis, and participation in research group meetings, culminating in a research paper. Confirmation of project eligibility and consent of supervising research mentor required at the start of the term. Pass/fail grading.

courses.title: Introduction to Independent Study in Biology

courses.title: Developmental Biology
courses.desc:
Basic concepts of developmental biology with emphasis on the molecular events underlying the morphological changes that occur during development. Examples will be drawn from a number of phyla to illustrate developmental mechanisms, e.g., gametogenesis, cleavage, organogenesis and determination, cell-cell interactions, induction, and programs of gene activation.
Recommendations: BIO 41 or 46.

courses.title: Molecular Biology
courses.desc: Gene structure and function in prokaryotes and eukaryotes, fundamentals of recombinant DNA technology. Molecular mechanisms of DNA replication and repair, recombination, transcription, and protein synthesis are emphasized. Advanced topics including regulation of gene expression during development, transposition, and regulation of chromatin structure are based on current literature.

sections.req: Requires completion of BIO 0041 or graduate standing.

courses.title: Endocrinology
courses.desc: A comprehensive introduction to the chemical and physiological principle of hormonal integration in animals. Topics include endocrine regulation of metabolism, growth and development, reproduction, neural functions, mineral and water balance, behavior, and nutrition.

sections.req: Completion of BIO 0014 or equivalent, or graduate standing.Sophomore Standing or Graduate Students

courses.title: Exercise Physiology
courses.desc: Functioning of the human body during acute and chronic exercise. Integration of fundamental concepts in functional anatomy and physiology with current knowledge on exercise. Anatomy of musculature associated with physical exertion; physiology of muscle systems; cardiovascular, respiratory, and nervous systems pertaining to the physical movement; and energetics of exercise. Emphasis on the impact of environmental factors, performance enhancers, and gender differences on performance (Group B: Biology of Organisms). Prerequisites: BIO 0013 and BIO 0014, or graduate standing.

sections.req: Completion of Bio 13 and Bio 14 or equivalents.

courses.title: Physiology – Circulation, Respiration, and Renal
courses.desc: Elements of homeostasis, circulation, respiration, and excretion are discussed at various levels, from the molecular to the organ system. Emphasis on critical thinking, integration, and application. BIO 116 is not required for this course. Requirements: BIO 014 or instructor permission, or graduate standing. Recommendations: BIO 013 or instructor permission.

sections.req: Completion of BIO 0014 or equivalent, or graduate standing.

Topics include probability, parameter estimation, inference, correlation, regression, analysis of variance, and nonparametric methods. (Group Q.) Required: BIO 13 and 14, or equivalent, plus one additional biology course above BIO 14.

Focus on rare and endangered species, as well as threatened ecosystems. Includes applications from animal behavior, captive breeding, and wildlife management. Readings from current texts and primary literature.

(Group A). Prerequisites: BIO 13 and CHEM 51.

sections.req: Requires completion of BIO 13 or BME 33, and CHEM 51, or graduate standing.

courses.title: Biophysics of Macromolecules
courses.desc: Biophysical properties of proteins and macromolecules as they relate to biology, biochemistry, medicine, and biomedical engineering. Physical rules that govern protein structure and function, protein folding and stability, and ligand binding. How tools of spectroscopy, kinetics, and thermodynamics can be applied to these concepts and lead to new mechanisms of function. Fulfills the group A requirement for the Biology major, and satisfies an elective for the Biochemistry and Biotechnology major. Prerequisites: BIO 13 or BME 33, PHY 1 or PHY 11, and BIO 152 or CHEM 171, or graduate standing or instructor consent.

(Cross-listed as BME 162 and CHBE 162.) Overview of key aspects of molecular biology and engineering aspects of biotechnology. Lecture topics include molecular biology, recombinant DNA techniques, immunology, cell biology, protein purification, fermentation, cell culture, combinatorial methods, bioethics, and bioinformatics with review and discussion of primary literature. Comprehensive technical paper on an emerging topic.
Students may not receive credit for both BME/CHBE/BIO 162 and BME 33.
Recommendations: CHEM 1, BIO 13 or permission of instructor.

courses.title: Seminar In Marine Biology
courses.desc:
Exploration of the primary scientific literature in areas selected by mutual consent. Topics may include symbiotic interactions, migration and dispersal, larval ecology, adult feeding and locomotory biology, responses to pollutants, and physiology of deep-sea animals. Strong focus on developing critical reading skills and effective writing through frequent, short assignments.
Recommendations: Junior standing and BIO 164 or permission of instructor.

sections.note: This seminar will explore ways by which anthropogenic changes in the ocean are shaping marine ecosystems. Warming of the upper ocean has many complex results that include range expansions and changes in phenology of many marine organisms, with further consequences to the distribution and abundance of life in the sea. Through targeted readings and discussions, we’ll develop an understanding of how physical changes in the ocean drive ecological changes in habitats ranging from coral reefs to the deep ocean ecosystems.
sections.req: BIO 13, BIO 14 or equivalents or graduate students

courses.title: Tropical Ecology And Conservation
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed as ENV 181). Ecology and evolution of biodiversity in
the tropics. Discussions of original literature; presentations of particular ecosystems, communities, or organisms; team design of research project to be completed during two weeks of intensive fieldwork in December/January in Costa Rica. Meets two times per week during the semester and is followed by a required research trip to Costa Rica. Funding may be available for those in need. Group C. Recommendation: BIO 14L or equivalent. Permission of instructor required. This course is offered during the following semesters: Fall Semester/ alternate years.

sections.note: This course requires an application in order to enroll. Please email colin.orians@tufts.edu or anne.maxime@tufts.edu to obtain the application or for additional information.

courses.title: Chimpanzee Behavioral Ecology
courses.desc: (Cross-listed with Anth 177) Advanced seminar on current topics in behavioral research of chimpanzees and bonobos. Topics may include foraging, dominance, cooperation, adolescence, reproduction, culture, ranging, cognition, molecular ecology, and social relationships. Discuss behavioral flexibility of chimpanzees among different communities across Africa. Learn to collect and analyze behavioral data. Compare the behavior of chimpanzees and bonobos with that of humans and examine how these species might serve as models for human evolution. Prerequisite: ANTH 0044/BIO 0044 or consent.

sections.note: Graduate students may join the waitlist and will be able to move into the class as space allows starting 4/15/2026.

courses.title: Darwinian Medicine Seminar
courses.desc:
The mechanistic vs. evolutionary causes of diseases and modern medical practice. Focus on the evolutionary causes of disease as a means of sharpening research skills and the understanding and application of Darwinian thought. Evolutionary hypothesis creation and testing in both oral and manuscript form. (Group C.)
Prerequisites: BIO 130 or permission of instructor.

sections.req: Completion of BIO 130. Open to undergraduate students only.

courses.title: Food For All: Ecology, Biotechnology & Sustainability
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed w/ENV 182) An interdisciplinary examination of the pros and cons of two divergent approaches to meeting the increasing global food demand: organic farming and genetic engineering. Contrasting crops grown in developing and industrialized countries serve as case studies to evaluate: (1) how ecological knowledge makes food production more sustainable; (2) what existing and emerging approaches can, in the face of climate change, contribute to a reliable supply of nutritious food; and (3) the political and economic drivers that shape who has access to these technologies. An important focus is developing communication skills for negotiating stakeholder-specific perspectives (growers, advocacy groups, industry, governmental agencies). 
Please see departmental website for specific details.
Recommendations: Intro Bio or Intro Chemistry or equivalent

sections.note: Class starts at 1:30

courses.title: DNA From Structure To Function
courses.desc: Molecular genetics and genomics through the study of the fundamentals of DNA structure and function. Topics include DNA secondary and tertiary structures, DNA topology and topoisomerases, mechanisms of protein-DNA recognition and the structure of the chromatin; how the principles of DNA organization are employed in key genetic transactions, including DNA replication, transcription, repair, and recombination. Seminar course combining lecture and discussion of scholarly literature. Prerequisite: BIO 105 or graduate standing.

Students should demonstrate autonomy in literature reading, experimental design, and data collection/analysis. Undergraduates should have prior research in a related project and written science communication experience equivalent to Bio 93; graduate students without prior research experience should be familiar with literature in the field prior to enrollment. Title: Exploratory research in developmental biology and environmental toxicology
Description: A laboratory-based inquiry course examining aspects of developmental biology and environmental toxicology.  Participants will investigate amphibian embryogenesis and the effects of several teratogens on normal development, which may include reactive oxygen species, microplastics, or other emerging pollutants. sections.note:
Title: Pharmacology and Therapeutics
Description: This course is an exploration of how therapeutic drugs exert their effects across various disease settings. Core content includes principles of how drugs affect the human body (pharmacodynamics), how the body affects drugs (pharmacokinetics), and how these fundamental pharmacologic principles affect drugs’ safety and efficacy. Students will explore how these concepts affect clinical care by using problem-based learning to analyze and present patient cases. Prerequisites: BIO 013, BIO 014, and at least 2 courses above BIO 021; or graduate standing.

Instructor: Frank Massaro, PharmD, Tufts Medical Center.

courses.title: Exploratory Topics in Biology - Biological Oceanography:Diversity & Func Life
courses.desc: Exploration of special topics in biology though seminars or lecture.

sections.note:
Full course title: Biological Oceanography: Diversity and Function of Life in Marine Ecosystems

The ocean is comprised of connected biological networks, from microorganisms to whales. Chemical and physical processes and interactions between biotic and abiotic components fuel this engine. The course will explore diversity and biological activities of oceanic life, with emphasis on microbial aspects, across contrasting ecosystems (open oceans, deep-sea, coral reefs). We will address topics that drive research, including: the role of diversity and interactions in sustaining healthy ecosystems, climate change, and human impacts. Students will gain a working knowledge and skill set such that they can participate in oceanographic cruises and analyze data from complex sampling programs. Requires relocation to Maine for Fall semester 2026; courses take place at the Bigelow Laboratory for Ocean Sciences. Programmatic housing options are available.

For more info, contact: tufts@bigelow.org

courses.title: Exploratory Topics in Biology - Ocean Biogeochemistry on a Changing Planet
courses.desc: Exploration of special topics in biology though seminars or lecture.

sections.note:
Full course title: Ocean Biogeochemistry on a Changing Planet

The ocean plays a key role in mediating climate and supporting Earth's life. In this course, students will build on topics covered in previous Bigelow courses to explore the biological, chemical, and physical processes that affect the cycling of elements in the ocean, e.g. photosynthesis and respiration, oxidation-reduction (redox) reactions, calcification and silicification, and ocean-sediment interactions, with emphasis on processes that directly affect global climate. The role of humans will be addressed through topics such as ocean acidification, coastal eutrophication and hypoxia, marine pollution, and geoengineering. Laboratory activities will investigate carbonate chemistry, redox reactions, metabolic energy transfer, and carbon cycling. In an extended laboratory activity students will work with Bigelow’s communication professionals to compose short videos to explain ocean biogeochemistry topics. Requires relocation to Maine for Fall semester 2026; courses take place at the Bigelow Laboratory for Ocean Sciences. Programmatic housing options are available.

For more info, contact: tufts@bigelow.org

courses.title: Exploratory Topics in Biology - The Ocean Environment: A Cross-Discip Foundation
courses.desc: Exploration of special topics in biology though seminars or lecture.

sections.note:
Full course title: The Ocean Environment: A Cross-Disciplinary Foundation

The study of marine systems requires an understanding of multiple intersecting disciplines, including physics, chemistry, biology, geology, and human systems. This course will set the stage to cover how these processes interact to create a variety of marine systems, from estuaries to the open ocean to the sea floor. The course will introduce modern methods of ocean observing, including data collection and analysis in a programming environment. Students will become proficient in using the primary scientific literature to inform their research and understanding, and build an understanding of how oceanic processes link to human activities, such as policy, geoengineering, and sustainability. Requires relocation to Maine for Fall semester 2026; courses take place at the Bigelow Laboratory for Ocean Sciences. Programmatic housing options are available.

For more info, contact: tufts@bigelow.org

courses.title: Exploratory Topics in Biology - Oceanographic Field Methods and Independent Rsrch
courses.desc: Exploration of special topics in biology though seminars or lecture.

sections.note:
Full course title: Oceanographic Field Methods and Independent Research

Exposes students to oceanographic research through field work and two projects. The field component includes 6 research cruises where students will collect physical (temperature, light penetration), chemical (macro-nutrient) and biological (bacterial, phytoplankton and zooplankton) data at 4 stations from within the Damariscotta River Estuary to the open ocean. Students will process, analyze, and interpret the oceanographic data they collect in the first project for this course, and present it in a poster session at Bigelow. For the second project, students will work with a faculty mentor to develop an independent research project that includes designing and executing a plan with experiments and data analysis. There will be 4 “Roundtable on Research” meetings led by course instructors, culminating in a scientific talk at a research symposium. By the end of the semester, students will have experienced the full range of activities involved in oceanographic research. Requires relocation to Maine for Fall semester 2026; courses take place at the Bigelow Laboratory for Ocean Sciences. Programmatic housing options are available.

For more info, contact: tufts@bigelow.org

courses.title: Exploratory Topics in Biology - Computing for Bioinformatics
courses.desc: Exploration of special topics in biology though seminars or lecture.

sections.note:
Title: Computing for Bioinformatics 

Introduction to principles and practices for scalable and reproducible computing in bioinformatics, focusing on version control, workflow automation, and use of shared and high-performance computing (HPC) environments. Students will apply these methods to real bioinformatics use cases, including genomics, transcriptomics, and other large-scale biological datasets while developing practical skills in pipeline design, computational collaboration, and research reproducibility. Skills will include Git/GitHub, workflow management (Nextflow), Linux command line, and containerization (Docker/Singularity), as well as introductory skills in Python/R

courses.title: Electrical Circuits and Biomedical Applications
courses.desc:
Fundamentals of electrical circuits, resistors, basic laws, methods of analysis, and network theorems. Capacitors, inductors, and impedance. Transient and steady-state sinusoidal analysis of electrical circuits. Laplace and Fourier analysis. Frequency response of circuits and transfer function. Basic concepts of amplifiers and operational amplifiers. Biomedical applications of electrical circuit concepts and methods.
Prerequisite: prior completion of MATH 34 and PHY 12

courses.title: Biomechanics: Solids and Fluids
courses.desc: Solid and fluid mechanics as related to biological systems. Stress, strain, motion and constitutive relations; force, mass, and momentum balances; equilibrium, universal solutions and inflation; extension and torsion, beam bending and column buckling; nonlinear solid biomechanics methods; exact solutions for biologically relevant fluid flow; coupled solid-fluid problems. With demonstrations of methods for measuring mechanical properties of biological systems. Prerequisite or concurrent enrollment in PHY 11 and MATH 34.

sections.req: Prior completion or concurrent enrollment in PHY 11 and MATH 34.

courses.title: Biomedical Concepts at the Molecular, Protein and Cellular Scales I
courses.desc:
First course of a two-course sequence on biomedical concepts at the molecular, protein and cellular level scales: nucleic acid structure and function, recombinant DNA techniques, genome sequencing, CRISPR gene editing, protein structure and function, regulation of protein expression, signal transduction, cellular receptors. Mix of didactic lectures, case studies, experimental/computational labs, and clinical/industrial presentations/visits.
Students may not receive credit for BME 33 and BIO 13, BME 162, or BME 163

courses.title: Biomedical Concepts at the Tissue, Organ and Systems Scales II
courses.desc:
Mechanics of solids, lever systems and moments as applied to bones, joints and muscles; linear and nonlinear circuit theory as applied to computational models of the respiratory and cardiovascular systems; mechanics of fluid flow through pipes as applied to vessels and airways; work and thermodynamic cycles as applied to pressure-volume systems of the heart and lungs; and basic control systems theory as applied to regulation of mean arterial pressure in the cardiovascular system. Applications to the musculoskeletal system, motor neurons, the cardiovascular system, the respiratory system, the lymphatic system, metabolism, the renal system and the digestive system. Instruction using a mix of didactic lectures, case studies, experimental/computational labs and clinical/industrial presentations and visits.
Prerequisites: BME 44

(Cross-listed as EE 131 and BIO 131.) This interdisciplinary course presents the principles of medical imaging techniques such as diagnostic ultrasound, radiography, X-ray computed tomography (CT), and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). For each imaging modality, topics include the physical principles, key aspects of instrumentation design, mathematical methods, and the anatomical/physiological information content of the images. Representative medical images will be discussed and interpreted. This course cannot be taken for basic science requirement for engineering students.
Recommendations: MATH 32 (formerly MATH 11), PHY 2 or 12, or permission of instructor.

courses.title: Analytical Tools For Biomedical Engineering
courses.desc:
Statistical methods of data analysis with emphasis upon biomedical applications. Topics include Fourier analysis, probability, Bayes' theorem, interpretation of diagnostic tests (sensitivity, specificity, predictive values), random variables, covariance and correlation, normal distribution, samples, statistical tests, linear systems, spectral analysis, correlation, coherence, phase analysis, independent component analysis and principal component analysis. Data analysis will be performed with MATLAB.
Recommendations: MATH 42, experience with MATLAB, or permission of instructor.

sections.req: Junior, Senior, or Graduate students only

sections.note: Recitation is required

courses.title: Biological Systems Analysis
courses.desc:
Mathematical and computational methods of biological systems at molecular and cell levels including regression, logic, statistics, kinetics, dynamical systems, pharmacodynamics, and agent-based modeling. Biological questions coordinated with appropriate mathematical modeling approach. 
Recommedations: Junior standing, CHEM 2, BIO 13, MATH 42, or permission of instructor

courses.title: Computational Systems Biology
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CS 166) Computational modeling of complex biological systems to analyze their emergent properties and understand or predict system behavior. Molecular and protein modeling in the context of biochemical networks. Application of these models across a select set of applications such as metabolomics, gut microbiome analysis, modularity analysis, flux balance analysis, and biological discovery. Introductions to machine learning, linear systems, and statistical concepts that are commonly used in systems biology.

sections.note: Students wishing to enroll in Computational Systems Biology should register under CS 166.
sections.req: CS 15 and at least one CS class numbered above 100 or graduate standing

courses.title: Biomaterials and Regenerative Medicine
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed as CHBE 164 and MSE 151). Fundamental concepts of biomaterials and regenerative medicine (biomaterial types, synthesis, properties, mechanisms of degradation, biological interfaces, inflammation and related issues). Specific focus on biomaterials related to regenerative medicine. Course independent of, but complementary to, BME 154. 
Recommendations: Junior standing, BIO13, CHEM 1, or consent of instructor

sections.req: Junior, Senior, or Graduate students only

courses.title: Bio-surfaces and Interfaces
courses.desc:
Physical chemistry of biological surfaces and bio-synthetic interfaces including surface tension, surface free energy, adsorption, diffusion, bio-molecular interactions, chemical/mechanical/electrical aspects of cellular interfaces. Applications to biomedical engineering such as biosensing, immunostaining, drug design, tissue engineering, bioMEMS, and electrophysiology.

Recommendations: BME 12, or permission of instructor.

courses.title: Molecular Biotechnology
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed as CHBE 162 and BIO 162) Overview of key aspects of molecular biology and engineering aspects of biotechnology. Lecture topics include molecular biology, recombinant DNA techniques, immunology, cell biology, protein purification, fermentation, cell culture, combinatorial methods, bioethics, and bioinformatics with review and discussion of primary literature. Comprehensive technical paper on an emerging topic.
Students may not receive credit for both BME/CHBE/BIO 162 and BME 33.
Recommendations: CHEM 1, BIO 13 or permission of instructor.

sections.req: Junior, Senior, or Graduate students only
Junior, Senior, or Graduate students onlyJunior, Senior, or Graduate students only

courses.title: Principles Of Controlled Release And Drug Delivery
courses.desc:
Fundamentals of drug product development and formulation with particular emphasis on novel and developing technologies for controlled release and drug delivery for biopharmaceuticals. Course includes coverage of formulation principles and discussion of the interplay between physiology, pathophysiology and dosage form development, pharmacokinetics, and novel materials used in controlled release.
Recommendations: CHEM 1 or 16, BIO 13 or ES 11, ES 2, and MATH 34

sections.req: Junior, Senior, or Graduate students only

courses.title: Biotechnology Processing Projects Lab
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CHBE 168) Laboratory experience with techniques in biotechnology processing: fermentation of recombinant E. coli cells, hybridoma cell culture, purification of protein and antibodies and related analytical procedures. Laboratories accompanied by lectures and relevant readings to cover the underlying principles.

sections.note: Graduate students require instructor permission.
sections.req: (BIO 13 or BME 33) & junior standing, no grads

courses.title: Orthopaedic Biomechanics
courses.desc: The effects of mechanical stress and strain on musculoskeletal tissues during growth, function, and repair. The impact of loads acting on the musculoskeletal system alone and with orthopedic interventions. Applications of classical mechanics for modeling and solving problems encountered in orthopedic surgery and evaluation of orthopedic implants. Forces and moments acting on human joints; composition and mechanical behavior of orthopedic biomaterials; design and analysis of joint replacement (hip, knee, shoulder, spine, and fracture fixation).

sections.req: BME 11 or ME 21 or Graduate Standing

courses.title: Cellular Agriculture & Biofabricated Foods
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as NUTR 253) Introduction to the concepts of cellular agriculture, food science and the use of biotechnology in food production. Laboratory experience in cell culture and biomaterials processing from cell isolation to generation of in vitro meat using tissue engineering techniques. Course culminates in a scientific, creative proposal based on student interests.

courses.title: Tissue Engineering Research Laboratory
courses.desc:
To gain hands-on experience in the field of tissue engineering by preparing and characterizing scaffold biomaterials, expansion and handling human adult stem cell, preparation and use of bioreactors and assembling a functional system to grow a tissue. In addition, safety, ethical, and general laboratory protocol issues are covered.
Students may not receive credit for both BME 175 and BME 34.

sections.req: Junior, Senior, or Graduate students only

courses.title: Special Topics - Sustainable Materials
courses.desc: Guided study of an approved topic.

sections.note: Exploration of materials used in everyday products through the lens of environmental sustainability, human health, and global impact. Students will examine how traditional plastics and other materials are evolving toward more sustainable alternatives, including the motivations, methods, and progress driving this shift. Topics include material synthesis, sources, processing, breakdown, reuse, sustainability assessment, lifecycle analysis, emerging strategies, and future directions. Course also incorporates current developments in the field and project-based work focused on innovative solutions.

courses.title: Optics And Wave Motion
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed as PHY 31). Propagation of electromagnetic waves; geometrical optics; polarization; optical properties of metals, insulators, and semiconductors; Fraunhofer and Fresnel diffraction; interference; Fourier optics. Lectures and laboratories.
Recommendations: PHY 2 or 2N or 12 or 12N. Corequisite: MATH 42 (formerly MATH 13)

courses.title: Principles Of Biomedical Engineering
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed as EE 250). The role of biomedical engineering in the diagnosis and treatment of various pathologies such as cardiovascular disease, cancer, diabetes, and neurological disorders. For each disease model, biomedical engineering principles are used to examine the function of the organ, 
mechanisms of the disease, diagnostic tools, and treatment approaches. Covered biomedical engineering areas include biomaterials, implantable devices, bioimaging techniques, gene therapy, and biosensors.
Recommendations: ES 121 or equivalent, or permission of instructor.

courses.title: BME Graduate Internship
courses.desc:
Off-campus experiential learning related and integral to BME field of study.
This course does not fulfill requirements towards graduate degree completion.

courses.title: BME Non-Thesis Research
courses.desc: Guided research on an approved topic suitable for a graduate-level scientific exploration. Students may not receive credit for BME 0289 and BME 0295, BME 0296, BME 0297, or BME 0298

courses.title: BME Graduate Project
courses.desc: Execution of a major, graduate project under the guidance of a faculty adviser. Each project must address a substantive engineering analysis or design problem. Students are required to submit a written report and make an oral presentation of their project work. Students are expected to enroll in this course in the last term of their degree program.

courses.title: Graduate Seminar
courses.desc: Biomedical engineering seminar series and presentation of individual reports to a seminar group for discussion.

courses.desc: Preparation of an original research proposal under the guidance of a faculty adviser. Proposals must address a substantive engineering analysis or design problem. MS students are required to submit a written report; PhD students are required to submit a written report and make an oral presentation.

courses.title: Fundamentals of Biostatistics
courses.desc: (Cross listed as CH 116) Examination of statistical methods used in biomedical and public health studies. Descriptive statistics, probability, basic hypothesis testing, ANOVA, linear regression, logistic regression, and an introduction to survival analysis. Instruction in the use of statistical software will be provided throughout the course. CEE 6 and CEE 156 cannot both be taken for credit

courses.title: Structural Analysis
courses.desc: A first course in the application of mechanics to the analysis of structures, with a major emphasis on structural forms important to civil engineering. Deflection calculations of beams and frames using differential equations and momen1t-area theorems. Deflection of trusses, beams, and frames using virtual work. Indeterminate structural analysis using flexibility and stiffness methods. Hands-on experience with industry-standard software and practical applications in structural engineering. With laboratory.

courses.title: Reinforced Concrete Design
courses.desc: Analysis and design of reinforced concrete members. Working stress and ultimate strength theories are applied to beams, girders, slabs, columns, walls, and footings. Use of these elements in various structures is studied.

courses.title: Engineering for a Sustainable and Resilient Society
courses.desc: Quantitative description of natural and engineered processes affecting environmental sustainability at local, regional, and global scales. Principles of ecology, material and energy flows, environmental quality, climate change, and resiliency in a civil and environmental engineering context.

sections.req: At least simultaneous enrollment in: MATH 34, (CHEM 1 or CHEM 11 or PHY 11), and (ES 2, CS 10, or CS 11)

courses.title: Pollutant Fate and Transport
courses.desc:
Basic principles of fate and transport related to environmental engineering. Thermodynamics, equilibrium, kinetics, mass balance, chemical partitioning, advection, dispersion and reactions for predicting behavior of pollutants in air, water, and soil. Techniques for measuring dissolved oxygen, biochemical oxygen demand, nutrients, sewage indicator bacteria, airborne particles and 
 hydrocarbons, and other pollutants. Applications to environmental processes. With laboratory.

sections.req: Prior completion of CHEM 2, BIO 13, CEE 32 & ES 7

courses.title: Introduction To Geotechnical Engineering
courses.desc: The engineering properties of soils and the behavior of soil masses subjected to loads and fluid flow. Flow of water through and stress in soil. Investigation of permeability, compressibility, and strength of soil. With laboratory.

courses.title: Public Health
courses.desc:
An introduction to the public health approach is provided. The epidemiological model of the disease process is used to study a variety of infectious and noninfectious diseases. The wide variety of nonmedical approaches to disease control is emphasized. The public health aspects of vital statistics, evaluation, and administrative decision making are introduced and applied to current problems in public health.
Recommendations: Consent of instructor.

courses.title: Cataldo Scholar Research
courses.desc: Supervised research through the Cataldo Scholars Program within Civil and Environmental Engineering. Department consent and Senior standing required

instructors: Babak Moaveni, Brian Brenner, C. Andrew Ramsburg, Daniel Kuchma, Deborah Sunter, Eric M Hines, Farshid Vahedifard, John Germaine, John L Durant, Jonathan Lamontagne, Laurie Baise, Luis Dorfmann, Masoud Sanayei, Paul Dombrowski, Wayne Chudyk

courses.title: Nano Course - FE Exam Review
courses.desc: Focused study of a selected engineering topic such as an engineering skill, method, or software package. Cannot be counted toward the Major Requirement for BSCE, BSEvE, BSE-EH or BSE-Arch.

courses.title: Independent Study
courses.desc: Supervised, independent study of topics related to civil and environmental engineering. Departmental consent required.

instructors: Ana Martha Fernandes, Babak Moaveni, Brian Brenner, C. Jen, Luis Dorfmann, Mark Albert Woodin, Masoud Sanayei, Robert Christian Viesca, Shafiqul Islam, Wayne Chudyk

courses.title: The Energy Transition
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as STS 101, ME 174, UEP 133 & ENV 161) Consideration of engineering concepts relevant to the global transition from fossil fuels to renewable sources of energy. Interface between policy and technology in the energy sector and its relevance to decision making. Offshore wind energy is used as an example to illustrate the convergence of technology, infrastructure, policy, and markets that is necessary to achieve a just and equitable energy transition. Course is open to juniors, seniors, and graduate students from across the university.

sections.req: Junior, Senior, or Graduate students only

courses.title: Structural Dynamics
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ME 0178) Fundamentals of vibration theory with applications important in structural engineering. Free, forced, and transient vibration analysis. Time and frequency domain analysis of single and multi-degree of freedom systems. Natural frequencies and normal modes of vibration. Vibration mitigation and base isolation. Understanding behavior of structures subjected to various dynamic loads such as wind, earthquake, machine vibration, and ambient vibration. Hands-on experience with industry-standard software and practical applications in structural engineering.

sections.req: CEE 22 or ME 41 or graduate standing

courses.title: Hydrology of the Built Environment
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ENV 112) Processes and land surface characteristics that affect stormwater flows, including land-use intensification influence on flooding, geomorphic stability, and nonpoint source pollution. Design of mitigation measures based on drainage and detention, as well as land-use planning, low impact development, best management practices, and green infrastructure.

sections.req: Prior completion of CEE 32 & ES 8, or graduate standing

courses.title: Advanced Structural Systems Analysis
courses.desc:
The application of mechanics to the analysis of indeterminate structural forms important to civil and aeronautical engineering, with emphasis on modern structural types. The analysis of fundamental structural forms, including curved beams, arches, rings, thin-walled cell-type structures, and members with variable inertia, for stress and deflection by the classical methods. Influence lines for indeterminate structures. Introduction to matrix analysis and vibration of structures.
Recommendations: CEE 22.

courses.title: Data Science for Sustainability
courses.desc: (Cross-listed w/ DS 143 and ME 173). Emerging topics in data science and statistical learning with applications to the three pillars of sustainability (environmental, economic, and social). Building, estimating and interpreting models used in energy and environmental decision-making with emphasis on social justice. Development of critical consumers and responsible producers of data-driven analysis through: learning a suite of data-driven modeling and prediction tools; building the programming and computing expertise to use those tools; and, developing the ability to formulate analyses to answer questions pertaining to sustainability.

sections.req: (ES 2, CS 10 or CS 11) and (ES 56, CEE 156, EE 24, EE 104, BME 141, MATH 166, or ME 102); OR graduate standing

courses.title: Site Remediation
courses.desc: (Cross-listed w/ CHBE 143). Conventional and innovative remediation technologies are examined under the remedial investigation/feasibility study (RI/FS) process. Knowledge of fundamental processes governing remedy implementation is integrated with an understanding of site characterization and applicable regulations to enable design of site-specific treatment systems for clean-up of the contaminated subsurface environment.

sections.req: (CEE 12 and CEE 32), or CHBE 22, or graduate standing

courses.title: Environmental Health Data-Lab
courses.desc: Use of publicly available environmental and health data for in-depth analysis of environmental health topics such as air pollution, exposure disparities, water quality, and contaminant source contributions, with knowledge of contaminant fate and transport, statistics, and data visualization.

sections.req: (ES 55 and (ES 56 or CEE 156)) or graduate standing

courses.title: Principles Epidemiology
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed as CH 114.) Methods that quantify disease processes in human populations. Topics include study design, sources of inaccuracy in experimental and observational studies, the methodology of data collection, and an introduction to the statistical evaluation of epidemiological data.
Cannot receive credit for both CEE 154 and CEE 54

courses.title: Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene (WASH) Design
courses.desc: User-centered design of WASH systems for low-cost, community- and household-level treatment. Topics include technologies, health impacts, societal contexts, and monitoring for achieving sustainability. Emphasis on applying topics to develop a WASH design for a self-selected project.

sections.req: CEE 32 and CEE 52 or graduate standing

courses.title: Geographical Information Systems
courses.desc: Spatial analysis with Geographic Information Systems (GIS), including their use for engineering applications. GIS data structure and management, techniques for spatial analysis. Applications including seismic hazard, water resources, and environmental health. Laboratory exercises in GIS.

sections.req: ES 56 or CEE 156 or graduate standing

courses.title: Special Topics - Timber Analysis and Design
courses.desc: Topical courses offered within civil and environmental engineering.

courses.title: Special Topics - Urban Analytics & Visualization
courses.desc: Topical courses offered within civil and environmental engineering.

courses.title: Internship In Civil And Environmental Engineering
courses.desc:
Internship in a field related to Civil and Environmental Engineering practice.
Application of knowledge and skills developed in the classroom in a professional
situation having practical significance

courses.title: Applied Probability and Data Analysis in CEE Systems
courses.desc: Foundational treatment of probability, statistical inference, and prediction for small or censored datasets from asymmetric, heavy-tailed distributions for which standard statistical procedures are inappropriate. Emphasis on CEE applications like natural hazard analyses and modeling censored observational data. Probability theory, Monte Carlo analysis, statistical prediction, and probability distributions commonly used to model natural hazards. Additional topics related to CEE data analysis can be covered based on student interests. It is recommended that students have taken undergraduate statistics and calculus before enrolling.

courses.title: Chemical Principles In Environmental & Water Resources Engineering
courses.desc:
Basic principles of water chemistry related to environmental and water resources engineering. Thermodynamics, chemical equilibrium, acid-base reactions, alkalinity, complexation, precipitation, dissolution, sorption, and reduction-oxidation reactions. Quantitative problem solving. Fall.
Recommendations: CHEM 1 or equivalent.

courses.title: Advanced Soil Mechanics
courses.desc:
Soil composition, index properties, classification. Mohr circles and stress paths. Consolidation behavior; consolidation theory including radial and 3-D solutions; secondary compression. Shear strength of soils; effects of soil composition, stress history, drainage conditions, and rate of loading. 
Recommendation: CEE 42 or equivalent

courses.title: Geomechanics
courses.desc: Introduction to the mechanics of solids focused on earth materials as porous, deformable media. Strain, stress, and equations of motion. Elasticity and seismic wave propagation. Failure, inelastic deformation, and plasticity. Role of pore fluid in deformation and failure. Consolidation. Fluid flow and Darcy’s law; seepage forces and design considerations. Recommendations: ES-9, CEE-42

courses.title: Unsaturated Soil Mechanics
courses.desc: Principles of unsaturated soil mechanics. Topics include stress state variables, soil-water retention properties, soil suction measurements, hydraulic conductivity, effective stress, shear strength, and volume change theory in partially saturated soils. Appropriate for graduate students with backgrounds and interests in geotechnical and geological engineering, soil science, environmental engineering, and groundwater hydrology.

courses.title: Introduction to Ceramics
courses.desc:
An introduction to sculptural, painterly, and functional approaches to ceramics. Explores techniques in wheel-throwing and construction for hand-building and examines the basic use of fire, glazes at low and high temperatures, and raku. No prerequisites. 

Non-SMFA students and MAT Art Education students will receive a letter grade.

courses.desc:

Non-SMFA students will receive a letter grade.

courses.desc: See departmental website for details.

Advanced techniques in vessel making are introduced with special attention to the relationship between surface and form of the pot. Projects focus on designing and constructing dynamic vessel forms, using combined methods of hand-building and the potter’s wheel. Projects will emphasize honing surface considerations, including slip application, texture, glaze research, firing methods, and more, to enhance the finished pot. This is not a beginner class; students should have taken CER-102, CER-103, or receive instructor permission via portfolio. This course is open to graduate and undergraduate students.

courses.title: Introduction To Community Health
courses.desc: Examines the relationship between health, health care, and community. Considers the determinants of health and illness in contemporary society. Major emphasis on how communities define and try to resolve health-related problems explored through case studies.

courses.title: Introduction to the U.S. Healthcare System
courses.desc: Problems and issues encountered in the planning, organization, and regulation of health services. Health policy formation and its implications for service delivery. Health care financing; health insurance; the changing role of physicians; technology; poverty and health; the mix of planning, regulation, and competitive strategies; and consumer organizations. Problems of implementation and administration; federal, state, and local interests.

courses.title: Introduction to Global Health
courses.desc: Introductory course in global health. Focus on health in low- and middle-income countries. Principles of global health along with additional topics such as health determinants and disparities, socioeconomic status and health, human rights, culture and health, maternal and child health, water and sanitation, parasitic diseases and the Neglected Tropical Diseases (NTDs).

courses.desc: Fundamentals of research on population-level health and development of skills important for understanding and improving community, public, and global health. Emphasis on accessing and critically evaluating public and community health research; developing research questions and hypotheses identifying appropriate research designs; addressing ethics in research; conducting measurement and sampling; applying qualitative and quantitative research methods; and disseminating findings.

courses.title: Health Economics
courses.desc: (Cross-listed w/ EC 48) An examination of major topics in the economics of health and health care, both in the United States and abroad, using the basic theoretical and empirical tools of economics. Covers the medical and nonmedical determinants of health, markets for medical care services and health insurance, and proposed ideas for health care reform. Prerequisites Economics 5 or Economics 8.

courses.title: Principles Epidemiology
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed as NUTR 204 and CEE 154.) Methods that quantify disease processes in human populations. Topics include study design, sources of inaccuracy in experimental and observational studies, the methodology of data collection, and an introduction to the statistical evaluation of epidemiological data.
Cannot receive credit for both CH 114 and CH 54

courses.title: Fundamentals of Biostatistics
courses.desc: (Cross listed as CEE 6) Examination of statistical methods used in biomedical and public health studies. Descriptive statistics, probability, basic hypothesis testing, ANOVA, linear regression, logistic regression, and an introduction to survival analysis. Instruction in the use of statistical software will be provided throughout the course. CEE 6 and CEE 156 cannot both be taken for credit

courses.title: Disability and Difference in Children
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CSHD 190) Overview of some of the special needs of preschool and elementary-age children who show a variation in physical, sensory, emotional, cognitive, and social development, through the lens of a positive model of identity. Focus on educational implications, family support, and adaptations to promote inclusive environments. Class lectures, observations of children, media portrayals, hands-on adaptations of materials, and visiting speakers.

sections.req: CSHD 1 or PSY 1 or Junior Standing

courses.title: Health in the Spanish-Speaking World
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CH 124 & LAS 148) Examination of the determinants of health in Latin American countries and among Latino communities in the United States. Focus on disease, drugs, maternal and child health, nutrition, poverty, and health. Texts include scholarly articles, narrative, poetry, and film. Conducted in Spanish. Recommendations: Two courses above Spanish 22 or consent of the instructor.

courses.title: Applied Qualitative Research Methods
courses.desc: Qualitative research methods including frameworks for research; data collection methods such as focus groups, interviews, and direct observation; key data analysis techniques; data organization software; results dissemination; and story-telling in qualitative research. Emphasis on acquisition of qualitative research skills. Topics include language, logic, theory, and ethics; study design and common data collection techniques; basics of qualitative analysis and interpretation; writing and presenting.

courses.title: Internship in Community, Public, & Global Health
courses.desc: Structured and supervised community health work in a health organization, government agency, community group, or healthcare-related company that 1) provides opportunities to gain professional skills and experience, 2) facilitates application of community health curriculum and 3) provides exposure to community, public, and global health career possibilities. Students select Boston area sites in the public or private sector and at the local, state, or federal level. Class meetings with Internship Administrator and department faculty. Prerequisite: Major in Community Health, second semester junior standing and consent of department.

sections.note: CH majors only with required pre-requisites, Department Consent required
sections.req: CH 1, CH 2, CH 30 & CH 36 or instructor permission

courses.title: Research in Community Health
courses.desc: Student participation in an ongoing research program led by a Community Health faculty member. Emphasis on faculty mentoring of students to promote acquisition of research skills. Skills taught may include conducting literature reviews, participant outreach and recruitment, measurement tool development, qualitative and quantitative data collection, data analysis, and development of written products and presentations. Weekly lab meetings instead of class sessions. Students produce a tangible product (e.g., presentation to the lab group on their work, academic poster, literature review).

sections.note: Dept Consent required. Please email instructor if interested. liana.woskie@tufts.edu

courses.title: Promise & Peril of New Technology in Healthcare
courses.desc: Scientific and technological advances in genomics, synthetic biology, big data, and artificial intelligence show promise in health care. Discussion of ethical issues pertaining to safety, appropriateness, and impact. Topics related to the ethical, legal and social issues of technology may include xenotransplantation; algorithmic bias and fairness in clinical prediction models; telehealth, and biomedical devices. Prerequisites: CH 1, CH 2, CH 11, CH 30, CH 34, & CH 36 or instructor permission.

sections.note: CH majors who have taken the core courses or instructor permission

courses.title: Disability & Public Health Policy
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as OTS 110 & CVS 113) Examination of the interactions between individual, community, and policy-level factors among populations with potentially disabling health conditions. Develop and evaluate a policy-level intervention proposal to improve the lives of individuals or communities faced with potentially disabling health conditions. Topics may include the changing demographics and dynamics of disability, political levers in public health and social policy, the measurement of disability, and potential determinants of disability. Prerequisites: CH 1, CH 2, CH 11, CH 30, and CH 34.

sections.note: CH majors who have taken the core courses or instructor permission

courses.title: Beyond the Food Desert: Access, Health and Justice
courses.desc: Critical inquiry into the theories, measures, and policies that influence how we think about and define "healthy food access." Predominant models of food access in the US, evaluations of place-based policies to improve food access, and structural and historical factors that influence the food environments of today. Engagement with active policy discussions about the future of food access in the US through class discussions and debates. Prerequisite: CH 1.

courses.title: Chemical Process Principles
courses.desc: Introduction to chemical and biological process calculations emphasizing unit operations, process stoichiometry, material and energy balances, states of matter, and continuous steady state and transient processes. Introduction to computational tools for process engineering calculations.

courses.title: Transport Phenomena II
courses.desc:
Principles of heat and mass transfer. Steady-state conduction and diffusion processes. Convective transport of heat and mass in laminar and turbulent flows in conduits and over various surfaces. Applications to design of heat exchangers. Natural convection. Combined heat and mass transfer applications.
Recommendations: CHBE 10, 11; MATH 42 (formerly MATH 13).

courses.title: Applied Numerical Methods For Chemical & Biological Engineering
courses.desc: Numerical analysis methods and their implementation using commercially available software are reviewed. Scientific programming methodology. Application of commercial process simulation software to the analysis of chemical and biological process models.

courses.title: Chemical And Biological Engineering Laboratory
courses.desc: Laboratory experiments related to fundamental concepts characterizing chemical and biological systems and processes. Experience is gained in planning and executing the experiments and critically analyzing the collected data to achieve a deeper understanding of the underlying concepts. Oral presentations and written reports are an integral part of this laboratory course.

instructors: Araoluwa Adachim Adaramola, Laura Walker Place
Araoluwa Adachim Adaramola, Laura Walker Place

courses.desc: Preparation of a report based on personal research, design, or experiment.Please see departmental website for specific details.

courses.title: Honors Thesis Research A
courses.desc: Supervised research in chemical and biological engineering leading to the completion of the undergraduate honors thesis. Please see the Departmental website for specific program details and qualification requirements.
