courses.title: Art Ed, Human Dev, and Culturally Sustaining Teach
courses.desc: Creating a cohesive, culturally responsive, and culturally sustaining art curriculum in PK-12 schools. Focus on the role of art in human development and learning; ways to cultivate a classroom culture centered on cultural diversity, inquiry-driven learning, and empathy. How art educators can engage youth in studying, critiquing, and creating visual art in the context of culturally sustaining education theory.

courses.title: Current Issues in Art Education
courses.desc: Integration of studio practice with individual teaching style to design meaningful and relevant art lessons that support the diverse needs of K-12 learners. Studio work, contemporary artworks, readings, and lectures to build understanding of the evolving needs and goals of 21st-century art education.

courses.title: Foundations In Art Education, Pre-k - 8
courses.desc:
(Fall 2010 & Beyond). In this course students investigate the history and philosophies of Art Education, recent issues of educational reform, and the effects of national and state achievement standards on art programs. They explore child and adolescent development as they study early developmental and psychological approaches to Art Education. More recent developments in the field inspire discussions of student diversity, multiculturalism, visual and critical studies, and aesthetics. Course requirements include weekly readings and class discussions, a research paper, and formulation of a personal philosophy of Art Education.
Recommendations: MAT students only unless granted special permission.

courses.title: Foundations In Art Education: 5-12
courses.desc:
(Fall 2010 & Beyond). Students examine middle school and secondary art education by studying historical, psychological, social and theoretical developments. A range of educational researchers and their theories are explored. Students will research and present a project that focuses on an art education issue, either historical or contemporary. Topics will include components of Discipline Based Art Education, Multiple Intelligences, Visual Culture, Interdisciplinary Instruction and Postmodernism. Students will identify areas of research which influence the practice of art education. They will examine the psychological and artistic development of pre-adolescents and adolescents and the influence of art education. Studying and analyzing personal creativity and process, the course combines academic inquiry with art making activities. Through discussions, presentations, and art making, we will explore how theories and research can enhance the classroom learning experience for all art students. There will be a special emphasis on the development of your own personal vision of art education leading towards authentic instruction, activities and assessment.
Recommendations: MAT students only unless granted special permission.

courses.title: Field Studies In Art Education: Pre-k - 8
courses.desc:
(Fall 2010 & Beyond). Students participate in school and community art programs for children in grades preschool through grade eight. Fieldwork includes internships at the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston and focused observations one day a week in public school settings. Emphasis is placed on reflection and discussion of lesson planning and presentation, assessment strategies, classroom management, and student diversity. Course work includes individual field site visits, readings, journal writing, and presentations.
Recommendations: MAT students only .

courses.title: Field Studies In Art Education 5-12
courses.desc:
(Fall 2010 & Beyond). This course will focus on the development and presentation of standard-based lesson plans. Perspectives will range from modernism's focus on the elements of art and principles of design to the postmodernism empasis on interdisciplinary approaches, cultural context and societal influences. Drawing from Wiggins & McTighe (2005), we will develop Essential Questions that stem from Enduring Understandings to bring meaning to content and skills in the art classroom.We will explore creative and worthwhile ideas and themes, choosing appropriate materials, visual resources, constructing sample products, and developing a personal teaching style. Students will work in cooperative groups to design a lesson plan bringing their individual talents and interests to the process. The cooperative groups will present their lesson plans to the whole class. Field work will require focused observation and participation in both museum settings and public school settings. Students will work with classroom teachers and also have the opportunity to participate in the Museum of Fine Arts's educational program. These dual settings will expand the students' exposure to different teaching styles, content, skills and environments.The class will also cover assessment strategies, classroom management issues, instruction strategies and organizational issues. Artful Thinking guidelines will be introduced to help students understand the importance of continual assessment. Course work includes pre-practicum internships in the field, readings, reflective journal writing, lesson plan construction and presentation, and attendance.
Recommendations: MAT students only .

courses.title: Quantum for Engineers
courses.desc: Fundamentals of quantum mechanics for the modern electrical engineer to begin engaging with topics from quantum computing to quantum networking. Topics include: particle-wave duality; de Broglie waves; wave packets; uncertainty principle; observables; solutions to the Schrödinger equation (free particle, particle in a box, potential steps/barriers, harmonic oscillator, hydrogen atom); spin; multiple particles; exclusion principle; entanglement; atomic elements; molecular bonding; quantum statistical mechanics (Fermions and Bosons); applications of quantum mechanics to electronic materials (electrical conduction, and theory, semiconductors, p-n junctions). Students may receive credit for EE 13 or PHY 13, but not both. Students in the School of Arts & Sciences are directed to PHY 13.

sections.req: SOE students who have completed PHY 12 and MATH 34

courses.title: Electromagnetic Fields And Waves W/lab
courses.desc:
Coordinate systems and transformations, base vectors, scalar and vector point functions, gradient, divergence, curl, Laplacian, divergence theorem, Stokes theorem, source-point and field-point notation, electrostatic and magnetostatic fields and laws, scalar and vector potential functions, continuity equation, Maxwell's equations in differential and integral form, boundary conditions, wave equation, time-harmonic fields, plane waves, electromagnetic radiation, dipole antenna, Poynting theorem, distributed circuits and transmission lines. Associated laboratory work. 
Recommendations: ES 3, PHYS 12, MATH 51 (formerly MATH 38).

courses.title: Introduction to Circuits and Electronics
courses.desc: Definitions of circuit elements, fundamental laws, selected network theorems, controlled sources, energy and power, response of first order circuits, operational amplifiers, semiconductor materials and doping, diodes, MOS field effect transistors, MOS logic circuits, oscilloscope, measurements and instrumentation, computer-aided circuit analysis and design. Associated laboratory project work. Recommendations: MATH 34

courses.title: Computer Organization
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed w/ CS 45) Computer organization including performance measurement, instruction set architectures, digital arithmetic, processor datapath, control, pipelining, memory hierarchy, caches and input/output. 
Prerequisite: ES 4

courses.title: Junior Design Project - Engineering Project
courses.desc: Junior level team project with ECE faculty direction and guidance. Introduction of the engineering method: concept, planning and analysis, design, test. Integration of theoretical concepts from circuit theory, digital and analog electronics, signal processing, engineering economics, and engineering design practices to deliver a working prototype. Use of microcontroller and peripherals, analog-to-digital converters, digital signal-processors, memory and computer aided design tools. Students are expected to provide schedules, schematics and specifications; build prototypes; present their projects orally; and deliver a working system. Pre-reqs: EE or Comp-Eng Majors. EE 14 and EE 20

courses.title: Junior Design Project - Engineering Project
courses.desc: Junior level team project with ECE faculty direction and guidance. Introduction of the engineering method: concept, planning and analysis, design, test. Integration of theoretical concepts from circuit theory, digital and analog electronics, signal processing, engineering economics, and engineering design practices to deliver a working prototype. Use of microcontroller and peripherals, analog-to-digital converters, digital signal-processors, memory and computer aided design tools. Students are expected to provide schedules, schematics and specifications; build prototypes; present their projects orally; and deliver a working system. Pre-reqs: EE or Comp-Eng Majors. EE 14 and EE 20

courses.title: Senior Design Project I
courses.desc: A comprehensive design project undertaken during the senior year as a team under the guidance of a faculty supervisor or external sponsor. The work is spread over two terms. Please see departmental website for specific details.

courses.title: Undergraduate Internship In Electrical Engineering
courses.desc: Supervised internships at suitable locations in industry and government. Jobs offered on basis of availability. Term paper required. Credit not given retroactively. Prior arrangements necessary.

instructors: Aseema Mohanty, Eric L Miller, Karen A Panetta, Mai Vu, Marco Donato, Mark David Hempstead, Paul J Simmonds, Sameer Sonkusale, Shuchin Aeron, Thomas E Vandervelde, Valencia Margie Joyner Koomson, Yingjie Lao

courses.title: Introduction To Vlsi Design
courses.desc:
An introduction to CMOS VLSI design. Topics include the structure of the MOS transistor, theory of operation, fabrication methods, CMOS circuit design, subsystem design, the PLA and finite state machines, introduction to memory design, system timing techniques. Students will design a circuit of modest complexity.
Recommendations: Senior standing or permission of instructor.

courses.title: Probabilistic Systems Analysis
courses.desc:
Advanced analysis in probabilistic systems with strong emphasis on theoretical methods. Development of analytical tools for the modeling and analysis of random phenomena with application to problems across a range of engineering and applied science disciplines. Probability theory, sample and event spaces, discrete and continuous random variables, conditional probability, expectations and conditional expectations, and derived distributions. Sums of random variables, moment generating functions, central limit theorem, laws of large numbers. Statistical analysis methods including hypothesis testing, confidence intervals and nonparametric methods. Undergraduates may not take both EE 0024 and EE 0104 for degree credit.
Prerequisite: Math 0042 or equivalent. 
Recommendation: Senior or graduate standing or consent of instructor.

sections.req: Open to online CS or DS postbac, OR online CS or DS MS students

courses.title: Feedback-control Systems
courses.desc: Modern control and fundamentals of state-feedback including matrix differential equations, controllability, state transformations, canonical forms, and control matrix design. Classical control and output-feedback with topics including transfer functions, s-plane analysis, stability criteria, PID controllers, root locus, controller design using op-amps, and compensation networks. Prerequisite: EE23 and Math 70; OR graduate standing

courses.title: Semiconduct Device W/lab
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed w/ MSE 110) Introduction to semiconductor physics; quantum mechanics, equilibrium distribution; charge transport; P-N junction theory; diodes; bipolar junction transistors; field-effect devices; heterojunction devices; novel semiconductor devices such as carbon nanotubes.
Recommendations: EE 21 and MATH 51 (formerly MATH 38).

courses.title: Bioelectricity
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed with BME 123) Fundamental physical basis of bioelectricity; understanding its role in various living organisms. Action-potential creation and transmission in the nervous system. Analysis of the heart as a distributed, highly fault-tolerant electrical system. Potential bioelectrical role in morphogenesis (creation of bodily shape) and cancer. Application of engineering concepts to understand molecular processes associated with bioelectricity. 

Recommendation: differential and integral calculus

courses.title: Digital Signal Processing
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed as ME 136) Discrete signals and systems, digital simulation of analog systems. Z transforms, recursion equations, finite-order systems. Fourier transforms, line spectra and Fourier series, discrete Fourier series and Fast Fourier Transforms (FFT). Sampling and interpolation, mean-square approximations. Nonrecursive and recursive filters. Selected topics on algorithms, design and applications of digital signal processing.
Recommendation: Previous experience with Matlab or Python.

sections.req: (EE 23 or ME 31 or BME 10) or graduate standing

courses.title: Information, Inference, and Learning
courses.desc: (Cross-listed CS 149) Modern methods for inference and learning through the lens of information theory and statistics. Entropy, relative entropy (KL divergence), mutual information, information inequalities, and their operational interpretation in terms of data compression/rate-distortion. Rigorous bridge through large deviations and statistical inference to variational inference, latent variable models such as Variational Auto-Encoders (VAE), and modern diffusion-based generative models. The unifying theme is the interpretation of inference and learning as optimization of information-theoretic objectives, understructural or computational constraints.

sections.req: MATH 70 and (EE24 or EE 104 or MATH 165) or graduate standing

courses.title: Computer Communication Networks
courses.desc:
Data communications concepts. Communications networking techniques: switching and broadcast networks, access protocols, local networks. Design issues, overview of current products. Computer communications architecture: hardware/software issues, protocols and architecture, layered approach and hierarchical approach. Prerequisite: senior or graduate electrical engineering degree candidate, or consent.
Recommendations: Senior or graduate electrical engineering degree candidate, or permission of instructor.

courses.title: Advanced Electromagnetics
courses.desc:
Stationary electric and magnetic fields. Differential and integral forms of Maxwell's equations. Time-harmonic fields and potential functions. Electromagnetics of circuits. Transmission line transients and coupling. Plane wave propagation. Guided wave propagation. Electromagnetic radiation. Electromagnetic properties of materials. Practical applications. Fall.
Recommendations: EE 18 or equivalent.

courses.title: Software Engineering for Regulated Industries
courses.desc:
Fundamentals of software engineering for regulated industries. Identifying user needs, mapping user needs to requirements, processing software design, coding, verification, and validation. Emphasis on quality and documentation to meet regulatory standards. Hands-on experience with tools used in developing high-quality software products.
Recommendation: CS 15 or CS 40

courses.title: Real-Time Embedded Systems
courses.desc: Hardware and software considerations for fast, predictable response time in embedded systems. Real-time operating systems and multi-threaded programming for managing multiple time-sensitive tasks. Comparison of industrial-grade versus hobbyist-grade embedded-system infrastructures. Examples are drawn largely from medical equipment (e.g., electrocardiography and electromyography) Recommendation: some experience working with embedded processors (e.g., equivalent of EE14 or ME30, or experience with Arduino programming).

sections.req: CS 11 or CS 15 or graduate standing

courses.title: Power Systems
courses.desc:
Analysis and design of AC transmission and distribution systems, transmission lines, transformers and generators. Understanding, modeling, operating and controlling such systems; basics of voltage control and power flows in electricity networks. Graduate students are expected to complete and present an additional class project. 
Recommendations: EE 22 or graduate student standing

courses.title: Product Design and Innovation
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ENT 181) Product design & development, marketing, operations, sales, quality assurance, field service, and customer support to make an impact with customers and society. Iterative design approach—observe, think, plan, do, test, and demo. Critique and reflection on failure assessment for customer, product, and technology adoption insights to structure and accomplish design problem definition, implementation, and success criteria. Influence of imagination and creativity across a design team. Interdisciplinary collaboration with focus on project management, time to profit, market product penetration, organization, and the challenges and obstacles of getting a product into the marketplace.

sections.note: Open to seniors and graduate students only.

courses.title: Societal Aspects of Design: Integration, Innovation, and Impact
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CVS 149 and ENT 109) Multi-disciplinary perspective of innovative technology-based design process for societal, community influence, and civic engagement. Elements and principles of design from product development process and societal value systems thinking, thought and emotion, ethics and responsibility. Experiments to explore bias, failure, and iteration, reflection for self-discovery and innovation. Articulation and expression via written, oral and pre-recorded audio and video presentations showing measurable impact of solutions as societal benefits.

sections.note: Open to seniors and graduate students only.

courses.title: Advanced Quantum Engineering
courses.desc: Graduate level quantum mechanics for the modern electrical engineer. Topics include Particle-wave duality; de Broglie waves; Wave packets; Uncertainty principle; Observables; Solutions to the Schrödinger equation (free particle, particle in a box, potential steps/barriers, harmonic oscillator, hydrogen atom); Spin; Multiple particles; Exclusion principle; Entanglement; Atomic elements; Molecular bonding; Quantum statistical mechanics (Fermions and Bosons); Applications of quantum mechanics to electronic materials (electrical conduction, and theory, semiconductors, p-n junctions). Weekly problem sets and a semester-long project on current research in quantum computing or communication. Content requires proficiency in differential and integral calculus as well as electricity and magnetism. Not appropriate for students in the Graduate School of Arts & Sciences.

courses.title: Optoelectronic Characterization
courses.desc: (Cross-listed with MSE 201) Tools and techniques used to characterize optoelectronic materials and devices. Photoluminescence, ellipsometry, scanning probe microscopy, electron microscopy, and AC/DC electrical characterization. Theoretical underpinning of and practical experience with the measurement techniques. Laboratory.

courses.title: Biomedical Engineering
courses.desc: An introduction to the interdisciplinary nature of biomedical engineering. The biological, chemical, electrical, and mechanical principles involved in the design and operation of medical devices. Biopotentials, electrodes, transducers, biocompatibility of materials, and patient safety.

courses.title: Foundations in Financial Accounting and Corporate Finance
courses.desc: An introductory course to corporate finance from the perspective of the chief financial officer (CFO). The first part of the course deals with financial planning and budgeting, financial analysis, and short-term financial management. The second part of the course develops a valuation framework for making investment decisions (capital budgeting) for new equipment, the launch of new products, mergers and acquisitions and LBOs... and the funding/financing decisions to be coordinated with those investment decisions. Special attention is given to the cost of capital and valuing stocks, bonds, convertible and preferred.

courses.title: Data Analysis and Statistical Methods
courses.desc: This course provides an introduction to data analysis and statistical methods, focusing on concepts related to descriptive statistics, data visualization, probability, and hypothesis testing. The objective of this course is two-fold. First, the course equips students with tools to understand, analyze, and effectively present data. Students will learn to create summary statistics and data visualizations using Microsoft Excel. They will also learn how to craft a narrative based on their insights. Through hands-on exercises, students will gain practical skills in analyzing real-world datasets. Second, this course serves as an introduction to hypothesis testing and causal inference. In this course, students will explore basic concepts related to probability, hypothesis testing, and causal inference, preparing them for more advanced courses such as Econometrics and Econometric Impact Evaluation.

courses.title: Financial Statement Management
courses.desc: Accounting is an economic information system, and can be thought of as the language of business. Accounting information provides individuals with a starting point to understand and evaluate the key drivers of the firm, its financial position and performance. This can then be used to enhance decisions, as well as help predict a firm’s future cash flows. The present (or current) value of those cash flows provides an estimate for the value of the firm. This course will cover the basic vocabulary, concepts, procedures and mechanics of financial and managerial accounting and the role of accounting information in society.

courses.title: Entrepreneurial Leadership: Starting New Ventures
courses.desc: This course takes a global approach to entrepreneurial leadership, drawing on lessons from the Indo-Pacific, Africa, Latin America, the Middle East, and the Arctic Ocean region, including indigenous perspectives on sustainability and entrepreneurship. This course is designed to prepare Fletcher students to develop an entrepreneurial mindset and to launch and nurture their own ventures – including private sector startups, social enterprises, and non-profits, as well as initiatives launched by academic entrepreneurs, policy entrepreneurs, and leaders of “tiger teams” in government agencies.

courses.title: Informal and Underground Finance
courses.desc: This course aims to study the role of the informal (off- the-books) and underground (criminal) sectors in the global economy, from multiple perspectives ranging from economic development to law enforcement and global security. In the past decades, the removal of financial controls, combined with technological advances, has allowed deviant globalization (drug trade, piracy, cybercrime, counterfeiting, human trafficking, terrorist financing, etc.) to prosper, creating governance and law enforcement challenges to governments and corporations alike.

courses.title: Global Investment Management
courses.desc: This course investigates the global dimensions of investment management. The course combines technical and theoretical tools with practical illustration and application of critical investment concepts. The course will open with an overview of global institutional investors and the business of investment management. Following sessions will focus on developing an understanding primary asset classes, including foreign exchange, global equities, global fixed income securities, alternative investment vehicles, and derivatives. On this foundation, subsequent class sessions will focus on introducing and developing portfolio skills in the areas of risk management, investment performance and attribution, and finally portfolio construction and asset allocation.

courses.title: Managing NGOs and Social Enterprises
courses.desc: This course examines how to create, develop and scale high-performing social sector organizations — be they for-profit, nonprofit, or hybrid organizations. In this course, student will learn how to: a) design an organization’s mission, theory of change, and strategy in order to deliver social results; b) develop performance management systems useful for internal learning, while managing complex demands for accountability from diverse stakeholders; c) understand how to scale impact through multiple strategies including growth, collaboration, and policy influence; and, d) examine capital markets and the challenges of obtaining resources. Taken together, students will acquire the understanding, skills and knowledge necessary to lead and sustain high performance in enterprises dedicated to addressing some of the most challenging problems facing the world today.

courses.title: Strategic Management
courses.desc: Effective strategists can: size up the dynamics of the external environment of a firm, covering its economic, political, and social contexts; take a holistic view across all functions and configure all of a firm’s internal choices to give it a competitive advantage; sustain this advantage over time and leverage it into adjacent business and geographic opportunities; use acquisitions and alliances when these are the more effective approaches to support a strategy; create the right organizational context to execute the chosen strategy efficiently; ensure the continuous renewal of the firm in anticipation of and adapting to its changing environment. The objectives of this short course are to master the field’s core concepts and to build the skills needed to be an effective strategist.

courses.title: Sustainable Finance and Investment
courses.desc: Designed for students with prior coursework and/or practice in finance and investments and interested in understanding the effects of environmental, social, and governance factors on financial decision-making. These include risks posed to the firm and its stakeholders resulting from such factors, as well as risks posed by the firm to its extended stakeholders. The course is structured as an intermediated seminar, i.e. sessions will be facilitated by lecture slides with active engagement expected. The course will examine key themes and developments in regulation, financial reporting, sustainability assessment (or ratings), investment analysis, and capital sourcing across a range of financial markets and asset types, including public equities, public debt, private equity, and infrastructure. Across asset types, key themes include climate risks and financing climate transition, blended capital and innovations in development finance, and fintech, financial inclusion and democratization. Central to the course design is to examine financial strategies and vehicles as tools to advance sustainability and impact objectives whether at the investor, state, or multinational level. To this end, it will introduce and leverage a variety of analytic tools to understand the basic decision models of sustainable and impact investing.

courses.title: Marketing Management
courses.desc: It is not an overstatement to say that all non-monopolistic companies, NGOs and even government-sponsored organizations live or die by their ability to effectively market their products and services. In today’s hyper-competitive global markets, organizations that excel at identifying their customers, determining how to meet their interests and needs, and delivering an outstanding experience will be the winners. This course will cover six key market functions and responsibilities: understanding the roles and responsibilities of a marketer; segmentation: identifying and targeting your best customers; strategic social media: when, how, what and with who; sales enablement and support; brand strategy; delivering a superior customer experience. We will look at marketing issues facing both private and non-profit sector organizations. All the topics in the course will be discussed in an international context, including the unique issues that marketers face in global markets.

courses.title: Strategic Marketing for Non-Profit Organizations
courses.desc: This course offers a comprehensive coverage of the fundamental issues in marketing and branding in nonprofits. The aim of this course is to arm students with the analytical skills and knowledge necessary to make, evaluate, and critique marketing and branding strategy decisions facing nonprofit organizations in an increasingly global arena. The course addresses how to craft a nonprofit marketing strategy; implement a coherent marketing plan and optimize the use of marketing resources, develop brand identity and positioning statements; leverage brand alliances and partnerships; and perform financial brand valuations.

courses.title: Managing Operations and Supply Chains in Global Companies
courses.desc: A management-oriented, case study-based course on how companies design, manage, and measure operations around the globe today. The core topics will be: the exercise of competitive advantage through operational capability; business process design; supply chain management; lean operations; disruptive operations innovations; operations networks and connectivity; talent management; the managerial metrics revolution; etc. Readings and cases will focus on both the operations themselves and the management issues surrounding them. One-half credit.

courses.title: Introduction to Economic Theory
courses.desc: This course provides the foundation of modern economics with an emphasis on its applications. Topics include demand and supply analysis, consumer theory, theory of the firm, welfare economics, monopoly and antitrust, public goods, externalities and their regulation, unemployment, inflation and economic growth, national income determination, monetary and fiscal policy. This is an introductory course for non-specialists.

courses.title: Quantitative Methods
courses.desc: This module presents the mathematical methods that are used widely in economics, including logarithms, exponential functions, differentiation, optimization, constrained optimization, and an introduction to dynamic analysis. The mathematical material is presented in the context of economic applications and examples that illustrate the bridge between mathematics and economics. One-half credit.

courses.title: Microeconomics
courses.desc: Microeconomics does not address every question about the economy, but it does provide tools to answer numerous questions about the choices individuals and firms make. The set of tools microeconomics gives you can be used to solve almost any economic problem an individual person or firm faces. In this course, we will start with theories and models, explanations of how things work that help us understand and predict how and why economic entities (consumers, producers, industries, governments, etc.) behave as they do; we will also cover theories and models that help us understand and predict how competitive, oligopolistic, and monopolistic markets work, as well as situations in which markets might not work well (e.g., asymmetric information, externalities, and public goods). To learn the intricacies of the theories and models, we will use the tools of graphs and mathematics. We then use theories and models to look at how people and firms actually behave in real life (including some seemingly noneconomic situations). The interaction between microeconomic theory and the events, decisions, and empirical data from the real world lies at the heart of microeconomics (Goolsbee, Levitt, and Syverson, 2020). Students are required to be concurrently enrolled in EIB E210M, unless they have passed E210M or the Quantitative Reasoning equivalency exam.

courses.title: The Practice of Economic Policy Analysis
courses.desc: This seminar teaches skills that enable students to bridge the gap between coursework in economics and statistics and the creation and presentation of the types of analyses conducted in professional settings. Translating the material from these courses into useful, well-targeted analysis can be challenging. Providing practical policy and strategy advice requires an ability to identify the relevant theoretical concepts for the question at hand, to bring to bear on the topic appropriate and persuasive empirical analysis and to make these concepts understood to an audience with different levels of knowledge of economics.

courses.title: Managerial Economics
courses.desc: This course is a brief introduction to management issues presented from the perspective of economics. The focus is on the strategic responses a firm can make regarding both its internal organization and its external interaction with both consumers and other firms. Students will learn the role of economic analysis in determining organizational design and developing competitive strategies whether the organization is a for-profit firm or a non-profit enterprise. One-half credit.

courses.title: Advanced International Trade and Investment
courses.desc: This seminar presents the analytical economics and political economy of different integration strategies, and then applies these to WTO multilateral initiatives, Brexit, NAFTA, the Trans-Pacific Partnership, Mercosur, and the Trans-Atlantic Trade and Investment Partnership. Other topics this semester include the effects of Covid on trade and investment and international policy cooperation, supply chains and economic welfare, infra-structure and foreign aid, and multinationals and international taxation. The seminar format is a workshop with lectures, student presentations and discussions, a student research paper, and a conference. Open to students who have completed E220, other upper-level economics courses, or with permission by instructor.

courses.title: International Finance
courses.desc: This course examines the determination of income, the exchange rate, and the trade balance in economies that trade goods and services, as well as assets, with the rest of the world. Theory is developed and employed to study current events, as well as historical experience. Issues studied include exchange rate determination, monetary and exchange rate policy, the causes and consequences of external imbalances, international policy coordination, financial crises, and the global capital market. Open to students who have completed E201 or equivalent. E210m is suggested, and may be taken concurrently, but is not required.

courses.title: Development Economics: Policy Analysis
courses.desc: This course equips students for rigorous economic analysis of development problems and policies. The first half of the course develops tools for studying the decisions, markets and institutions that shape development outcomes. The second half develops an approach to policy analysis that draws on those tools. Students apply the approach in the study of policy questions related to cash and food transfers, agricultural pricing, infrastructure, education, agricultural technology, microfinance, and health. Emphasis is on rigorous reasoning, careful synthesis of empirical evidence, and effective communication of policy analysis results. Open to students who have completed E201 or the equivalent.

courses.title: Political Economy of Development Policy: Theory and Practice
courses.desc: Combines economic and political perspectives to develop an interdisciplinary understanding of selected topics in economic development. Each session addresses a particular question that arises as policymakers contend with the dynamic interplay between economics and politics as competing influences on policy choice. How can it be rational for policymakers to adopt policies that harm a majority of their own citizens? In what ways do institutions shape the development process? How does history shape the evolution of institutions? Do elections lead to better or worse policy choices? Does democracy benefit the poor and promote economic growth? Comprehensive answers to these types of questions require a political economy perspective -- one that combines an understanding of the underlying economics with consideration of the interests and political influence of various stakeholders and pressure groups. In addition, a central goal of this seminar is to bridge the gap between theory and practice by providing tools for incorporating political economy perspectives into development policy analysis.

courses.title: Econometric Impact Evaluation for Development
courses.desc: One of the primary challenges for policymakers, development practitioners, donors and non-governmental organizations (NGOs) is understanding what policies and interventions are the most effective in improving the welfare of the world’s poor. While monitoring and evaluation is useful in determining whether a program is on the “right track”, impact evaluation sets the focus on assessing the causal impacts of policies and interventions. For example, how does a program that sends cash directly to households living in extreme poverty affect food security, household assets, and psychological well-being? Does increasing female income improve the education and health of girls? What is the causal effect of attending secondary school on fertility and occupational choices? The objective of this course is to provide students with a set of theoretical, econometric and practical skills to estimate the causal impact of a policy or program, with a particular focus on development programs. The course will introduce students to a set of econometric techniques that are commonly used in impact evaluation, including randomized control trials, instrumental variables, difference-in-differences, and regression discontinuity. Examples will be drawn from a variety of sectors, including health, education, financial services and governance.

Prerequisite: Departmental Consent

courses.title: Teaching and Learning in Engineering II
courses.desc: Structures for responsive teaching as well as assessment of students’ competencies in engineering. Additional topics include foundational knowledge of current policy and research in K-12 engineering education. Design of a curriculum unit is required.

sections.note: This class is for participants accepted into the GETT program in the School of Engineering. The GETT program provides preparation for doctoral students and post doctoral associates interested in teaching-related careers. Part I focuses on foundational knowledge related to teaching and learning in college-level engineering education.

courses.title: Topics in Creative Writing - Writing the Climate Crisis
courses.desc: Introductory practice and instruction in creative writing through the lens of a particular topic in a workshop setting. Topics may relate to either a specific genre (e.g. fiction, poetry, nonfiction) or multiple genres. See department website for complete descriptions of courses offered in a given semester. Prerequisites: ENG 1 and 2 or completion of the College Writing Requirement.

sections.note: In a time of climate crisis, how can and should writers of nonfiction bear witness, provoke, motivate, provide hope, build resilience, cultivate gratitude, stoke anger, or tend grief? This generative workshop will combine critical consideration of these questions with creative exploration through assignments inviting personal reflection, engagement with science and other academic research, and experimental forms that weave various modes of truth-telling.
sections.req: Requires the completion of ENG 0001 and ENG 0002 or ENG 0003 and ENG 0004 or equivalent(s) and A&S, or ENG 0001 and SOE

courses.title: Creative Non-Fiction Writing
courses.desc: Practice and instruction in a creative non-fiction workshop setting. Focus on subgenres, including personal essay, travel writing, nature and science writing, humor, memoir, and lyric/hybrid essay. Supported and independent writing, and written and oral critiques of assignments. Prerequisites: ENG 1 and 2 or completion of the College Writing Requirement.

sections.req: Requires the completion of ENG 0001 and ENG 0002 or ENG 0003 and ENG 0004 or equivalent(s) and A&S, or ENG 0001 and SOE

courses.title: Writing Fiction: Advanced
courses.desc: An advanced course for students who have taken one or more semesters of ENG 5 or have equivalent fiction workshop experience. Focus on developing a sustained practice in reading, writing, workshopping, and revising. Prerequisites: One semester of ENG 5; ENG 1 and 2 or completion of the College Writing Requirement. Recommendations: Two semesters of ENG 5 or the equivalent fiction workshop experience.

sections.req: Requires the completion of English 0005 and college writing requirement.
Requires the completion of English 0005 and college writing requirement.

courses.title: Topics in Creative NonFiction/Journalism - Weirding the Essay
courses.desc: Workshop course in reading and writing creative nonfiction and/or journalism through the lens of a particular topic or genre. Topics offered on an ad hoc basis. Please see departmental website for specific course descriptions. Prerequisites: ENG 7 or ENG 10 and ENG 1 and 2 or completion of the College Writing Requirement

sections.note: In this advanced creative nonfiction workshop, we’ll read and write lyric essays, braided essays, hermit crab essays, speculative nonfiction, and hybrid or multimedia forms. We will explore how these experimental, unruly forms might help us approach the stickiest of truths–the vulnerable, the complex, the partial, and the contradictory. We’ll we push the bounds of nonfiction while taking seriously the ethics and expectations, the possibilities and perils, that come with the genre.
sections.req: Completion of ENG 7, ENG 8 or ENG 10

courses.title: Black World Literature
courses.desc: (Cross-listed w/AFR 22 and ILVS 20) Fiction, poetry, and drama written principally in English by black writers from Africa, the Caribbean, and South America. Relation of modern black writing to African folk literature, classical Greek drama, European existentialism, and other contexts. Attention to specific geographical areas illustrating the transition from traditional tribal values and forms of expression to the attempted accommodations to colonialism and industrialism. All works are read in English.

sections.note: Fulfills English major survey requirement.

courses.title:
Heroes, Lovers, and Demons: British Literature from Beowulf to
the Eighteenth Century
courses.desc:
An Introductory survey of English literature with attention to selected works from the Anglo-Saxon period through eighteenth century. One of the gateway courses to the major. Focus on the development of literature in England and on foundational skills of critical reading.
Recommendations: ENG 1, 2 or Fulfillment of College Writing Requirement.

sections.note: Fulfills English major survey requirement.

courses.title: Literary Studies Now
courses.desc: Introduction to how and why we study literature in the 21st century. Considers strategies for reading diverse genres and aesthetic forms; various conceptual and critical frameworks; historical, national, and trans-national contexts in the study of imaginative writing in English from around the globe. See department website for further detail.

courses.title: The English Bible
courses.desc:
A study of the Old and New Testaments from a literary perspective, examining the King James version as a work of the English Renaissance; with emphasis on the shaping and unity of the Bible's materials, the nature of its various genres and styles, the levels of its meaning, and the sources of its cultural influence. The particular approach is to the typological relationship of the Old and New Testaments to one another from an archetypal and structuralist point of view.
Recommendations: ENG 1, 2 or Fulfillment of College Writing Requirement.

courses.title: Shakespeare- F
courses.desc:
This course carefully examines eight or nine of Shakespeare's plays, both early and late. Although the plays are considered in a variety of historical and theoretical contexts, the primary focus is on a close reading of the texts. The same plays will not be read in both 50 and 51.
Recommendations: ENG 1, 2 or Fulfillment of College Writing Requirement.

sections.note: Fulfills the pre-1860 English major requirement.

courses.title: Modern American Poetry
courses.desc: A survey of major modern American poets, including Robert Frost, Marianne Moore, Wallace Stevens, Ezra Pound, T. S. Eliot, William Carlos Williams, Jean Toomer, Langston Hughes, Countee Cullen, Hart Crane, and e. e. cummings.

sections.note: Fulfills the post-1860 English major requirement.

courses.title: Surviving with Yeats and Auden
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ILVS 30) In-depth study of two of the 20th century’s major English-language poets, W. B. Yeats and W. H. Auden, with particular focus on the role of poetry during times of cultural upheaval and uncertainty. Examination of the relationship between poetic form, historical context, and personal experience, including questions of ethnicity and sexuality. No prior knowledge of poetry required.

sections.note: Fulfills post-1860 English major requirement

courses.title: Contemporary Asian American Lit & Popular Culture
courses.desc: Focus on intersections of race, gender formation, and sexuality in contemporary Asian American literary and popular culture across a range of genres and media, including literature, film, television, and stage. Interdisciplinary examination of concepts of feminism, queerness, and LGBTQ identity in relation to ethnicity, citizenship, power, activism, art, politics, resistance, representation, and collective and individual histories in selected 21st-century Asian American cultural production.

sections.note: Fulfills post-1860 English major requirement

courses.title: Postmodernism And Film
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed w/ FMS 87 and ILVS 89) Introduction to postmodernism through the study of late twentieth century and early twenty-first century film in relation to important texts of literary and cultural criticism. The movement from modern to postmodern, originality to mechanical reproduction, identity to difference. Readings from Baudrillard, Benjamin, Butler, Derrida, Foucault, Haraway, Lacan, and ¿i¿ek , along with films by Cameron, Gilliam, Polanski, Scott, the Wachowski brothers, and Welles.
Recommendations: ENG 1, 2 or Fulfillment of College Writing Requirement.

sections.note: Fulfills post-1860 English major requirement.

courses.title: Topics In Literature And Culture - Flight Of Fancy: Travel Am Lit
courses.desc: Courses offered on an ad hoc basis and open to all interested undergraduates. Please see departmental website for specific details: http://ase.tufts.edu/english/

sections.note: This course will focus on what multi-ethnic, early American literature has to say about travel, migration, captivity, escape (literal and metaphorical), and other versions of movement and stasis. Authors may include: Jane Schoolcraft, Harriet Jacobs, Zilpha Elaw, Charles Chesnutt, John Rollin Ridge, Sui Sin Far, Hannah Crafts, and Phillis Wheatley, among others. Fulfills pre-1860 English major requirement.

courses.title: Topics In Literature And Culture - Inventing Childhood
courses.desc: Courses offered on an ad hoc basis and open to all interested undergraduates. Please see departmental website for specific details: http://ase.tufts.edu/english/

sections.note: This course examines literary representations of children in the American 19th century, a period that shaped many of our contemporary notions of childhood and the child’s role in society. We will look at the iconic child characters of Louisa May Alcott’s Little Women and Mark Twain’s fiction, the racialization of childhood in texts like Harriet Jacobs’ autobiography, the haunted children of Ambrose Bierce’s civil war stories and Henry James’ The Turn of the Screw, and lesser-known works by 19th-century children themselves. In doing so, we will reveal the important part that children played—as agents and as symbols—in both the household and the young nation. Fulfills pre-1860 English major requirement.

courses.title: Topics In Literature And Culture - 19th C American Lit on Film
courses.desc: Courses offered on an ad hoc basis and open to all interested undergraduates. Please see departmental website for specific details: http://ase.tufts.edu/english/

sections.note: In this course, we will read 19th-century texts and watch their film adaptations. We will examine the ways 20th and 21st-century cinema adapts the historical conflict, literary styles, and cultural anxieties of the period. Pairings include Edgar Allan Poe’s short stories and the gothic visuals of Roger Corman, Solomon Northrup’s memoir Twelve Years a Slave retold through Steve McQueen’s stark representation of plantation life, Herman Melville’s Billy Budd seen through Claire Denis’ Beau Travail, and Edith Wharton’s Age of Innocence and Martin Scorsese’s interpretation of its aristocratic decadence. By reflecting on the ways that these texts engage with American ideals of freedom, rebellion, and progress, students will develop a vocabulary for reading both literature and film. Fulfills pre-1860 English major requirement.

courses.title: Internship in Literary Study
courses.desc: Practical experience in professional settings relevant to the study of literature, such as teaching, publishing, editing, public relations, librarianship, and other related fields. Students identify their own opportunities to integrate academic study with real- world training. Specific expectations for journal keeping, reflection paper, or other written components will be determined on an individual basis depending on credits assigned and other factors. Department approval required. Internships do not count toward the requirements for the English major or minor.

instructors: Amaris Brown, Amy Susan De'ath, Emily Strasser, Ichiro Takayoshi, Jess Keiser, John Lurz, Joseph D Litvak, Kevin Dunn, Lee Edelman, Modhumita Roy, Nathan Wolff, Rick Moody, Sara Deniz Akant, Sarah Anne Robbins, Simon Han, Sonia Hofkosh, Tonhi Lee
sections.note: Credit for an internship requires department consent. Students must apply and gain approval by submitting the "Internship in Literary Study Form" at https://as.tufts.edu/english/resources

courses.title: Ovid And The Ovidian Tradition
courses.desc: Close readings of Ovid's Metamorphoses, a bible of pagan mythology for later poets, and also his erotic poems, which explore the pathos and comedy of love, and invent an extraordinarily influential psychological vocabulary. Also a study of the Ovidian tradition, including two French works in translation, the Roman de la Rose and Les Liaisons Dangereuses, and a number of shorter works in English, by such authors as Chaucer, Marlowe, Shakespeare, and Spenser.

sections.note: Fulfills pre-1860 English major requirement.

courses.title: The Literary Imagination
courses.desc: Examination of the nature and function of the imagination in literary creation and reception, from antiquity through contemporary fiction. Interdisciplinary exploration of how writers and readers construct imaginary worlds, drawing on philosophy, psychology, neuroscience, and writers' reflections. Topics include theories of imagination from Plato through Romanticism to cognitive science; genre and world-building in fantasy, horror, and science fiction; and the relationship between imagination and empathy, childhood, and moral reasoning. Authors may include Lewis Carroll, J.R.R. Tolkien, William Blake, Jorge Luis Borges, H.P. Lovecraft, Philip K. Dick, Stanislaw Lem, Stephen King, and theoretical texts from classical to contemporary sources. Emphasis on close reading, collaborative discussion, and critical analysis through in-class writing and examinations.

sections.note: Fulfills post-1860 English major requirement

courses.title: American Women Writers
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed w/AFR 155, WGSS 152, CVS 135, and AMER 155) The complex and rich tradition of women writers of fiction and poetry in America from a multicultural perspective: major figures; important lines of influence; areas of challenge to the traditional canon; and reconstruction and discovery of neglected literary traditions.
Recommended that the student already have taken either ENG 20,21,22, or 23.

sections.note: Fulfills post-1860 English major requirement.

courses.title: Seminar In English - The Female Complaint
courses.desc: Courses offered on an ad hoc basis and open to undergraduates and graduate students. Please see English Department website for specific descriptions of courses in a given semester: http://ase.tufts.edu/english/ Recommendations: ENG 1, 2 or Fulfillment of College Writing Requirement.

sections.note: In this course, we will investigate the relationship between race, gender, and sentimentalism in 18th- and 19th-century American literature. Authors may include Phillis Wheatley, Lydia Maria Child, Catherine Maria Sedgwick, Harriet Beecher Stowe, Harriet Jacobs, Frances Ellen Watkins Harper, etc. Fulfills pre-1860 English major requirement.

courses.title: Seminar In English - #MeTheory
courses.desc: Courses offered on an ad hoc basis and open to undergraduates and graduate students. Please see English Department website for specific descriptions of courses in a given semester: http://ase.tufts.edu/english/ Recommendations: ENG 1, 2 or Fulfillment of College Writing Requirement.

sections.note: Why is so much contemporary writing all about “me”? From #Booktok to autotheory, avant-garde lyric poetry to Oprah’s Book Club, this course will consider how writing about the self shapes a wide variety of “cultured” and lowbrow feminized literary genres. We will explore how these new and emergent genres are gendered, racialized, and classed, and how they are different from more established forms of autobiography and memoir. Drawing on cutting-edge scholarship on women's writing and literary industries by Sarah Brouillette, Jane Hu, Eva Illouz, and Mark McGurl, we will discuss Wattpad fiction as a form of amateur bibliotherapy, misogynist dismissals of romance writing, data-driven systems of literary publishing, and more. Readings may include work by Juliana Spahr, Lola Olufemi, Anne Boyer, Britney Spears, Kay Gabriel, rupi kaur, Maggie Nelson, as well as texts drawn from Wattpad, #Booktok, and Workers’ Inquiry. Fulfills post-1860 English major requirement.

courses.title: Seminar In English - The Invention of Utopia
courses.desc: Courses offered on an ad hoc basis and open to undergraduates and graduate students. Please see English Department website for specific descriptions of courses in a given semester: http://ase.tufts.edu/english/ Recommendations: ENG 1, 2 or Fulfillment of College Writing Requirement.

sections.note: This course will trace the history of utopian literature back to Thomas More's Utopia (1516), paying close attention to the contexts in which More's seminal work had its meaning. Fulfills pre-1860 English major requirement.

courses.desc: Individual study of an approved topic guided by a full-time faculty member in the English Department. Students pursuing such study are normally expected to have already taken the department's available courses on the topic, as well as one survey course (ENG 20, 21, 22, or 23). Department permission required. One Directed Independent Study may be counted towards the English major or minor. Prerequisites: ENG 1 and 2 or fulfillment of the College Writing Requirement.

courses.desc: A series of 2-hour colloquia run by distinguished professors at other schools; each year, the invitees will be selected to cover a wide variety of specialties. In advance of each colloquium, a selection from the visiting professor’s work-in-progress is distributed; students discuss the work in detail at the colloquium, raising pertinent questions and offering feedback. Required of all graduate students currently in classes; those who have finished coursework are welcome to attend.

courses.title: Proseminar
courses.desc: The Proseminar is taught by various members of the faculty on topics of their choice (these include various aspects of professionalization, pedagogy, and current work). The Proseminar lasts one hour and will be held every other week. Attendance is mandatory. It will be graded Satisfactory/Unsatisfactory.

courses.desc:

courses.title: Methods for Human Factors Engineering
courses.desc:
Qualitative and quantitative methods and techniques used in human factors engineering research. Usability testing, structured observation, questionnaire design, focus group design, psychophysical methods, signal detection theory, and field studies. Examples of good and bad methods/techniques.

Recommendations: PSY53

courses.title: Undergraduate Research
courses.desc: Independent undergraduate research in the field of human factors. Proposal must be approved by faculty advisor and department. See departmental website for additional information. Course may not be repeated for credit.

courses.title: Internship In Engineering Psychology
courses.desc:
A mentored preprofessional experience in engineering psychology at an off-site organization. The internship must conform to all the requirements of the School of Engineering internship programs. The engineering psychology program will grant course credit for internships if the following conditions are met: 1) The student has junior or senior standing and has declared a major in engineering psychology. 2) The student has submitted a written internship proposal that has been approved prior to the semester in which the internship will be performed. No internships with course credit will be approved once the semester of the internship has started. 3) A faculty mentor in engineering psychology holds supervisory and technical control of any work that receives credit. 4) The student submits a written report that is to be evaluated by the faculty adviser and the outside institutional supervisor. Work of a proprietary nature cannot be used as a basis for the granting of course credit.
Recommendations: Junior or Senior standing or permission of instructor.

instructors: Chris Rogers, Daniel Hannon, Gary Leisk, Hoda Koushyar, James Intriligator, Jason Rife

courses.title: Assistive Technology Foundations
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as OTS 105). Examination of problems in designing and providing assistive devices to individuals with disabilities, to assist mobility, communication, positioning, and environmental control and daily living. Processes discussed include needs assessment, search for available devices, resources available, and creative problem solving. Students work with materials commonly used to create individualized devices, in cross-disciplinary teams on a design for a specific user or group. Problems of funding and delivery of devices also explored. For students in occupational therapy and engineering, and for educators, speech/language pathologists, and rehabilitation personnel.

instructors: Jennifer Connors Buxton, Loren Fields Mcmahon

courses.title: Human Factors in Medical Technology
courses.desc: Techniques for ensuring the safety and efficacy of medical technology ranging from over-the-counter devices to complex diagnostic and therapeutic workstations to clinical information systems. Global standards and regulations, usability engineering program planning, function and task analysis, user interface requirements, applied user interface design, user interface simulation, design verification, and design validation via usability testing. Pre-requisites: senior or graduate standing or permission of instructor.

courses.title: Ergonomic in Design
courses.desc: Topics related to the domain of physical ergonomics with emphasis on the quality of fit between humans and the things they interact with on a job site, in sports, or at home. Applications drawn from aspects of human-made environments and designed products. Extensive in-class activities, group work, and collaborative discussion. Project experiences involving analysis of real-life scenarios. Anthropometry, functional anatomy, ergonomics, body mechanics, and human factors research methods. Guest lectures with local industry and professionals. Recommendations: Junior, Senior or Graduate Standing

courses.title: Advanced Engineering Psychology
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed as PSY 130) Seminar on the various functions that humans perform in complex modern human-machine systems. Examination of psychological and engineering theories and models as they relate to these functions.
Recommendations: Three courses in psychology, including PSY 53.

sections.note:
Declared ENP/HFP or HFE major and have taken PSY53/ENP53. 
No Textbook.
sections.req: Prior completion of PSY 0053. Undergraduates only.Human Factors Engineering, Human Factors Psychology, or Engineering Psychology

courses.title: Human Factor Product Design
courses.desc:
Material relevant in consumer product design, biomedical engineering, architectural design, and machine design. Topics include design methodologies, user feedback techniques, performance measurements, sensory evaluation techniques, creative design, and prototyping. Extensive individual and group project design work. Emphasis on designing and creativity.
Recommendations: ENP 53, ENP 64 and junior standing

courses.title: Human-machine System Design
courses.desc:
Techniques for man-machine system designs in which cognitive and dynamic aspects are of major importance. Applications to computer-interface design, auto/semiautomated systems, biomedical systems, and others. Topics include information processing, decision making, reaction times, and signal detection theory. Individual and group projects, laboratory demonstrations.

Recommendations: ENP 64 and senior standing, or graduate standing.

courses.title: Applied Behavioral Statistics for Engineering
courses.desc: Behavioral statistics for human factors and applied behavioral research. Parametric, nonparametric, descriptive and inferential concepts. Small n and case study designs, factor analysis and power analysis. Use of modern statistical software package(s). Applications to product design and development, human performance, and survey methods.

courses.title: Computer Interface Design
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed as BME 166.) This hands-on course challenges students to design computer-based products and systems that are easy to learn and use. Lectures cover the user interface-design process, basic design principles, and design evaluation methods. In-class exercises and projects reinforce the students' understanding of the lecture material and provide practical design experience. Students use computer-based prototyping tools to model and demonstrate their design solutions. Frequent guest lectures by user-interface design specialists from industry.
Recommendations: EN 1, 2, and junior standing, or permission of instructor.

courses.title: Special Topics - Consumer Psychology
courses.desc: Guided individual study of an approved topic. Please see departmental website for specific details.

courses.title: Advanced Research Methods in Human Factors Eng
courses.desc: Human factors methods to propel product development. Literature review methodology, contextual inquiry, morphological ordering, affinity diagrams, journey maps, data visualization, traceability matrix, expert reviews, mental model development, psychophysics (differences, preferences, acceptability), psychomotor, and psychometrics. Advanced research planning, design, execution, analysis and impact. Applications, possibly including driver distraction, human performance and fatigue, video game testing, and addictive UI design.

courses.title: Master's Project
courses.desc: Completion of a project under the guidance of a faculty advisor. Proposal must be approved by faculty advisor and graduate director. Each project must address a substantive human factors engineering problem. Students are required to make an oral presentation of their project work. Enrollment is limited to students in the Human Factors Engineering Master of Science program.

courses.title: Leadership in Action
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as TML 10) Theory and practice of leadership. Development and application of leadership skills across a range of contexts including startups, corporations, and nonprofits and across different stages of a business. Frameworks to navigate conflict and leadership challenges. Development of inclusive teams. Strategies for developing self-awareness and leading with authenticity. Alignment of actions with goals and intentions. Connection of life experience and strengths to leadership approach.

courses.title: Mastering Money: Developing Financial Literacy
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as TML 11) Introduction to sound money management in personal and professional finance. Creation of greater financial awareness, and development of financial vocabulary. Financial requirements across life stages including student finances, purchasing the first home planning, and investing for life events and a comfortable retirement. Basic business finances, such as budgeting, accounting statements, and taxation.

sections.note: First year students welcome

courses.title: Planning Your Career Pathway
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as TML 14) Exploring the skills and knowledge needed across an individual's career. Planning for internships and placements, preparing for a job search and gaining the skills and confidence for interviewing and starting a job. Students will develop the skills and knowledge needed to plan for a successful and fulfilling career.

courses.title: Living a Life with Purpose
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as TML 15) Holistic view of a human life. Work-life balance, mindfulness, personal ethics, physical and mental health, setting achievable and meaningful goals, and developing the skills of personal effectiveness. How to contribute to global society with an ethical mindset and cultural sensitivity.

sections.note: Sophomore standing or above

courses.title: Paths to Entrepreneurship
courses.desc: Build knowledge about the many paths, skill sets, and strategies to early-stage entrepreneurship. Learn and unlearn what it means to be an entrepreneur while exploring different industries. Hear from experts in the field in a traditional corporate job, a startup, a social enterprise, or people running a side hustle and more. Engage in discussions and workshops to understand entrepreneurial narratives and envision an entrepreneurial future.

sections.note: First year students welcome

courses.title: Creativity, Innovation and Entrepreneurial Thinking
courses.desc:
Tools and techniques to promote creativity and innovation with application to everyday problem solving, launching new ventures, and working in businesses and non-profit organizations. Rapid ideation workshops for novel solutions and innovations. Tools to stimulate brainstorming and creativity. This class is designed for undergraduate students, particularly Freshmen and Sophomores, who have not taken an ENT core course and are interested in learning more about innovation and entrepreneurship.

Restrictions on Enrollment: No previous ENT credit

Recommendation: Students with significant design thinking, innovation or entrepreneurship experience should not take this introductory class.

sections.note: First year students welcome

courses.title: Entrepreneurship And Business Planning
courses.desc: This course focuses on investigating, understanding, and implementing the process of founding a start-up firm. Elements of searching out new venture opportunities, matching skills with a new venture, financing, competitive strategy, intellectual property, and operating a new venture will be explored. The focus of the course will be the development and presentation of a business plan created by teams of students with various academic backgrounds.

courses.title: Entrepreneurial Finance
courses.desc: Financial statement construction and analysis for new ventures. Financial business plan development; evaluation of disparate commercial enterprises; business valuation. Utilization of modern financial tools to support investment decisions. Skills development to define and create pathways to fund and grow a business to optimize results and minimize risks.

courses.title: Entrepreneurial Marketing
courses.desc: This course focuses on institutional and product marketing methods used by start-up to medium-sized companies. After an overview of basic marketing principles, the course will cover the spectrum from day-to-day marketing activities of the entrepreneurial business to positioning and strategy. Students will learn to analyze, formulate, and implement marketing strategies, explore concepts for understanding customer behavior and creating entrepreneurial marketing strategy, and learn the fundamentals of market research, pricing, and reaching and selling to customers.

courses.title: Entrepreneurial Leadership
courses.desc: This course is designed to help students develop the knowledge, confidence, skills, and self-image necessary to pursue entrepreneurial ventures in such domains as business, government, and public service. It provides a foundation in the fundamentals of entrepreneurial leadership, as well as a source of inspiration and energy in the art and science of taking visions and bringing them to reality.

sections.note: ENT101 is recommended as prereq; Sophomore standing or above
ENT101 is recommended as prereq; Sophomore standing or above

courses.title: Societal Aspects of Design: Integration, Innovation, and Impact
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CVS 149 and EE 185) Multi-disciplinary perspective of innovative technology-based design process for societal, community influence, and civic engagement. Elements and principles of design from product development process and societal value systems thinking, thought and emotion, ethics and responsibility. Experiments to explore bias, failure, and iteration, reflection for self-discovery and innovation. Articulation and expression via written, oral and pre-recorded audio and video presentations showing measurable impact of solutions as societal benefits.

sections.note: Open to seniors and graduate students only.

courses.title: Vocal Arts for Personal and Professional Life
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as TML 112) Development of effective verbal communications skills across a range of personal and professional scenarios, including public speaking, interpersonal communication, storytelling, public narrative, speeches, presentations, interviewing, and networking.

courses.title: Business in Action
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as EM 120 and TML 120) Examination of how business impacts the world. Exploration of different types of business and evolving roles and functions within business. Consideration of social, cultural, organizational, ethical, and technological factors affecting business organizations. Focus on the importance of purpose-driven, human-centered leadership.

courses.title: Introduction to Intellectual Property
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as TML 126 and EM 126) Comprehensive overview of the fundamental concepts and legal frameworks that govern intellectual property (IP) rights. Patents, trademarks, copyrights, and trade secrets. Key principles such as IP ownership, infringement, and enforcement, role of IP in innovation and economic growth. Impact of IP laws on industries including life sciences, artificial intelligence, material sciences, media, and the arts.

sections.req: Junior, Senior, or Graduate students only

courses.title: Entrepreneurship for Social Impact
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as AMER 141, TCS 141, and CVS 187) Learn how to address systemic social and environmental problems and generate financial returns. Choose a problem based on your why. Form a diverse team and interview stakeholders. Harness AI for marketing and product development. Execute a pilot project with real users. Create and present a pitch deck. Interact with impact entrepreneurs and investors. Emerge as a more confident leader with valuable career skills, a broader network, and maybe even an impact venture.

sections.note: Sophomore standing or above

courses.title: Nonprofits, Philanthropy, and Impact
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CVS 180) Nonprofits are a valued engine for community engagement and innovation across the country. This complex sector is built on the desire to do good through scalable, sustainable organizational strategies that deliver impact. Study of successful nonprofits and the connection between nonprofits, philanthropy, and impact. Grantmaking strategy and award.

sections.note: Sophomore standing or above

courses.title: Entrepreneurial Business Law
courses.desc:
Legal issues and considerations common to the business life cycle. Formation, seed and venture capital financing, mergers and acquisitions, initial public offerings, securities law, employment and intellectual property, and governance considerations. Negotiation of various financing and other transactions. Speakers from the private equity, venture capital, and investment banking worlds as well as executives who have exited through a public offering or sale of their company.
Enrollment Restriction: Sophomore standing

sections.note: Sophomore standing or above

courses.title: Introduction to Making
courses.desc:
Exploratory course for beginners that teaches practical, hands-on skills to make working prototypes of your products. Make physical things, make them work, and integrate them with electronics/software. Common fabrication techniques including foamboard, 3D printing, laser cutting, electronics, and Arduino programming. Demonstration of hands-on skills and entrepreneurial spirit in an individual final
project.

sections.note: First year students welcome

courses.title: Product Design and Innovation
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as EE 181) Product design & development, marketing, operations, sales, quality assurance, field service, and customer support to make an impact with customers and society. Iterative design approach—observe, think, plan, do, test, and demo. Critique and reflection on failure assessment for customer, product, and technology adoption insights to structure and accomplish design problem definition, implementation, and success criteria. Influence of imagination and creativity across a design team. Interdisciplinary collaboration with focus on project management, time to profit, market product penetration, organization, and the challenges and obstacles of getting a product into the marketplace.

courses.desc: Under the guidance of a faculty member, students apply concepts learned in the classroom and acquire new skills as they address real life challenges while working as an intern at a company. Internships typically involve students serving in a functional role with an entrepreneurial focus, such as product management, entrepreneurial marketing and sales.

courses.desc: This course enables students to apply the learning and skills acquired by other courses on entrepreneurship. Students have the option of starting a new business based on an actual business plan or consulting in an actual start-up operation. Students who select the new business option will be expected to submit a project-scope paper that outlines the elements of the launch that could be accomplished within the term limits.

instructors: Carol Denning, Elaine Chen, Peter Om
