courses.title: Introduction to Environmental Studies
courses.desc: A case study approach to integrating the natural and social sciences with the arts and the humanities when exploring environmental challenges. Draws on both major Western thinkers and indigenous, global, and emerging environmental thinkers.

courses.title: Environmental Studies Lecture Series
courses.desc: Tied to the Environmental Studies Lunch and Learn lecture series featuring presentations on environmental topics by speakers from government, industry, academia, and non-profit organizations. Opportunity to broaden knowledge beyond the curriculum, explore career paths, meet other faculty and students, and network with the speakers. Students submit short writings before and after each talk. Detailed information about speakers and a full schedule can be found on the Environment Studies website. Mandatory pass/fail.

sections.note: The Speaker roster will be published here: https://as.tufts.edu/environmentalstudies/news-events/hoch-cunningham-lecture-series

courses.title: One Health: The Environment-Animal-Human Triad
courses.desc: The “One Health” triad and the associated transdisciplinary approach to solving health-related challenges that impact the physical environment, domestic and wild animals, and humans. The climate crisis, vector-borne diseases, health implications of human and domestic/wild animal interactions, water resources, and chemical contaminants.

courses.title: Food Systems
courses.desc: Introduction to the structure and functions of past, present, and future food systems. Emphasis is placed on the psychological, biological, social, economic and political systems that impact food production, processing, distribution, and consumption. Examination of real-world issues facing stakeholders in the New England food system.

courses.title: Plants & Humanity
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as BIO 10.) Principles of botany accenting economic aspects and multicultural implications of plants, their medicinal products, crop potential, and biodiversity. Emphasis placed on global aspects of this dynamic science, with selected topics on acid rain, deforestation, biotechnology, and other applications. Also covered are medicinal, poisonous, and psychoactive species, as well as nutritional sources from seaweeds and mushrooms to mangos and durians. Three lectures. Spring.

courses.title: Introduction to Urban Studies
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as UEP 11) Introduction to cities and urbanization. Exploration of the intellectual foundations of the urban studies field (including anthropology, sociology, economics, history, political science, American studies, environmental studies, urban planning, and public policy). Key topics include gentrification, social justice, racism, housing affordability, neuro-architecture, immigration, and demographic analysis.

courses.title: Environment & Technology
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed as ES 25.) The impact and interaction of technology and the environment will be evaluated using historical examples. Environmental problems and their solutions will be evaluated from an engineering viewpoint. This course is a core requirement of the Environmental Studies program.
Recommendations: CHEM 1 or 16 and sophomore standing

courses.title: Music and Nature
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as MUS 36) Set against the backdrop of the present-day environmental crisis, an exploration of the relationship between music and the natural world from the 16th century to the present. Topics may include inspiration from landscapes across history, and how their music opens new perspectives on Western society’s shifting relationship to the idea of nature itself. Examination of the art and science of music created by animals, such as birdsong and whale song, and soundscape ecology.

courses.title: Special Topics - Writing the Climate Crisis
courses.desc: Please see departmental website for specific details.

sections.note: In a time of climate crisis, how can and should writers of nonfiction bear witness, provoke, motivate, provide hope, build resilience, cultivate gratitude, stoke anger, or tend grief? This generative workshop will combine critical consideration of these questions with creative exploration through assignments inviting personal reflection, engagement with science and other academic research, and experimental forms that weave various modes of truth-telling.
sections.req: Requires the completion of ENG 0001 and ENG 0002 or ENG 0003 and ENG 0004 or equivalent(s) and A&S, or ENG 0001 and SOE

courses.title: Environmental Internship
courses.desc: A period of service with an organization, either public or private, concerned with environmental engineering, research, protection, modification, legislation, or education. Required of all majors in the program, internship proposals must first be approved by track adviser or director. Many academic semester and summer internships are available. Adviser-approved participation in field courses and fieldwork, both at Tufts and elsewhere, may be substituted for this requirement. No credit. Completion noted on transcript.

sections.note: For more information go to: https://as.tufts.edu/environmentalstudies/academics/internships

courses.title: Sustainability in Action
courses.desc: An integrated multidisciplinary approach to the study and practice of sustainability. Introduction to the breadth of sustainability and the enormous career opportunities available, including data analysis, stakeholder engagement, and field work. Topics include: water, waste, energy, climate change, transportation, food & agriculture, informational interviewing and networking skills.

sections.note: This class is beneficial for students at any stage of their journey - first year undergraduate through any graduate program.

courses.title: Introduction to Geographic Information Systems
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as GIS 101). Broad foundation of Geographic Information Systems theory, capabilities, technology, and applications. Topics include GIS data discovery, data structure and management; principles of cartographic visualization; and basic spatial analysis and modeling. Assignments concentrate on applying concepts covered in lectures and class exercises to term projects in each student's fields of interest.

courses.title: Hydrology/water Resource
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CEE 111) Processes and land surface characteristics that affect stormwater flows, including land-use intensification influence on flooding, geomorphic stability, and nonpoint source pollution. Design of mitigation measures based on drainage and detention, as well as land-use planning, low impact development, best management practices, and green infrastructure.

sections.req: Prior completion of CEE 32 & ES 8, or graduate standing

courses.title: Introduction to Environmental Fieldwork: From Classroom to Community
courses.desc: Exploration of environmental fieldwork— how to gather, analyze and communicate data— in the natural and social sciences. Coverage includes Geographic Information Systems (GIS). Work with community clients to ask questions based on environmental concerns. Collect and interpret relevant data and report findings to stakeholders. Fieldwork will range from forests and urban areas to archival sources, maps, databases, surveys, and interviews. One laboratory session per week plus one discussion period. No pre-requisites.

sections.note: Students should be prepared to spend a significant portion of class time outdoors.
Students should be prepared to spend a significant portion of class time outdoors.

courses.title: Drones for Data Collection, Mapping & Analysis
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as UEP 121) Covers the foundations of Unoccupied Aircraft Systems (UAS, aka drones) for data collection; provides skills to manage, plan, and execute remote flight operations. Applications in many fields including ecology, environmental science, urban planning, agriculture, natural and cultural resources management, and emergency response. Legal aspects of flying UAS, including FAA requirements; collecting and processing imagery data for use in Geographic Information Systems (GIS); creating data for spatial analysis and remote sensing. Incorporates the use of Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) for field data collection.

courses.title: Environmental Policy - U.S. Challenges and Solutions
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as PS 194) Overview of environmental policy focusing initially on the United States experience, then linking to global environmental policy-making. Introduction to the ways in which environmental policies are made in the United States and abroad including major actors, key decisions, and future challenges.

courses.title: Population And Community Ecology
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed as BIO 142.) Introduction to population dynamics (population structure and growth), species interactions (predator-prey, competition, mutualism), and community structure (adaptations to the physical environment, patterns and processes governing the world¿s biomes).
Prerequisites: BIO 14 or equivalent, or permission of instructor.

sections.req: Completion of BIO 0014 or equivalent, or graduate standing.

courses.title: Beyond the Human: Creative & Critical Ecologies
courses.desc: Comparative ecologies that attend to the climate crisis’ relation to the legacies of colonialism, slavery and other forms of extraction, eradication, and racialized oppression. How does rethinking or decentering the human, and sustained attention to nonhuman life and the animacy of water and land reshape our ideas about responsibility, freedom, solidarity? Emphasis on black, indigenous and queer ecologies, relying on models of wild thought and imagination. Recommendations: RCD 50

sections.attrs: African Cult/Lang - Diasporas|BFA-Humanities|BFA-Language/Culture|BFA-Social Science|LA-Distribution-Humanities|LA-Distribution-Social Sciences|Native American Culture|SoE-HASS|SoE-HASS-Humanities|SoE-HASS-Social Sciences|World Civilization Requirement

courses.title: Environment, Communication and Culture
courses.desc: (Cross-listed with ANTH 155 and CVS 181) Explore the intersection of environmental issues, communication, and cultures. Examination of where our beliefs about environmental issues come from, how news and entertainment media cover environmental challenges, and why good coverage of critical issues is so rare. Exploration of green marketing and the relationship among politics, environmental issues, and the media, and discuss how media can be used by individuals and advocacy groups to effect social change.

courses.title: The Energy Transition
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as STS 101, UEP 133, ME 174 & CEE 101) Consideration of engineering concepts relevant to the global transition from fossil fuels to renewable sources of energy. Interface between policy and technology in the energy sector and its relevance to decision making. Offshore wind energy is used as an example to illustrate the convergence of technology, infrastructure, policy, and markets that is necessary to achieve a just and equitable energy transition. Course is open to juniors, seniors, and graduate students from across the university.

sections.req: Junior, Senior, or Graduate students only

courses.title: Environmental Data, Analysis, and Visualization
courses.desc: Provides skills in data management, study design, statistical analysis, and data visualization that are critical for those working in environmental fields through hands-on experience working with environmental datasets. Environmental data are unique in that they are often spatial in nature, containing multiple variables that interact. These types of data require a careful approach to analysis and visualization.Topics covered include best practices in data access and storage, data analysis and interpretation, and data visualization for relevant stakeholders. Prerequisite: An introductory statistics course.

sections.req: Completion of an introductory stats class: BIO 132, BIO 133, CEE 6, MATH 21, EC 13, or PSY 31.

courses.title: Dance and Environment
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as DNC 172) Explore how we experience, interact with, and construct our understanding of environment, whether it be natural or engineered, through dance. Areas of inquiry include: activation of site-specific environment; the translation of internal responses to external topography and landscape; and the inter-relationship of science and the arts in enhancing environmental awareness, activism, and empathy. Assignments include weekly indoor and outdoor movement experiences, and independent and collaborative reading, viewing, and research projects. Recommendation: DNC 71, but no dance and/or environmental science experience required.

courses.title: Food For All: Ecology, Biotechnology & Sustainability
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed w/BIO 185) An interdisciplinary examination of the pros and cons of two divergent approaches to meeting the increasing global food demand: organic farming and genetic engineering. Contrasting crops grown in developing and industrialized countries serve as case studies to evaluate: (1) how ecological knowledge makes food production more sustainable; (2) what existing and emerging approaches can, in the face of climate change, contribute to a reliable supply of nutritious food; and (3) the political and economic drivers that shape who has access to these technologies. An important focus is developing communication skills for negotiating stakeholder-specific perspectives (growers, advocacy groups, industry, governmental agencies). 
Please see departmental website for specific details.
Recommendations: Intro Bio or Intro Chemistry or equivalent

sections.note: Class starts at 1:30

courses.title: Impact Investing for Catalytic Impact: Filling Capital Gaps
courses.desc: (Cross-listed UEP 185) This course explores the impact investing capital continuum from government agencies to ESG funds, banks, advisors, endowments, impact funds and individual investors and ways they can bridge traditional investment expectations with those required by an economy focused on positive impact. The course focuses on the role impact investors can play to fill ‘capital gaps’ to advance sustainability and equity, defined by the intersectional needs of social entrepreneurs and impact investors. By drilling down into the practical correlations between mission, cost structure and financial returns, the course explores opportunities and challenges for impact capital to advance a sustainable and equitable agenda. Students will gain insight into capital limits and matchmaking opportunities for different segments of capital providers, including philanthropy, ESG funds, regulated financial institutions, place-based funders and other potential sources of impact funds. Given the rapid emergence of the field, students will be exposed to an array of contemporary learning experiences including case studies, workshops, lecture, and guest speakers. Students will leave this course with the conceptual and practical framework required to deploy catalytic capital and to distinguish this segment of the impact investing space from aligned and complimentary strategies.

courses.title: Selected Topics - Food Economics
courses.desc: Exploration of special topics of environmental importance through seminars, lectures, or guided study.

sections.note: This is an undergraduate cross-listing of NUTR 238: Economics of Food, Agriculture and Nutrition. The course helps students explain, predict and evaluate change in consumer behavior, agricultural production and food businesses, government policies and nutritional outcomes. The first half is a gentle introduction to economic principles, using analytical diagrams to represent individual choices and interactions between people. The second half is data analysis, using Excel to construct charts and tables using downloadable data from a variety of sources about food, agriculture and nutrition in the U.S. and worldwide. Presentation and discussion in class is reinforced by weekly exercises followed by either exams or a course project, building skills needed for careers in nonprofit organizations, for-profit enterprises and government agencies. Our teaching blog with links to the open access textbook (Food Economics, published by Palgrave Macmillan in 2024) is here: https://sites.tufts.edu/foodeconomics.

courses.title: Selected Topics - Climate Crisis Community Org
courses.desc: Exploration of special topics of environmental importance through seminars, lectures, or guided study.

courses.title: Senior Honors Thesis A
courses.desc: See Thesis Honors Program for details.Please see departmental website for specific details.

sections.req: Senior Standing (Juniors with permission). Completion of ENV 1, and ENV 120, and one of the following: ENV 150, ENG/ENV 160, ENG/ENV 0176, or ANTH 24

courses.title: Land Use Planning: Nonregulatory Tools and Techniques
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as UEP 200). Public and private attempts to manage and control land use without resorting to traditional regulatory options such as zoning, subdivision control and other government-imposed restrictions on private property. (Regulatory controls are the focus of Land Use Planning: Regulatory Tools and Techniques: - UEP 201.) Non-regulatory techniques include, but are not limited to: deed restrictions, easements, reverter clauses, bargain sales, and "limited development" projects. Graduate standing or consent.

courses.title: Corporate Social Responsibility
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as UEP 269) Corporate behaviors and the ways consumers, community members, employees, and future leaders hold corporations accountable for their impact on issues including water, energy, pollution, waste, human rights, and worker wellbeing. Corporate structures and emerging business models, codes of conduct, transparency and accountability, the social and environmental impact of global supply chains, regulatory and voluntary frameworks, reporting, strategy and communication, and technology as a driver for change. Practice key tasks of corporate social responsibility (CSR) professionals within corporate and consulting contexts in the apparel and other industries.

courses.title: Introduction To Digital Logic Circuits W/ Lab
courses.desc: An exploration of how microprocessors work. Topics include: Boolean algebra and logic gates; combinational logic; representing numbers and performing arithmetic with circuits; behavior and use of flip-flops; sequential circuits and state machines; instruction sets; and building blocks for constructing microprocessors. Associated lab exercises with FPGAs and modern design tools. Culminating design of a substantial digital system.

courses.title: Introduction To Mechanics- Statics And Dynamics
courses.desc: Introduction to analysis and problem solving in statics and dynamics. Equilibrium of particles and rigid bodies in two and three dimensions. Vector and matrix analysis. Force-moment balance equations. Applications include trusses, frames, machines, beams, and friction problems. Kinematics and kinetics of particles and rigid bodies. Newton's equation, impulse-momentum, work and energy, Centroids and moments of inertia.

sections.req: Prior completion of or current enrollment in MATH 32 and PHY 11

courses.title: Fluid Mechanics
courses.desc: An introduction to fluids at rest and in motion. Fluid properties. Pressure and velocity variations in flows. Mass, momentum, and energy conservation in a flowing fluid. Bernoulli's equation and inviscid flows. An introduction to viscous flows. Dimensional analysis. Drag and lift of moving objects. Fall.

sections.req: Prior completion of or simultaneous enrollment in MATH 42

courses.title: Modern Optics and Photonics
courses.desc:
An introduction to the world of optics and the use of light today. Application of the underlying physics behind light propagation, processing, and detection to practical technological/engineering applications. Concepts include imaging, LEDs, lasers, microscopy, optical coding, fiber optics,information transfer, nanotechnology, and nano-optics.

Prerequisites or co-requisites: PHY 12, or permission of instructor

courses.title: Computer Aided Design w/ Lab
courses.desc: Computer Aided Design (CAD) software typically used by infrastructure professionals for drafting, modeling, and visualization. Use of Autodesk programs for 2D and 3D geometry construction, engineering drawings, Building Information Modeling (BIM), and visualization renderings and animations. Includes mandatory laboratory. Students may not receive credit for both ES18 and ES19.

courses.title: Environment And Technology
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed as ENV 25.) The impact and interaction of technology and the environment will be evaluated using historical examples. Environmental problems and their solutions will be evaluated from an engineering viewpoint. This course is a core requirement of the Environmental Studies program.
Recommendations: CHEM 1 or 16 and sophomore standing

courses.title: Numerical Methods
courses.desc: Introduction to using computers to solve engineering-oriented mathematical problems. Topics include mathematical modeling, round-off and truncation error, root location, linear algebraic equations, optimization, regression, interpolation, numerical differentiation and integration, ordinary and partial differential equations. Applications using software and programming languages.

sections.req: Prior completion of (ES 2 or CS 10 of CS 11) & MATH 51

courses.title: Probability And Statistics
courses.desc: Application of the concepts of probability and statistics to problem solving in engineering systems. Topics include data reduction techniques, probability, probability distribution functions, error propagation, sampling distributions, estimation, hypothesis testing, simple comparative experiments, and linear regression. Examples are drawn from a variety of disciplines, including the environment, materials, manufacturing, computing, and process design.

sections.req: Prior completion of MATH 42 or graduate standng

courses.title: Advanced Music Recording and Production
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as MUS 142) Theory and techniques for recording, editing, and producing acoustic music, and principles of audio system design. Topics include acoustics, audio perception, physics and electronics of transducers, analog and digital audio principles, stereo and multitrack recording, mixing, virtual instruments, and synchronization. Additional material in circuit design, signal flow, and analog and digital audio theory. The aesthetics of recorded sound and how circuits and components influence the sound of a recording. Students may not receive credit for both MUS 140 and MUS 142/ES 65. MUS142 is required for the Recording & Production emphasis of the Music Engineering minor. Prerequisite: Instructor permission. Recommendations: Ability to play an instrument, musical literacy, MATH 30 or 32 or equivalent, PHY 1 and 2 or equivalent, and either MUS 61 or MUS 62.

instructors: Daniel Fox, David Lefkowitz, Paul David Lehrman

courses.title: Professional Preparation for Cooperative Education
courses.desc: Introduction to work-based learning, strategies to optimize work experience and learn skills and habits to best transition into a professional work environment. Writing an effective resume, strategic interviewing, professional networking strategies, and developing a list of goals to achieve and skills to develop in a professional environment. Effective approaches to oral and written communications.

courses.title: Electronic Musical Instrument Design
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed as MUS 141). Non-standard electronic musical instruments or "controllers," incorporating sensors that respond to touch, position, movement, finger pressure, wind pressure, and other human factors, and their translation to Musical Instrument Digital Interface (MIDI) data. Designing and building original systems using common materials and object-oriented music-specific programming languages and software-based synthesis. Students will complete several creative projects using music hardware and software.
Recommendations: Experience in one or more of the following--electronic music, electronic prototyping, mechanical engineering, computer programming.

courses.title: Experimental College - Forensics: Crime to Courtroom
courses.desc: See details below for descriptions/bios.

sections.note:
COURSE: Forensics: From Crime Scene to Courtroom.

You’ve seen it on TV, but how objective is forensic science? If it's not, how can you tell, and what steps can you take to make it more impartial?

The primary goal of forensic science is to provide objective, reliable information that can assist investigators, attorneys, and courts in understanding what happened during an event under investigation. This course will provide an introduction to various types of forensic science—e.g., DNA, arson, and fingerprint—examine the origins of each, how they are used, and the current assessment of their reliability. Readings, films, podcasts, guest speakers, and discussions will provide students with a range of perspectives on the issues, as well as materials and video from actual cases. By the end of this course, students will be able to: explain the role of forensic science in the criminal justice system, identify and classify several of the major types of forensic evidence, understand basic forensic laboratory techniques, evaluate the reliability and limitations of forensic methods, and understand ethical and legal issues in forensic science.

INSTRUCTOR: David A.F. Lewis is an Assistant District Attorney and Deputy Chief of the Integrity Review Bureau at the Suffolk County District Attorney’s Office. Prior to becoming a prosecutor in 2019, He was in private practice for over 23 years, specializing in civil and criminal appeals in state and federal court. Mr. Lewis received his JD from the University of Denver College of Law.

courses.title: Experimental College - Designing the Future
courses.desc: See details below for descriptions/bios.

sections.note:
COURSE: Designing the Future: Worldbuilding & Time Travel.

What if you could explore the future not by predicting it, but by designing it? This course invites students to learn how futurists, designers, and creative thinkers use curiosity, observation, and imagination to understand the present and create possible worlds. Together we will examine the hidden structures that shape daily life, analyze cultural signals, and explore how human needs and emerging change collide to form new possibilities.

Students will practice context mapping, worldbuilding, and speculative prototyping to design a preferred future based on a real human need or opportunity. Weekly studio work will involve hands-on making, discussion, and experimentation. The course culminates in a creative future project that blends research, imagination, and design.

No previous experience with design or futurist thinking is required. This course is for anyone who wants to see the world differently, challenge inherited assumptions, and imagine more humane and hopeful futures.

INSTRUCTOR: Antonio Viva is a Partner at Leadership+Design, bringing more than thirty years of experience as a designer, educator, and strategic advisor working at the intersection of creativity, learning, and organizational leadership. He helps schools, nonprofits and mission-driven organizations imagine new possibilities, design meaningful experiences, and navigate complexity with clarity and curiosity. Antonio previously served as Executive Director of Artisans Asylum, one of the largest makerspaces in the United States, and spent twelve years as Head of School at Walnut Hill School for the Arts. Earlier in his career, he worked as a Senior Research and Design Associate at the Education Development Center on national school design initiatives.

courses.title: Experimental College - AI & the Mind: Adverse Effects
courses.desc: See details below for descriptions/bios.

sections.note:
COURSE: Black Mirrors and Dark Psychology: The Adverse Effects of AI on the Mind.

AI is drastically changing our society, but what is AI doing to our minds?

Much good can be done with technology. This course is NOT about that. Instead, this course will delve into the unsettling aspects of technology, specifically AI’s capacity to exacerbate the dark facets of human psychology. Integrating psychology theories with cutting-edge advancements in human-machine interaction, our explorations will foster a critical perspective on our relationship with technology. Together we will examine the insidious phenomena of manipulation, polarization, engineered addiction, moral disengagement and social disengagement. We will discuss how these psychological dark forces are amplified by psychological targeting, mindless scrolling, filter bubbles, lethal autonomy, and artificial intimacy. Through this course, we’ll gaze into our “black mirrors” and dare to question: “Mirror, mirror on the wall, what’s most harmful of them all?” Our journey will illuminate the darker side of the human psyche, adhering to the belief that only by acknowledging and confronting both our own capacity for harm, and that of the technologies we create, can we truly prevent it. So, are you ready to step into the shadows?

INSTRUCTOR: Meia Chita-Tegmark is a researcher and activist focused on the impacts of artificial intelligence on human psychology. She is the co-founder of the Future of Life Institute, a non-profit organization aimed at steering transformative technologies towards benefitting life and away from extreme, large-scale risks. As a postdoctoral scholar she conducted research on human-robot interaction at Tufts, and holds a PhD in Psychology from Boston University.

courses.title: Experimental College - Punk Rock: History & Practice
courses.desc: See details below for descriptions/bios.

sections.note:
COURSE: Punk Rock: History, Theory, and Practice.

Punk Rock is many things—a set of interconnected music styles, fashion aesthetics, political ideologies and communities that have risen and fallen over the course of the past half-century.

This course explores the iconic and often misunderstood subculture. Beginning with the Windrush Generation’s introduction of Ska to Britain, we will follow Punk through its complex and surprising history. We will learn how to use Punk as a critical lens for analyzing how social, economic, and political realities impact youth culture and mental health. And we will conclude with creative final projects in which we recreate the core elements of a Punk Scene through DIY music, fashion, and original research. Students will have the opportunity to learn in a semester what has taken many former Punk Rockers decades: how to use art, philosophy and critical analysis to turn their relationship with challenging social, political and economic realities into a powerful tool for self-discovery.

INSTRUCTOR: Micah Huang (G19) is an educator and performing artist whose work has been supported by institutions including the National Endowment for the Arts, California Arts Council, and the Fulbright Commission, among others. Ongoing work as an artistic researcher and community organizer includes co-organizing the Los Angeles Hungry Ghost Festival in the critically underserved community of LA Chinatown, and a series of collaborations between Immigrant communities and Indigenous Nations in Southern California. Micah is a PhD Candidate in Creative Practice and Critical Inquiry in the Music Department at Harvard University. He earned a Masters in Music Composition at Tufts. Micah’s journey as a musician and performer began in 2000s-era Pomona, California as a guitarist in that city’s notable post-punk scene.

courses.title: Experimental College - Financial Innovation & Tech
courses.desc: See details below for descriptions/bios.

sections.note:
COURSE: Financial Innovation through Technology: New Ways of Building the Future.

There’s more to financial innovation than Venmo and CashApp! Did you know that financial innovation or “FinTech” can be a force for good, helping those who need it most and the wider society to live better and prosper? Regardless of your expertise, you have a role to play in this booming area. If you’ve ever wanted to learn more about finance, innovation, personal financial wellness, or to meet experts in these and other spaces, this course is for you.

FinTech is the application of technology in financial services to improve upon existing products and services. It’s been making waves recently thanks to more powerful technology and changing consumer trends. In this course, students will get a broad overview of the world of FinTech and delve into the perspectives of both large traditional financial institutions and small, fledgling startups. We will study different sectors and forces disrupting them. Students will learn about the latest technologies, trends, and how different players leverage them (and each other) to evolve. You will also meet experts from the Boston FinTech ecosystem and hear their takes on real use cases, careers, and opportunities for change (spoiler: you don’t have to be a numbers wizard or tech-guru to succeed here).

INSTRUCTOR: Dahiana Duarte Pena (A15) focuses on FinTech and digital product development as a Vice President on the Eastern Bankshares Labs team. She has worked in innovation and research globally across North and South America, Europe, and Asia, including for State Street Corporation and the Embassy of Uruguay. Dahiana is also an elected member of the Tufts University Alumni Council who has been recognized as a 30 Under 30 National Latino Lister by El Mundo Newspaper, a Top 30 MA Latin Leader (from Amplify Latinx), and who received her company CEO’s Chairman award. She graduated from Tufts with degrees in Economics and International Finance, and holds an MBA from the Questrom School of Business at Boston University.

courses.title: Experimental College - Medicine, Ethics & the Law
courses.desc: See details below for descriptions/bios.

sections.note:
COURSE: Medicine, Ethics, and the Law.

What new ethical and legal issues arise as medical technology advances? How do these issues shape our thinking about what is moral in medicine? 

Topics will include in-vitro fertilization, organ donation, and our current medical care system. Students will weigh in on real legal cases, participate in healthy debates and a mock trial, and hear from a variety of guest speakers—likely including an AI/biotech scientist, an organ donor, and a physician who has been sued for medical malpractice. 

Students may also have the opportunity to attend a medical malpractice trial. The course will encourage students to question their own moral thinking and see the gray in what once seemed black and white.

INSTRUCTOR: Pam Gilman (A81) has been a civil litigation attorney specializing in medical malpractice defense for over 40 years. Her work has allowed her to develop relationships with physicians, hospital risk managers, genetic scientists, machine learning engineers, and organ procurement specialists, all of whom have expanded her thinking on medical ethics. Pam holds a JD from Boston University School of Law and was inducted into the Massachusetts Lawyers Hall of Fame in 2025.

courses.title: Experimental College - Right to Privacy
courses.desc: See details below for descriptions/bios.

sections.note:
COURSE: The Right to Privacy in Modern America.

No-knock raids? Phone data and location tracking? Warrantless wiretapping? Access to abortion? What does privacy mean in the 21st century?

This interdisciplinary course challenges students to explore the constitutional “right to privacy.” Through introspective papers and interactive classroom discussions, students are asked to analyze the historical, political, economic, legal, and sociological factors that form the backbone of the seminal cases and legislative decisions affecting privacy rights in America today. Students will also evaluate past and present societal mores and individual behaviors and preferences to predict the likely outcome of future cases and legislative debates. 

The class will concentrate on three particular areas : (1) privacy rights “enumerated” in the Constitution, (2) privacy rights that the Supreme Court has construed through interpretation of provisions in the Constitution and the Bill of Rights, and (3) emerging areas that have or still may necessitate the extension or expansion of historically established concepts of privacy. Topics considered in the course include the Fourth Amendment’s search and seizure jurisprudence in the face of recent technological innovations including Artificial Intelligence; the ongoing battle between safety-focused government surveillance and individual privacy in light of the ever expanding threats on the United States; the delicate thread that intertwines privacy, free speech, the freedom of religion, and the freedom of association; the dimensions and protections of reproductive rights; the efforts to contract sexuality and gender-based rights across the country; and even the outer expanse of the privacy right through the “right to die” cases. 

INSTRUCTORS: Doug Martland and Steve Sharobem have taught at the Experimental College several times over the past decade. Besides their experience teaching in the Experimental College, they each have nearly 20 years of experience as lawyers for state and federal government entities. Doug is an Assistant Attorney General for the Commonwealth of Massachusetts, providing legal representation to the state on civil matters. Steve serves as an Assistant United States Attorney, representing the U.S. in criminal and civil matters, and previously served as an Assistant Attorney General for the Commonwealth.

courses.title: Experimental College - Fiber Craft Creation & Culture
courses.desc: See details below for descriptions/bios.

sections.note:
COURSE: Fiber Craft: Creation and Culture.

Why do people craft? Is it meditation, activism, community, or simply the satisfaction of making something with your own hands? 

This course combines hands-on making with critical thinking about craft’s role in culture and society. You’ll learn a fiber craft technique (no experience required; options include knitting, embroidery, quilting), examine traditions from across the globe, and investigate why fiber crafts have been dismissed as “women’s work” rather than art. Through discussions, cultural case studies, a field trip to a local craft store, and your own creative practice, you’ll explore questions about gender, class, and what we value as “art” versus “craft.” You will leave this course having created something with your own hands and developed new perspectives on why making matters. 

Students may need to purchase supplies for individual projects and should expect to spend about $25. The ExCollege is available to assist if the cost of materials poses a problem.

INSTRUCTOR: Heather Dwyer is Senior Associate Director at Tufts’ Center for the Enhancement of Learning and Teaching (CELT), where she supports faculty in developing inclusive teaching practices. She holds a PhD in Ecology from UC Davis and has been practicing fiber arts for over 15 years, including knitting, quilting, and embroidery. She is passionate about creating equitable learning environments where students engage actively and reflect on their own growth as learners.

courses.title: Experimental College - Dark Tourism & Human Tragedy
courses.desc: See details below for descriptions/bios.

sections.note:
COURSE: Dark Tourism: The Attraction of Human Tragedy.

Why are people drawn to sites of death, violence, and suffering? Why do we vacation at places marked by trauma? This course explores the motivations behind dark tourism—the visitation of sites shaped by persecution, death, or disaster—and examines how visitors engage with these places and their histories. Using Boston-area case studies, such as the Boston Strangler murder sites, the Lizzie Borden House, and the Great Molasses Flood of 1919, students will consider ethical approaches to interpreting tragic pasts and analyze how and why societies commemorate, memorialize, and sometimes fetishize trauma.

INSTRUCTOR: Kristin Gallas is an award-winning museum educator and public historian. As principal of MUSE Consulting, she specializes in developing inclusive interpretation of challenging histories. She is a 2025–2026 Omohundro Institute Coffeehouse Fellow and is the author of Interpreting Slavery with Children and Teens at Museums and Historic Sites (2021) and co-editor of Interpreting Slavery at Museums and Historic Sites (2015), among other publications. Kristin has worked with sites around the country, including Mount Vernon, multiple National Park Service units, the Old North Church, and the USS Constitution Museum. She earned a MAT degree in Museum Education at George Washington University.

courses.title: Experimental College - Chinese Games, Chinese History
courses.desc: See details below for descriptions/bios.

sections.note:
COURSE: Chinese Games, Chinese History.

What does it mean to play, and how can play help us understand the past? 

This course explores the history of games in China and the possibilities and limits of using games to represent history. In the first half of the class, we’ll learn about (and play!) games that were central to Chinese cultural life, including go (weiqi), mahjong, competitive riddle-making, and other literati pastimes. We’ll then use these to investigate questions of social hierarchy, leisure, gender, and value systems in China from the Song dynasty (960–1279) through the early Republican period (20th century). 

The second half of the class turns to how we use games as tools for historical interpretation. We’ll study (and play!) board games and digital games and engage in a class-wide role-play simulation based on Chinese history, examining how game designers translate historical processes into mechanics and how games promote (or distort) historical arguments. Throughout the semester you will work in a group to design an original game rooted in an aspect or period of Chinese history. This class is hands-on, and much of the learning will come through play itself: competition, collaboration, and the challenge of experimenting with how games can model the past. No prior knowledge of Chinese history is required.

INSTRUCTOR: Sarah Bramao-Ramos is a cultural historian of China. She earned her PhD in History and East Asian Languages from Harvard University, where her dissertation examined the history of the Manchu language, the native language of the rulers of Qing China (1644–1911). Her research focuses on books printed in Manchu and has taken her to libraries in Norway, Mongolia, California, and many places in between. Her teaching emphasizes experimentation, collaboration, and the potential of experiential learning.

courses.title: Experimental College - Books Unbound
courses.desc: See details below for descriptions/bios.

sections.note:
COURSE: Books Unbound.

Want to learn how to make a book—both inside and out?! 

This studio/seminar hybrid will focus on the artist book in all shapes and forms: from initial design to final binding, students will learn the basics of bookbinding and how artists have used the form for centuries. We’ll explore book design, sequence, and structure using tools like Adobe InDesign. Project assignments focus on the relational aspects of books with an emphasis on accessible processes and demystifying bookbinding as a practice. Demonstrations include softcover and hardcover binding structures, Adobe InDesign, and digital printing. We’ll cover how bookmaking has evolved alongside and responded to historical shifts in technologies, with an eye to the contemporary potential of self-publishing. Students will gain familiarity with the artist book field and its impacts in art history through trips to the SMFA Library and Special Collections. No former studio art experience required, only a curiosity about books! 

Students may need to purchase some supplies for individual projects and should expect to spend about $20. The ExCollege is available to assist if the cost of materials poses a problem.

INSTRUCTOR: McCall Hollister (G24) is a museum worker, visual artist, and bookbinder. Working primarily through handbound photobooks, Hollister combines writing and photography to explore psychogeographical landscapes. Hollister received their Masters in Fine Arts and Museum Studies from the School of Museum of Fine Arts at Tufts University where they completed a Postgraduate Teaching Fellowship in 2025. Prior to graduate school, Hollister worked as a museum educator focused on youth and family arts programming with an emphasis on accessibility. They currently work as a freelance art handler and bookbinding instructor.

courses.title: Experimental College - Engineering in Ancient World
courses.desc: See details below for descriptions/bios.

sections.note:
COURSE: Engineering and Technology in the Ancient World.

Enter the world of Ancient engineers whose monumental works and technologies impressed audiences, both ancient and modern. 

This course explores, in thematic succession, the inventions and innovations that led to some of the most extensive building programs undertaken by pre-modern states. Through case studies ranging from particular structural elements and technologies (e.g. columns, domes, cranes, catapults) to overall structural systems (e.g. theaters, temples, aqueducts) this class investigates the history of materials, methods, and knowledge behind Greek and Roman innovations, and their role in communicating socio-cultural and political identity. Students apply course themes to the modern world and the architecture around them through biweekly short essays. Hands-on group activities allow for direct engagement with the technologies and innovations discussed in class. For their final project, students form small groups to build a to-scale working model of an ancient machine or technology. Students navigate the challenges of reconstructing an ancient artifact from various material and textual sources, and in the process gain insights into the collaborative process of design and innovation. Through the group project, students learn to collaborate by drawing on each other's diverse strengths and become closer as classmates and community members. No engineering background required.

Students may need to purchase some supplies for individual and group projects and should expect to spend about $10-20. The ExCollege is available to assist if the cost of materials poses a problem.

COURSE: Max Peers is an archaeologist and architectural historian who recently earned a PhD from the Joukowsky Institute for Archaeology and the Ancient World at Brown University. Peers has served as the lead instructor and teaching assistant for a wide variety of courses on the art and archaeology of the ancient world, including specialized upper-level courses on engineering and technology, and the history and archaeology of pandemics. He has participated in fieldwork in Italy, Greece, and Jordan, and practices stone carving, all of which informs his classroom techniques.

courses.title: Experimental College - Global Journalism in 21st Cen
courses.desc: See details below for descriptions/bios.

sections.note:
COURSE: Behind the Reporter’s Notebook: Global Journalism in the 21st Century.

What is it like to work as a foreign correspondent? How do journalists across the globe operate, what challenges do they face, and how does their work shape our understanding of today’s world?

This course, taught by a veteran reporter, will use some of the best works of contemporary journalism to explore the craft of international reporting and the changing nature of the global media industry. We’ll study the work of both Western and non-Western journalists, including print, radio, and television reporters, war correspondents, travel writers, photographers, videographers, and documentary filmmakers. We’ll delve into the risks posed by hostile governments, examine how the internet and social media have upended old business models, and discuss how the global media’s ongoing evolution impacts what we see and hear about the world around us. Along the way, we’ll gain a knack for the reporting process by taking a critical eye to others’ work and completing our own journalistic assignments.

INSTRUCTOR: Jonathan W. Rosen (A04) is a freelance journalist who’s been reporting overseas for more than fifteen years, mainly from sub-Saharan Africa. His writing has been published by National Geographic, The New York Times, The Atlantic, The Economist, MIT Technology Review, and many others. Jon has a BA from Tufts and an MA from the Johns Hopkins University School of Advanced International Studies.

courses.title: Experimental College - Fashion & Clothes Histories
courses.desc: See details below for descriptions/bios.

sections.note:
COURSE: Fashion Histories: Thinking With Clothes.

How can a study of clothing enrich an understanding of history? Why can producing, consuming, wearing, or displaying dress offer new insight to the past? 

This course will examine how historians use dress and fashion to interpret the past and will explore the theories, concepts, and questions that drive dress history and material culture studies. We will use a comprehensive definition of dress to include clothing, adornment, and embellishment. Clothing, makeup, earrings¿all of these can offer a useful lens into cultural, political, economic, and gender dynamics of a time and place. While this course focuses on the historical discipline, dress and fashion history is a highly interdisciplinary field. We will draw from fields beyond history including art history, anthropology, and museum studies. Examining the production, consumption, and display of dress, we will explore how clothing is integral to understanding personal and political identity. This course encourages us to see dress as a way to uncover perspectives and stories that otherwise may be obscured. What kinds of answers can dress and fashion offer about the past that written sources cannot? 

INSTRUCTOR: Margot Rashba (A18, G21) is a PhD candidate in History at Boston University. Her dissertation “Britishness on the Runway: Dress and Identity from Punk to the Present” explores Britishness and national identity in the collections of designers Vivienne Westwood, John Galliano, and Alexander McQueen from 1970 to 2015. Margot received both her BA and MA from Tufts University, with her Master’s in history and museum studies. She has worked in the museum and public history world for the past eight years in institutions including the Peabody Essex Museum and the Boston Symphony Orchestra Archives.

courses.title: Experimental College - Humans and Animals
courses.desc: See details below for descriptions/bios.

sections.note:
COURSE: Humans and Animals: New Perspectives.

What is the relationship between animals, humans, and the planet? And how can we challenge speciesism and anthropocentrism through a critical lens? 

This course will explore how animal oppression intersects with other forms of environmental and social injustice. Topics explored will include animal public policy and advocacy, food systems, social justice, and environmental conservation. Students will then be challenged to apply the critical and compassionate lens developed in the first section of the course to real world institutions and systems through hands-on and immersive experience. Students will explore and analyze organizations such as animal sanctuaries, aquariums and zoos, shelters, and school systems, and critically examine whether and how these organizations ultimately impact positive social change. 

INSTRUCTOR: Stephen Strout is an animal activist and graduate student at Tufts studying education with a sub-concentration in animal public policy and humane education. He is a Community Advocacy Leader with the MSPCA and lobbies for animal welfare. He also has extensive experience in the farmed and exploited animal rescue and sanctuary space, where he is currently conducting research related to humane education programs within animal sanctuaries.

courses.title: Experimental College - Investing, Psych & Behavior
courses.desc: See details below for descriptions/bios.

sections.note:
COURSE: Investing, Psychology and Human Behavior. 

What is the impact of psychology and human behavior on individual investment decisions? Why do most professional investors fail to perform better than the market averages? Companies are managed by people; understanding the role psychology and human behavior play is instrumental when formulating an opinion on a company’s share price. How did some investors anticipate the 2008 financial crisis? And why did so many Wall Street Investment Banks fail to see such disaster looming? Does the pursuit of profits distort Wall Street’s behavior towards acting in a clients’ best interest? What are the warning signs (red flags) of bad behavior and how can investors become armed to avoid falling for Ponzi schemes and/or outright fraud?

There has been a small select group of investors over the years that have superior long-term investment records. How do the likes of Warren Buffett, Charlie Munger, Peter Lynch and John Maynard Keynes achieve their exceptional long-term results? A stock represents an actual business, and the ability to value the assets of a particular business is crucial to forecasting the direction of its stock price. Students will learn basic financial metrics and valuation tools to aid their understanding of the investment process. Students will also study behavioral analysis and learn how psychology plays an important part in one’s investment success as well as failure. The goal of this course is to expose students to basic investment tenets and help them develop a foundation that will guide them to become better educated investors in the future. The course will also include the role financial markets have in society. Students will explore how access to financial capital serves as a multiplier effect to human capital, social capital, and real assets, and will explore the ways financial innovation meets the needs of society.

INSTRUCTORS: Douglas A. Rachlin (A85) is a Managing Director, Senior Portfolio Manager and founder of the Rachlin Group within the Neuberger Berman Private Asset Management group. The Rachlin Group manages energy and renewable focused investment strategies for private wealth and institutional clients. From 1996 to 2005, Doug was a Portfolio Manager with Lehman Brothers. Prior to joining Lehman Brothers, he served as the president of Rachlin Investment Management, and had previously worked as a securities analyst for Standard & Poor’s Corporation. Doug has been quoted or featured in several publications and news media including The Financial Times, The Wall Street Journal, Barron’s, CNBC, and Forbes magazine. He holds an MBA from New York University’s Leonard N. Stern School of Business. He is a Trustee of Tufts University.

Raphael A. Leeman recently retired from Morgan Stanley, where he was a Portfolio Manager and Analyst on the High Yield Bond Team. During Rafe’s 20-year career in finance, his experience included managing the Calvert (ESG-focused) High Yield Bond Fund, and covering the automotive, cable and broadcasting, media and entertainment, equipment rental, and transportation industries. Prior experience includes eight years of systems integration and consulting, as well as seven years of product development and marketing, for both large companies and startups. He holds an MBA from Harvard University.

courses.title: Experimental College - The World of Crosswords
courses.desc: See details below for descriptions/bios.

sections.note:
COURSE: The World of Crosswords.

Half-semester, meeting 6 times on Sept. 9, 16, 23, 30, Oct. 7, 14.

Have you ever wondered what it takes to make a crossword? In this course, you’ll learn about the rules of crossword construction, the challenges of finding the perfect theme, and take a peek inside the world of puzzlemaking. You will finish the course with your own original crossword puzzle, which you can submit to a professional outlet, publish in The Tufts Daily, or share with your friends.

INSTRUCTOR: Nate Hall (A25) is a Tufts alumnus, former ExCollege peer teacher, and freelance crossword constructor. His crossword has been published in The New York Times.

courses.title: Experimental College - Reading in a Digital Age
courses.desc: See details below for descriptions/bios

sections.note:
COURSE: Reading in a Digital Age. 

(Cross-listed as CLS 0186 and DH 150) Introduction to reading in a digital age: survey of digital methods for engaging with the human record. Applications of AI (such as large language models), more traditional computational methods and core statistical concepts needed to provide intellectually transparent and defensible conclusions, and key concepts from research on the impact of digital methods on learning and memory.

INSTRUCTOR: Peter Nadel is the Digital Humanities and Natural Language Processing Specialist with Research Technology. He works with both students and faculty on a wide variety of projects. With his Master’s in Classical Studies as well as a wealth of programming experience, he is well suited to work with everyone from hardcore computer scientists to humanities scholars. He is particularly interested in how computational methods can be used to extract sub- and intertextual meaning, especially in understudied corpora like that of post-classical Latin.

courses.title: Experimental College - Designing Your Career Journey
courses.desc: See details below for descriptions/bios.

sections.note:
COURSE: Designing Your Career Journey.

This course is a perfect introduction for first and second year students who are getting started on their career journey. This course is a half-semester and runs for the first 7 weeks of the semester. Throughout the 7 weeks, you’ll learn how to use design thinking to find meaningful experiences in college and jumpstart your career exploration. Included will be fun and engaging activities, and an opportunity to build a supportive community with other students. By the end of this course, you will have created a plan to kick off your career exploration while at Tufts. 

INSTRUCTOR: Sheryl Livsey is an Associate Director in the Tufts Career Center with 15 years of experience in career coaching for college students. Originally from California's Bay Area, Sheryl holds a Master of Education in College Student Development Administration from Seattle University. Prior to working at Tufts, she led career programs at Bottom Line, a nonprofit focused on supporting first-generation and low-income college students in the Boston area, and at Wellesley College. Sheryl loves helping students understand the career development process, make meaning of their college experiences, and launch their professional lives after Tufts.

courses.desc: See details below for descriptions/bios.

sections.note:
COURSE: Parchment to Print: Special Collections Workshop

A hands-on introduction to rare books and special collections at Tisch Library and the SMFA. Explore medieval manuscripts, early printed books, contemporary artists books, and printmaking. The course will be team-taught in Tisch Library Special Collections, and will feature readings, discussion, and in-class activities. Students will have the opportunity to engage in a hands-on project. There will be six class meetings beginning on Thursday, October 29, 2026.

INSTRUCTORS: Elettra Conoly (A21) is a librarian in the Special Collections department of Tisch Library. She holds an MA in Medieval Studies from King’s College London where she learned how to read old books. 

Christopher Barbour is the Head of Special Collections at Tisch Library. His areas of expertise include rare books, history of the book, medieval and early modern studies, and letterpress.

courses.title: Experimental College - Writing Fellow Seminar
courses.desc: See details below for descriptions/bios.

sections.note:
COURSE: Writing Fellows Seminar.

This course is only open to students who have already been accepted into the StAAR Center Writing Fellows Program. This pedagogy seminar focuses on the history, theory, and practice of writing instruction and writing tutoring at the college level. Together we will read and discuss scholarship, engage in reflective and analytical writing, and practice hands-on activities to apply theoretical concepts as a writing tutor. By the end of the seminar, you will be able to apply a critical lens to writing instruction, discuss prevailing theories for writing tutoring, and create your own tutoring philosophy. Throughout this process, we will build a community of writers and developing educators: peers supporting peers as writers and as writing tutors. 
 
INSTRUCTOR: Hannah Weildon is the Writing Resources Specialist at the Student Accessibility and Academic Resource (StAAR) Center, where she coordinates the Writing Fellows Program and provides individual writing support to Tufts students. She received her PhD from Tufts in English in 2024. Previously at Tufts, she served as a Graduate Writing Consultant and taught in the First Year Writing Program. She has also taught literature at other local institutions, including Emerson College and the Osher Lifelong Learning Institute. Hannah enjoys helping students find empowerment through writing as a collaborative process.

Explore the history of these processes and their uses in contemporary art and gain a basic understanding of each technique by focusing on their sculptural capabilities. Non-SMFA students and MAT Art Education students will receive a letter grade.

courses.desc: Studio/seminar looks at craft as a political and personal tool. Explore, through historical and contemporary research of community groups, artists, political movements, material studies, and students’ individual practice how fiber/textile practice acts as a form of resistance, protest, and self-empowerment. courses.desc: See departmental website for details.

sections.note:

Examines natural dye as a material, ecological, and cultural practice through sustained studio work in a fiber garden setting. Using the SMFA Dye & Fiber Garden as a primary material resource, students explore plant-based dye processes from cultivation and harvest through dye extraction, fiber preparation, and application. Emphasis is placed on seasonal cycles, sustainable material systems, and place-responsive making. Technical workshops introduce historical and contemporary natural dye methods while supporting individual material research and experimentation. Students produce dyed fibers and yardage for use in independent studio projects, with opportunities for collaborative work connected to the garden’s ongoing care and sustainability. Level: Intermediate. Prerequisites: One CER, FIB, SCP or MTL class

Introduces various design methods such as patternmaking and improvisation. Identifies histories of global trade, migration, colonialism, and other sources of cultural contact that influence existing quilt forms. Prerequisite: Intro to Fibers (FIB 0102), or other prior Fibers course, or by permission of the instructor.

Discussion of the extent to which cinema's aesthetic features are shared by television, as well as what is artistically distinctive about television. Theoretical concepts relevant to moving image art, principally genre, authorship, and character identification.

courses.title: Global History of Cinema
courses.desc: (Cross-listed w/ ILVS 52) History of cinema beginning with the emergence of the technologies for making and exhibiting films around 1894 and the major genres of early cinema (1895-1904); the development of "classical" narrative film in the US in the 1900s and 1910s; the creation of alternatives to classical cinematic storytelling in the 1920s in France, Germany, the Soviet Union and elsewhere; the rise of documentary and experimental film; and the coming of synchronized sound in the late 1920s. European responses to the increasing political turmoil in the lead-up to WWII in the 1930s; Japanese popular traditions of filmmaking, the impact of WWII on film history; the emergence of Italian Neo-Realism and "modernist" art cinema in the late 1940s and 1950s; the New Waves of the late 1950s; and political modernist, post-colonial, feminist and other radical forms of filmmaking that arose in response to the political crises of the 1960s. Survey of world cinema since the 1970s, focusing on the changes that have occurred in mainstream Hollywood filmmaking and the work of filmmakers in Hong Kong and other non-western countries.

courses.title: Intermediate Film & Media Production
courses.desc:
Advanced work in narrative filmmaking, building on FMS 10. Development of skills in producing, directing, cinematography, editing, sound mixing, and color grading through hands-on exercises drawn from professional preproduction, production, and postproduction workflows. Collaborative production of a 10–12 minute narrative film based on an original or adapted script. Emphasis on iterative practice, collaboration, and creative decision-making in story development, visual design, image-making, and sound.
Prerequisite: FMS 10

sections.note:
Formerly From Script to Screen. Intermediate Film and Media Production: Building on FMS10, students will develop a deeper skillset as producers, directors, cinematographers, editors, mixers, and color graders. Through a series of hands-on exercises drawn from real-world preproduction, production, and postproduction scenarios, students will be exposed to professional workflows. In addition, students will work in small teams to produce a 10–12 minute narrative movie, either from an original or adapted script.

Students who complete this course will gain the ability to move from concept to finished film through iterative practice, collaboration, and creative decision-making regarding story, design, image-making, and sound.

courses.title: Experimental Filmmaking: Concept to Practice
courses.desc: Exploration of experimental filmmaking techniques and practices as an alternative outlet to the commercial film industry. Various traditions from the cinematic avant-garde, including experimental film as medium for personal expression, as exploration of film form, or as critique of mass media and culture. Introduction to the tactile nature of film with the use of 16mm Bolex cameras and DIY cameraless filmmaking techniques. Screenings of notable work, readings, and discussions of contemporary film issues, as well as visiting artists lectures will provide additional context needed to engage with experimental film communities, film festivals, and exhibition spaces locally and abroad. Production of a project through in-class workshops, culminating in a class screening at the end of the semester. Prerequisites: FMS 1 or instructor permission.

courses.title: Screenwriting I
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as TPS 79). Immersive workshop in the craft of writing short, engaging scripts. Introduction to screenwriting and dramatic construction, taking the short film from concept to screenplay. Screenings and analysis of narrative shorts from around the world supplement weekly script development and roundtable discussion of student work.

courses.title: Costume Design
courses.desc: (Cross listed w/ TPS 71) Development of the skills of script analysis, rendering, and process for the design of costumes.

sections.note: Lab Fee $100. TDPS is committed to making our courses accessible to all and will assist students who need support with lab fees. Please email TDPS Associate Department Chair Linda Ross Girard for more information.

courses.title: Creative Writing: Journalism
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed w/ENG 7) A course open to all interested students who want practice and instruction in journalism in a workshop situation.Open to all who have completed the College Writing Requirement. Each section is limited to fifteen students.
Pre-requisites: Completion of the College Writing Requirement
