Requires the completion of ENG 0001 and ENG 0002 or ENG 0003 and ENG 0004 or equivalent(s) and A&S, or ENG 0001 and SOE

courses.title: Introduction to Branding and Marketing
courses.desc: Examination of how brands are created, communicated, and sustained through strategic branding and marketing. Brand building and the marketing tools used to bring brands to life. Analysis of brand identity, messaging, consumer insight, and media planning as core tools in brand development. Emphasis on experimentation, discussion, and applied work in translating ideas into cohesive brand experiences.

sections.note: Formerly Public Relations and Marketing. Introduction to Branding and Marketing: Brands shape how we see, feel, and engage with the world around us. This course explores how brands are created, communicated, and sustained through strategic branding and marketing. Students will learn the fundamentals of brand building and the marketing tools used to bring brands to life, including identity, messaging, consumer insight, and media planning. Highly interactive and hands-on, the course emphasizes experimentation, discussion, and real-world application, giving students practical experience turning ideas into compelling brand experiences.

courses.title: AI in Motion: Ethics & Impact in Media Industries
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CVS 13 & STS 36) Examination of the transformative role of artificial intelligence (AI) in digital media industries, with a particular focus on cinema and television. Engagement with theoretical and empirical literature and discussion of the history and current ethical debates surrounding AI, including AI’s impact upon contemporary media practices. Hands-on experience with cutting-edge AI tools for text, sound, image, and motion picture generation. Development of skills in critically analyzing and creatively engaging with the future of AI in media.

courses.title: Online Video: Algorithms, Creators & Social Impact
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CVS 47) The evolving landscape of online video platforms, the power dynamics that shape them, and the broader social impact of their content. The role of algorithms, surveillance capitalism, and the attention economy in the production and sharing of video content on platforms like YouTube, TikTok, Instagram, and more. Through a combination of social analysis and hands-on experience, engagement with key questions about why content goes viral, why people are compelled to share online, how platform design influences creators, and the social and political impact of these videos. Creation of an original video series, including production and marketing, with a critical reflection on the ethical implications of the work, as well as readings and written responses.

courses.title: Imagining The Holocaust On Stage And Screen
courses.desc: (Cross-listed w/TPS 25, JS 25 and TPS 125) Plays and films dealing with the Holocaust, From Nazi-era propaganda to contemporary reflections on genocide. Special emphasis on the ethics of Holocaust represented and the responsibilities of artists (and audiences) who engage the Holocaust story. Texts include such plays as Camp Comedy, Ghetto, Kindertransport, Good, Bent, Who Will Carry the World?, and Annulla, as well as critical and theoretical readings. Triumph of the Will, Night and Fog, The Architecture of Doom, Partisans of Vilna, The Boat is Full, My Mother's Courage, Schindler's List, Life is Beautiful and Shoah are among the feature films and documentaries considered. (Graduate Students should register for TPS 125).

courses.title: Composition for Film
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed as MUS 17) Introduction to composing music for a variety of visual media, including film, video games, and advertising. Access to the music lab where students produce their work hands on.
Recommendations: Working knowledge of notation and sequencing software (such as Finale or Sibelius and DigitalPerformer or Pro Tools) helpful. Music 5 or equivalent, or permission of instructor.

courses.title: Love and War in French Film
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as FR 75 & WGSS 75) Focus on the themes of love and war in French films from the 1930's to the present. Film theory and basic cinematic techniques, as well as the historical, social, and cultural contexts of films of the poetic realism, nouvelle vague, and more contemporary movements, by directors Renoir, Clément, Carné, Resnais, Malle, Truffauat, Godard, Rohmer, Keislowski, and others. Films include: La grande illusion, Les jeux interdits, Les enfants du paradis, Hiroshima mon amour, Jules et Jim, Les parapluies de Cherbourg, Pierrot le fou, Lacombe Lucien, Les roseaux sauvages, Trois couleurs: Bleu; De rouille d'os, and Amour. In English.

courses.title: Classics Of World Cinema
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ILVS100 and ILCS 80.) Worldwide survey of major films from the silent era to the present. Trends in filmmaking styles and genres; the impact of modern history on cinematic art; cultural, theoretical, and philosophical issues related to the study of film. Filmmakers covered may include Eisenstein, Chaplin, Renoir, Welles, DeSica, Ray, Ozu, Bergman, Fassbinder, Sembene, and Zhang Yimou.

courses.title: Arab And Middle Eastern Cinemas
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ILVS 87 and ARB 57). An overview of the social role of cinema in the Arab world and the broader Middle East focusing on a historical perspective on the development and expansion of cinema in these parts of the world, as well as several thematic windows through which the relationship of cinema to these societies is examined. In English.

courses.title: Introduction to Media Culture and Theory
courses.desc: (Cross-listed with TPS 22 and ILVS 54) Qualitative media studies, its history, intellectual development, and theoretical milestones. Introduction to study of popular media culture. Covers major areas of study, theoretical principles, methodologies, and debates that have shaped popular media studies. Theoretical approaches to issues and case studies (including representation, labor and authorship, contemporary media convergence, fandom and participatory culture, media globalization, reality television, game studies, industry research and more). Students acquire knowledge of the major theories that define the field and contemporary application of these theories in critical engagements with media texts and practices.

courses.title: Postmodernism&film
courses.desc: (Cross-listed w/ ENG 81 and ILVS 89) Introduction to postmodernism through the study of late twentieth century and early twenty-first century film in relation to important texts of literary and cultural criticism. The movement from modern to postmodern, originality to mechanical reproduction, identity to difference. Readings from Baudrillard, Benjamin, Butler, Derrida, Foucault, Haraway, Lacan, and ¿i¿ek , along with films by Cameron, Gilliam, Polanski, Scott, the Wachowski brothers, and Welles.

sections.note: Fulfills post-1860 English major requirement.

courses.title: Special Topics - Diasporic Cinema
courses.desc: Please see departmental website for detailed course information.

sections.note: The course explores an array of global cinematic representations of diasporic experience while relying on writings on the concepts of hybridity, migrancy, external and internal colonialisms and transculturation. We will discuss a broad range of filmmakers, styles and cross-cultural encounters, as well as the works’ social implications. In addition to the films and readings, students will research their own family background and contribute their creative projects to our discussion of dislocation challenges, understanding of difference, the sense of place, and socio-economic effects of migration.

courses.title: Special Topics - Individualism and Nonconformity in Film
courses.desc: Please see departmental website for detailed course information.

sections.note:
Class dates: 9/17, 10/15, 11/5, and 12/3

Hosted by the Center for Expanding Viewpoints in Higher Education (CEVIHE) in collaboration with the Film and Media Studies Program (FMS), this four-part film series invites Tufts students to examine the themes of individualism and nonconformity through screenings of landmark films drawn from a range of historical periods, political contexts, and cinematic traditions. Each session features a full-length film paired with faculty framing and guided discussion, allowing participants to analyze how individuals navigate the tension between personal conscience and collective pressure, and how political and social institutions respond to dissent. The series asks participants to think critically about moral independence, civic responsibility, and the costs and consequences of resisting conformity. Popcorn and pizza will be served. Students do not need to sign up for course credit to attend, but enrolled students will have guaranteed seats. The series is open to students from all disciplines and majors who are interested in exploring contested ideas, competing loyalties, and acts of principled resistance that shape public life. Faculty and staff are also welcome to join

courses.title: FMS Media Internship - 4 Credits
courses.desc: Internships in media teach you about the industry and give you valuable hands-on experience. This course provides faculty support and academic credit for media-related internships in all areas, including broadcasting, film, journalism, public relations, marketing, advertising, publishing, web and multimedia, social media, and other fields. 4-SHU course includes 3 short papers, short weekly reflections, regular meetings with the instructor, and 150 work hours onsite at the internship. 2-SHU course includes 2 short papers, short weekly reflections, regular meetings with the instructor, and 75 work hours onsite at the internship. Available to rising sophomores, juniors, and seniors. FMS major or minor not required. Pass/Fail. Prerequisites: Consent.

courses.title: FMS Media Internship - 2 Credits
courses.desc: Internships in media teach you about the industry and give you valuable hands-on experience. This course provides faculty support and academic credit for media-related internships in all areas, including broadcasting, film, journalism, public relations, marketing, advertising, publishing, web and multimedia, social media, and other fields. 4-SHU course includes 3 short papers, short weekly reflections, regular meetings with the instructor, and 150 work hours onsite at the internship. 2-SHU course includes 2 short papers, short weekly reflections, regular meetings with the instructor, and 75 work hours onsite at the internship. Available to rising sophomores, juniors, and seniors. FMS major or minor not required. Pass/Fail. Prerequisites: Consent.

courses.title: FMS Media Internship - 1 Credit
courses.desc: Internships in media teach you about the industry and give you valuable hands-on experience. This course provides faculty support and academic credit for media-related internships in all areas, including broadcasting, film, journalism, public relations, marketing, advertising, publishing, web and multimedia, social media, and other fields. 4-SHU course includes 3 short papers, short weekly reflections, regular meetings with the instructor, and 150 work hours onsite at the internship. 2-SHU course includes 2 short papers, short weekly reflections, regular meetings with the instructor, and 75 work hours onsite at the internship. Available to rising sophomores, juniors, and seniors. FMS major or minor not required. Pass/Fail. Prerequisites: Consent.

courses.title: Children And Media
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CSHD 167 and CVS 147). Why educators, broadcasters, advertisers, and politicians consider children a special audience of media. Examination of children’s media content—television, video, film, podcast, games, social media, and print—and its effects on children and adolescents. Student projects may include remix, media literacy, and related topics.

courses.title: How to Pay Attention
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as STS 189 & ANTH 189) Collective investigation of attention as a sociocultural phenomenon. Reading-, writing-, and discussion-intensive seminar, supplemented by experimental exercises in and out of class. Topics include information overload, distraction, boredom, enchantment, expertise, social media, attention economies and ecologies, attention deficits and surpluses, and ideologies of attention in politics, education, and ethnographic fieldwork. Recommendations: Junior standing and one sociocultural anthropology course, or permission of instructor.

sections.req: Junior, Senior, or Graduate students only

courses.title: Religion and Film
courses.desc: (Cross-listed w/ REL103) Analysis of religion and religious issues through their portrayal in contemporary film. Focus on approaches to film taken by scholars of religion, including mythological, theological and cultural studies, with consideration of film theory. Genres include drama, comedy, animation and science fiction.

courses.title: Women and Film in Latin America
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as SPN 181) Critical study of the representation of women in Latin American cinema. Beginning with Mexico's edad de oro (1930-1940) to the present, an exploration of the positioning of a gendered spectator, the role of melodrama, as well as issues of race and class in the construction of women's identity through film. Includes a variety of films, primarily from Argentina, Brazil, Cuba, Mexico and Peru. Conducted in Spanish. Recommended: Two 30-level Spanish courses or consent of the instructor.

courses.title: Storytelling: Radio/Podcasts
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as MDIA 166) Intermediate-level studio seminar on audio storytelling as an interdisciplinary field spanning podcasting, radio, literature, music, theater, poetry, journalism, activism, politics, cinema, and contemporary art. Tell stories through sound and words, using narrative structures, audio recording and editing techniques, sound design, collective listening sessions, and seminar discussions. Histories and genres of narrative sound formats. No experience in sound necessary. Prerequisites: Sophomore standing and above.

sections.note: SMFA students should register for MDIA 166.

courses.title: Children and Media Seminar
courses.desc: (Cross-listed with CSHD 162 and CVS 188) Examination of why children have long been considered a "special" audience by broadcasters, advertisers, politicians, educators, and researchers. Critical study of theory and research on children's media use and its effects. Exploration of how media consumption relates to developmental issues, patterns of use, and the content and context of children's media, including television, film/video, advertising, games, podcasts, and social media. Analysis of both theoretical frameworks and empirical evidence to explore topics including gender and ethnic stereotyping, sexual and violent content, educational and "pro-social" effects of media, and the links between media use and increases in childhood obesity. Projects, media assessments, research critiques, and an original research proposal.

courses.title: Television in the Age of Change
courses.desc: (Cross listed as ILVS 72 & TPS 121) Examines how new technologies and shifting viewing habits are transforming television; how storytelling is changing in light of TV’s industrial and technological evolution and our global, networked, media environment; and how contemporary viewing habits are reshaping our theories of audiences, styles, and viewing pleasures. Focuses on story creation, changing genres, programming conventions and global trends, shifting technologies, social media, TV fans, and streaming content—and how all these influence television narratives and our media culture.

courses.title: Special Topics - Cult Cinema
courses.desc: Please see departmental website for detailed course information.

sections.note:
Course Fee: $60 for tickets to screenings at the Somerville Theatre.

New for fall 2026. Defined as social, cult cinema is about the enthusiastic audience a movie acquires over time. Devotees argue it's also about late night screenings, dialogue that brands itself onto your brain, and a taste for the unusual. Cult cinema is marked by an ethics of endurance and the cultural politics of oppositional tastes. In this course, we will explore the fascinating history, theory, and cultural impact of films with dedicated, often fringe, fanbases that defy traditional, mainstream tastes. Key topics include midnight movies, genre cinema (horror/sci-fi), exploitation, camp, censorship, and audience reception. Films to be studied may include Blade Runner, Eraserhead, Monty Python and the Holy Grail, Pink Flamingos, The Princess Bride, and The Rocky Horror Picture Show. This course partners with Somerville Theatre in a new fall 2026 series curated to align with this new FMS offering. Attendance at a selection of screenings at the cinema is required. Together we will experience cinematic works on the big screen that not only afford memorable viewing experiences but also create rich possibilities for discussion and debate.
Weekly required screening - see course description for details.

courses.title: Directed Study
courses.desc: Independent study conducted under close supervision of an FMS faculty member. For FMS juniors and seniors who have a strong interest in an area of study in which there are no courses being offered, or who want to do advanced work beyond regularly offered courses. Requires regular meetings with a faculty member and in- depth research. Result is typically a long research paper or creative work. Departmental consent required.

instructors: Denise Kristen Cummings, Howard Steven Woolf, Jennifer Burton, Julie Dobrow, Malcolm Turvey, Mat Rappaport, Natalie Minik

courses.title: Elementary French I
courses.desc: Introduction to the French language with emphasis on acquiring basic vocabulary and grammar structures for daily interactions in a variety of settings. An immersive experience to gain introductory proficiency and basic reading, writing, listening, and speaking skills. Topics may include talking about family, school, food, sports, the weather, and parties.

courses.title: Elementary French II
courses.desc: Builds on skills acquired in FR 1. Interactive language use in situations, such as making vacation plans, going to the doctor, or ordering in a restaurant. Expansion of cultural knowledge based on discussion of various Francophone locations. A comprehensive foundation with opportunities to practice writing, reading, listening, and speaking. Weekly recitations required. Recommendations: FR 1 or instructor permission.

courses.title: Intermediate French I
courses.desc: Brings students to an intermediate level of French language proficiency in listening, speaking, reading, and writing. In-class activities centered around contemporary Francophone culture with historical context while practicing interactive language use. Discussions of short readings and films for proficiency through vocabulary expansion, grammar review, short compositions, and video production. Recommendations: FR 2 or instructor permission.

courses.title: Intermediate French II
courses.desc: Discussion of readings and films on topics ranging from the political and historical to the social and cultural to develop proficiency. Interactive language use in situations, such as choosing a profession, traveling, or defining happiness. Vocabulary acquisition, expansion of grammar topics, short compositions, oral practice, and weekly recitations to gain confidence in communicating in French. Recommendations: FR 3 or instructor permission.

courses.title: French Language through Culture I - Crimes et sentiments
courses.desc: Practice of oral proficiency and a review of complex grammatical structures in the context of French and Francophone cultures. Cultural references connected to diverse themes. Improvement of proficiency in listening comprehension, speaking, and writing through films, in-class presentations, varied writing assignments, and weekly recitations.. courses.title: Voices of France: Middle Ages to the Enlightenment
courses.desc: Examination of how social, political, and cultural forces influenced French thought, language, and identity from the 12th to 18th centuries. Analysis of literary texts and cultural artifacts to explore broader historical developments, such as the evolution of ideas about reason, individualism, and progress. Comprehensive understanding of the intellectual and cultural foundations that shaped modern France. Not for students returning from programs abroad. Prerequisite: FR 22 or equivalent, or instructor permission.

sections.note: Will be taught by Bastien Craipain

courses.title: Connections in French Literature and Culture
courses.desc: Exploration of French and Francophone literary texts, cultural movements, and historical transformations from the 19th century to the present, emphasizing their connection to broader political and social contexts. Study of texts, film, and visual art to examine how key literary and aesthetic movements both reflect and challenge their historical moments and assess their lasting effect on contemporary debates. Topics may include Romanticism, Impressionism, Theatre of the Absurd, Existentialism, feminist thought, class and social struggle, as well as shifting relationships between France and its former colonies. Not for students returning from study abroad. Prerequisite: FR 22 or equivalent, or instructor permission.

courses.title: Love and Marriage in Medieval French Literature
courses.desc: Examination of the cult of love in twelfth-century France, with focus on the process of psychosexual development and on efforts to reconcile the happiness of the individual with the common good. The ideal of amorous fulfillment in The Romance of Tristan and Iseut; the role of extramarital relationships in Lancelot by Chrétien de Troyes; the contrasting perspective on marriage in Chrétien’s Yvain and Erec and Enide; the link between growth in love and the spiritual quest in his Perceval; and Marie de France’s unconventional approach in matters of fidelity to lover, spouse, and God .In English.

courses.title: Love and War in French Film - Classics Of French Cin
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as FMS 63 & WGSS 75) Focus on the themes of love and war in French films from the 1930's to the present. Film theory and basic cinematic techniques, as well as the historical, social, and cultural contexts of films of the poetic realism, nouvelle vague, and more contemporary movements, by directors Renoir, Clément, Carné, Resnais, Malle, Truffauat, Godard, Rohmer, Keislowski, and others. Films include: La grande illusion, Les jeux interdits, Les enfants du paradis, Hiroshima mon amour, Jules et Jim, Les parapluies de Cherbourg, Pierrot le fou, Lacombe Lucien, Les roseaux sauvages, Trois couleurs: Bleu; De rouille d'os, and Amour. In English.

courses.title: Advanced French Language: Acting French
courses.desc: Theatre and acting as vehicles for improving French communication skills. Explore questions related to theatre and performance and engage in role-playing activities. Materials include French plays and films. Active participation, grammar assignments, exams, papers, and performance-based assessments. No theatre experience required. In French. Recommended: FR 22 or instructor permission.

courses.title: Business French
courses.desc:
Fundamental French as used in the business world, as well as background and information to enable students to communicate effectively in a business context in France and other Francophone countries. Technical terminology and practices in such fields as banking, government, industry, and advertising, and understanding of French political, financial, economic, and educational institutions. Writing business letters, job application letters, and résumés. Impacts of recent and current developments such as the European Union and euroscepticism, immigration, and climate change. Students may opt to take the Paris Chamber of Commerce exam for the "diplôme de français des affaires." 
Recommended: French 31 and 32 or consent

courses.title: Femmes criminelles
courses.desc: Women criminals in French literature and film as expressed in 20th- and 21st-century texts, films, and contemporary French-language true-crime television series and podcasts. Crimes attributed to women, the social and legal responses the crimes provoke, and the specificity of criminals’ motives. How female criminals are portrayed—as evil figures, tragic heroines, morally ambiguous subjects, or wrongly accused–including the cultural, historical, and ethical frameworks that shape these representations. In French. Recommendations: FR31 and FR32, or instructor consent.

courses.title: Resistance and Collaboration in Occupied France
courses.desc: Literature and films of the French experience of Nazi Occupation to better understand the horrors of this period, the morally ambiguous stance of many in the French population, the heroic actions of the resistance, and the murderous actions of collaborators. Readings may include memoirs, novels, letters, speeches, essays, and political tracts by Hélène Berr, Lucie Aubrac, Marguerite Duras, Lucie Aubrac, Joseph Kessel, Patrick Modiano, Robert Brasillach, Vercors, Simone de Beauvoir, Pierre Drieu La Rochelle, and Hannah Arendt. Films may include Le chagrin et la pitié, L’armée des ombres, Lacombe Lucien, Au revoir les enfants, La bataille du rail. In French. Recommendations: FR31 and FR32 or instructor permission.

courses.title: Special Topics
courses.desc:
(Conducted in French.) Courses on various topics in French literature or civilization. Topics may include love, marriage, and sexuality in medieval French literature; Balzac, George Sand; Jean Giono; Marguerite Duras; Ionesco; Beckett; Nathalie Sarraute; the Oedipus myth in French literature; and others. Please see departmental website for specific details.
Recommendations: FR 31 and 32, or permission of instructor.

sections.note: Will be taught by Bastien Craipain

courses.title: Special Topics - 50 years of French television
courses.desc:
(Conducted in French.) Courses on various topics in French literature or civilization. Topics may include love, marriage, and sexuality in medieval French literature; Balzac, George Sand; Jean Giono; Marguerite Duras; Ionesco; Beckett; Nathalie Sarraute; the Oedipus myth in French literature; and others. Please see departmental website for specific details.
Recommendations: FR 31 and 32, or permission of instructor.

sections.note: This course explores French television as a space where cultural norms, political debates, and collective imaginaries are produced, negotiated, and challenged. Case studies span fifty years of programming and include variety shows, beauty pageants, political satire, sitcoms, talk shows, reality television, late-night entertainment, cartoons, serial drama, local and regional broadcasting, and the Olympic Games. Through these, we examine how television has staged and shaped conversations around immigration, secularism, class, gender, and postcolonial memory in contemporary France, while also reaching audiences across Belgium, Switzerland, and North Africa, where French-language television remains a shared cultural reference. Students will apply approaches from media studies, cultural studies, and reception theory to analyze how television circulates ideologies, manufactures emotion and consensus, frames controversy, and shapes spectatorship. We will pay particular attention to the politics of representation on screen (race, class, gender, sexuality), the role of reality television in reproducing class and gender ideologies, the economics of public vs. private broadcasting, television as an industry and as a labor market, and the recent transformations brought about by the arrival of streaming platforms like Netflix. Recommended: 2 courses taught in French above FR-0022, or instructor permission. Taught in French.

courses.desc: Corporate Finance in Global Capital Markets: This is an introductory course to corporate finance from the perspective of a company’s chief financial officer (CFO). The first part covers financial planning and budgeting, financial analysis, and short-term financial management. The second part will help you develop a valuation framework for making investment decisions (capital budgeting) for new equipment, launching new products, managing mergers and acquisitions and LBOs, and making funding/financing decisions to be coordinated with those investment decisions. Special attention is given to the cost of capital and valuing stocks, bonds, convertible debt, and preferred stocks in the context of global capital markets.

courses.title: Data Analytics and Statistical Methods
courses.desc:
Data Analytics and Statistical Methods: In 2017, The Economist declared that the world's most valuable resource is no longer oil, but data. With each passing day, more data is generated. Within these data are insights to drive operational efficiencies, solve global health emergencies, and more.

To prepare you to leverage that data, this course will focus on two approaches to data-driven decision making: visual analytics and statistical methods. The course introduces you to data analysis, combining an overview of traditional methods of statistical inference with an introduction to visual analytics. The goal of the course is to provide you with the skills to make decisions and succeed in a data-rich and increasingly data-driven world.

courses.title: International Macroeconomics
courses.desc: International Macroeconomics: This course examines the determination of income, the exchange rate, and the trade balance in economies that trade goods, services, and assets with the rest of the world. Theory is developed and employed to study current events and historical experience. You will study exchange rate determination, monetary and exchange rate policy, the causes and consequences of external imbalances, international policy coordination, financial crises, and the global capital market.

courses.title: Decision Analysis for Business
courses.desc:
Most students will find themselves in positions to make or provide advice regarding difficult business decisions in their work. This course provides the opportunity to help you develop a toolbox of analytic techniques that can be indispensable in understanding complicated problems and arriving at the best possible decision such techniques and methods.

You will learn about different types of decision models and how to choose the model that best represents the problem and tradeoffs at hand. Throughout the course, you will learn and practice these analytic techniques through examples and cases from different countries involving a wide variety of business problems. You will construct and solve these models in class and in problem sets. This course does not require a background in economics, statistics, or advanced mathematics.

courses.desc: (Cross-listed as WGSS 70) The Grimm brothers as nineteenth-century collectors and authors. Significant focus on women’s issues. In English. Upper-level offering of GER 70. Extra assignments and class meetings in German. Recommendation: One of GER 22, 34, 44, or 61. courses.title: A Pact With the Devil: Faust's Modernity
courses.desc: How far would we go—making a pact with the devil—to attain power, knowledge, or (sexual) pleasure? Examination of Goethe's "Faust" and its resonances in literature (Bulgakov, Mann), visual arts, and film (Delacroix, Murnau), and music (Gounod, Berlioz), from the 19th through the 21st centuries. Challenges students to reflect on the ethical (or unethical?) underpinnings of modernity by opening a window onto the rich cultural tradition of "Faust" across artistic genres and media. In English. No prerequisites.

courses.desc: Computational methods and tools to both acquire new urban data from social media, crowdsourcing, and sensor networks, and using these tools to represent, understand, and visualize complex urban environments. courses.desc: The aim of this year-long lab is to link the leadership and negotiation skills introduced in the first residency and subsequent terms to the strategies and practices of GMAP students themselves. Our hope is that armed with the knowledge of their own leadership styles and negotiation strategies, they will leave Fletcher with a firm set of goals and action steps that will assist them in achieving their vision of a meaningful career.

courses.title: Cyber Policy Analysis and Risk Management
courses.desc: Looks at cyber policy, risk management, and compliance challenges facing global leaders today, ranging from data breaches and cyber attacks to issues of online speech, censorship, and intermediary liability. It will cover tools for how organizations manage cyber risk, as well as approaches to crafting both public and private sector cybersecurity policies with a particular focus on dealing with an evolving threat landscape and designing realistic, tech-informed policy.

courses.title: The International Legal System
courses.desc: This course will aim to provide participants with a handle on public international law extending to the basic structure and foundational principles that govern the interactions between the major participants in international law, most especially as they pertain to states and to international organizations. The course is designed to address two related objectives. First, it seeks to avail students of a workable framework to enable them to access and understand the major principles and rules governing international relations. Second, it also aims to provide students with skills in legal research, reasoning, argumentation and decision making in the context of international law and relations. Although anchored in international law, this course will be suitable for a multi-disciplinary cohort.

sections.attrs: Fletcher - This course is for GMAP students only.

courses.title: Global Security Governance: International Law and Institutions
courses.desc: Focuses on the law and practice of global governance institutions in the field of peace and security. It introduces the concept of global governance and the various institutions involved: formal inter-governmental organizations (such as the United Nations); informal inter-governmental institutions (such as the G-20); non-governmental actors (both NGOs and business); and public-private partnerships. The course then turns to selected issue areas: the use force, conflict management, human security, and health security. In each issue area, we look at institutions, law, and practice – painting a picture of how global governance actually functions.

The course is intended to help you develop your own personal style by deepening your understanding of the persuasive tools, recommendations, refutations, modes of analysis, and variations in audiences that motivate listeners to turn business, policy and diplomacy ideas into action.

courses.desc: The goals of this course are to understand the intersection of complexity theory in addressing global environmental challenges; assess and compare the role that leadership can play in solving environmental problems; explore three of the most pressing environmental challenges: plastics, climate, and water; learn and apply three types of skills that leaders will use regardless of sector in addressing these and similar challenges.

Readings and hands-on projects explore visual meaning, legibility, and the complexities of seeing.

Relevant works, artists, and technologies will be explored through readings, lectures, and demos. Free and open-source software, Adobe CC, and some coding will be used.

Key course components include:
Textual Fluency: Intensive reading of original Greek texts, supported by English translations for context.
Metrics: A deep dive into the mechanics of Greek verse, teaching students how to scan and appreciate the aural dimensions of the plays.
Modern Methodology: An introduction to the critical use of digital humanities tools, equipping students with 21st-century research methods for classical studies.

courses.title: History Of Ancient Greece
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CLS 37.) The historical development of ancient Greece and the interaction of society, politics, and culture in Greek civilization, from the Mycenaean civilization commemorated by Homer to the conquests of Alexander the Great and the diffusion of the Greek way of life in the succeeding Hellenistic Age. Special attention given to the relationship of the Greeks to other peoples of the ancient Mediterranean and Near East and to examination of literary and documentary sources. Fall.

sections.note:
8 seats reserved for CAP advising.

The ancient Greek world was never a single country, empire, or people—and that is precisely what makes it so influential. From Bronze Age palace societies and warrior-kings to small city-states experimenting with democracy, philosophy, and art, Greek societies developed ways of living together that continue to shape how we think about politics, culture, and human possibility.
This course explores the society, economy, material culture, and legacy of the Greek world from the Bronze Age through the rise of Roman power. Rather than telling a simple story of “Greek greatness,” we will ask how real communities—farmers, traders, soldiers, women, enslaved people, and elites—organized their lives in environments that were often harsh, fragmented, and unstable. Greece was a world of limited resources, fierce competition, and constant interaction with neighbors across the Mediterranean. Out of these pressures emerged remarkable creativity in politics, art, religion, and thought.
We will move across time and space: from the palaces of Mycenae to the marketplaces of classical Athens, from rural sanctuaries to overseas colonies, from the dramas staged in city theaters to the economic networks that linked Greek communities to Egypt, Anatolia, and Italy. Archaeology and material evidence—buildings, pottery, inscriptions, coins, and landscapes—will be just as important as literary texts, helping us see how Greeks actually lived, worked, worshipped, and imagined their place in the world.
A central theme of the course is connection. Greek history cannot be understood in isolation. The Greek world was shaped by exchange, migration, conflict, and borrowing. Its achievements were not the product of timeless ideals but of historical choices made in specific social and economic conditions. Just as important, Greek culture did not end when Greece lost its political independence. Instead, it was transformed, adapted, and carried forward—especially under Roman rule—becoming one of the foundations of later Mediterranean and European civilizations.

courses.title: Special Topics - What is History
courses.desc: Please see departmental website for detailed course information. http://ase.tufts.edu/history

sections.note: What is History? There are many answers to this question and many of those answers depend on individual views and experiences. In this class we will try to understand the challenges faced by the historian and to try and figure out what history actually represents. Who tells the story? How do they tell it? What biases are in play? How do the times a historian writes in shape their attitudes? Does the historian make the history or does the history shape the historian? By the end of the semester, you will have a better sense of your own view of history as well as the power and responsibility that comes with telling and understanding history, the story of humanity.

sections.note: The Mau Mau War in 1950s Kenya was one of the bloodiest chapters in the history of the British Empire after World War Two. This foundation seminar examines the different theoretical and methodological approaches that historians have employed to study the war, including feminism, Marxism, and peasant studies. It also explores the wide variety of sources that exist for the war, such as films, novels, news reports, colonial records, and the memoirs of Mau Mau guerrillas, government troops, and European settlers. The seminar thus introduces students to the historian’s craft by teaching them how to critically analyze primary and secondary sources, how to assess the validity of competing historical narratives, and how to develop new avenues of research on a widely studied topic.

courses.title: Advanced Special Topics, North America - W.E.B. Du Bois and the Problem of the Color Line
courses.desc: Please see departmental website for detailed course description.

sections.note:
7 seats reserved for CAP advising 

W.E.B. Du Bois and the Problem of the Color Line 

In 1903, W.E.B. Du Bois wrote that "the problem of the twentieth century is the color line." By that time, Du Bois had already published multiple works examining the lived experiences and political struggles of Black people in the United States. He continued to write on these topics for the nearly sixty years. This course examines the interdisciplinary scholarship of W.E.B. Du Bois. Reading across his sociological, historical, and literary works, we will study how he employed multiple research methods and genres of writing to explore how Black people in the United States understood, experienced, and sought to redress "the color line." Readings will include fiction and non-fiction books, essays, poems, and newspaper articles written by Du Bois.

courses.title: Independent Study, World/transregional - Resource Politics
courses.desc: Please see departmental website for detailed course information.

sections.note:
Class meets on the following dates: 9/16, 9/30, 10/14, 10/28, 11/18, 12/2 
 
FULL TITLE: Looting or Livelihood: Resource Politics, from Forests to Fossils 

Why did colonial governments in Madagascar call it arson when indigenous communities practiced the same slash-and-burn agriculture they had for centuries? Why is digging up fossils treated as looting in Argentina, while in Morocco it employs tens of thousands of workers in the country's poorest province? Why does fishing, foraging, or farming a shared resource become “theft” once someone declares it public property? 
 
This reading group considers who makes these decisions, and how they get made. We will trace diverse cases where practices become labelled as poaching or profiteering, and test those interpretations against competing arguments. What does the case for resource extraction and market access look like across these case studies? What about the defense of indigenous practices, the repudiation of environmental degradation, or opposition to the loss of cultural heritage? Do artifacts, as Indiana Jones claims, belong in a museum? If they do, should it matter whether that museum has the resources to preserve them? Meeting every other week, we will consider one case of resource use and ownership to explore competing interpretations on what is at stake.

courses.desc: Please see departmental website for specific details.

sections.note: This course will explore the profound transformation of global life that came in the course of the twentieth century. World Wars, Cold Wars, and political upheaval were dramatic moments but they occurred against a backdrop of tectonic cultural, economic, and technological change. These diverse forces and along with the power of ideas and ideology reframed how people lived or suggested how they might live. The scope of these changes, that reached all corners of the globe, in international affairs as well as within particular societies will be investigated as a means to give students a foundation to conduct their own research project. The class will provide instruction in research methods by extending student understanding of primary and secondary research materials as means to construct grounded historical analysis. The course will shape undergraduate research and writing skills with a semester long focus on a project of the student’s choosing.

courses.title: Research Seminar, North America - Slavery&Tufts: Archival Rsrch
courses.desc: Please see departmental website for detailed course information.

sections.note: Since its founding in 1853, Tufts University has been a center of progressive education with deep ties to Universalist and anti-slavery traditions. Yet, this history has obscured the university's ties to the Atlantic slave trade, to colonial exploitation, and to the African American and Afro-Native communities in Medford and Boston. Tufts' Slavery, Colonialism, and their Legacies Project explores this complex history, as part of a recent wave of universities reckoning with their slave-owning past. This class, co-taught by scholars spearheading the project, provides students an opportunity to study Tufts' historic ties to slavery and colonialism through archival research and intense engagement with the SCL research team.

Major topics and themes include the varied nature and outcomes of combat on the different fronts, civilian experience of the war, the impact of the war on Europe’s colonies, the problematic peace settlement, and the cultural, psychological, and political consequences of the conflict. The course aims to develop students’ research and writing skills by guiding them through a semester long project that culminates in an oral presentation and a 20-25 page capstone paper based on primary source research.

courses.title: Introduction to Literary and Cultural Studies
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ILVS 60) An introduction to the major critical and theoretical approaches for the study of literatures and cultures, especially of foreign cultures. Issues studied include: How do we analyze cultural productions, whether our own or those of other societies? What do we learn in comparing texts from different cultures with each other? courses.desc: Special topics in the humanities. Please see departmental website for specific details.

sections.attrs: BFA-Humanities|BFA-Language/Culture|East Asian Cult/Lang-Diasporas|East Asian Cult/Lang-Reg Orign|LA-Distribution-Humanities|SoE-HASS|SoE-HASS-Humanities|World Civilization Requirement
sections.note:
This course combines film, poetry and fantasy literature to journey into one of the most age-old and important issues in Japanese culture: How should humans relate to the natural world? Japanese culture has answered this question in a myriad of creative ways. The great Zen poet Matsuo Basho’s most famous poem depicts, from a subtly human perspective, a non-human setting brought to life by “the sound of the water.” In modern times what westerners refer to as “Green Shinto” attempts to construct a positive, even activist, engagement with nature, based on ancient indigenous beliefs. 
The course examines the role animism and the environment have played across Japanese culture and history, beginning with an exploration of Shinto and Japan’s other main religion, Buddhism, in relation to these issues. We will start with medieval Zen poetry but the bulk of the course will concentrate on the 20th and 21st century, starting with a look at the prewar writer Miyazawa Kenji’s poetry and fantasy, analyzing how Miyazawa connects literature with science in visions such as his concept of the “blue illuminations” of molecular energy. Moving on to post war films, we will look at Imamura Taihei’s The Ballad of Narayama, with its searing portrait of cycles of life and death in a mountain village, and Shinkai Makoto’s elegiac treatment of natural disaster and trauma, Your Name. Works from Studio Ghibli will include Nausicaa of the Valley of the Wind, Princess Mononoke, Ponyo and Pompoko and we will discuss the role of animation in defamiliarizing the natural environment.

courses.title: Special Topics - Iran: Modern Lit. & Culture
courses.desc: Special topics in the humanities. Please see departmental website for specific details.

sections.note: This course presents an introduction to the study of the literary and visual cultures of modern Iran (from the 19th century to the present day). Through engaging with a wide range of literary, visual, and cinematic texts, the course charts a path exploring the role of cultural expression as an arena of political and social resistance—not only to variety of forms of domestic authority (political tyranny, patriarchy, religious theocracy) but also to the influence and hegemony of colonial and imperialist forces. The course begins with the early literary and visual cultural innovations that fed into the revolutionary forces of the 1906 Constitutional Revolution, then explores the rise of nationalist and anti colonialist ideals expressed in literary and visual arts in the mid-20th century, to the variety of voices that came together in the 1979 revolution, and ends with more contemporary expressions of cultural resistance such as the Women Life Freedom movement and the 2026 uprising. Alongside the reading and viewing of primary texts—short stories, poems, novels, works of visual art, cinema—we will read secondary works of cultural and social theory that address how societies foster cultures of resistance to authoritarianism and repression. In particular. we will look to theorists and critics from Iran to provide frameworks for the study and analysis of the primary texts in the course.

courses.title: The International Legal Order
courses.desc: This introductory course deals with structural aspects of the international legal system, including the jurisprudence of international law and differing cultural and philosophical perspectives; the history of the international legal system; customary international law; treaty law; statehood and recognition; the United Nations and international organizations; and the relationship of the international legal system to domestic legal systems, using the United States as a primary example.

courses.title: International Human Rights Law
courses.desc: This course will trace the legal and political development of international human rights law. It will begin by exploring the philosophical bases of this body of law in the context of the positivist legal tradition of the 19th and early 20th centuries. It will examine the nature and structure of the international legal system, and provide an overview of the early development of international human rights law within the context of the evolution of that system. The course will focus on the scope and substance of modern human rights law, and will analyze the application of these standards in the context of case studies encompassing issues of hate speech, extraterritorial application of human rights law, and discrimination on the basis of sex and sexual orientation. It will also survey the extensive array of human rights mechanisms created under the auspices of the UN and regional intergovernmental organizations. In addition, the course will provide a brief introduction to related areas of international law, including the international law of armed conflict (also known as international humanitarian law) and international criminal law in the strict sense, and the interaction of these bodies of law with international human rights law. The format of the course will consist primarily of lectures, structured discussion, and role-playing activities.

courses.title: International Humanitarian Law
courses.desc: This seminar offers an introduction to international humanitarian law, the body of law regulating armed conflicts. It retraces its evolution, focusing on efforts to mitigate human suffering in war and on the protection of civilians. It considers the challenges posed to the application of IHL by the changing nature of armed conflicts. The topics discussed include: the principles underpinning IHL, the definition and types of armed conflicts, the distinction between combatants and civilians, the regulation of private military and security companies, humanitarian action during armed conflict, the use of child-soldiers, rape as a ‘weapon of war,’ and other war crimes.

courses.title: International Law and Migration
courses.desc: The number of displaced persons worldwide has reached record highs, and practitioners and policymakers working in situations of humanitarian crisis are confronted with increasingly complex legal, policy, and practical challenges related to displacement. In particular, migration flows are more than ever characterized by overlap between contexts and categories of persons with heightened vulnerabilities and protection needs. As a law course, it will focus on the analysis of relevant international legal frameworks applicable to migration and displacement, including international refugee law, international human rights law, international humanitarian law, international criminal law (in both the general and strict senses), the law of the sea, and international labor law. It will also examine the practice of relevant international organizations, and will consider the significance of the recently adopted Global Compact on Refugees and Global Compact on Migration and their follow-up mechanisms. The course will consider application of the above frameworks in the context of specific phenomena, including migration by sea, human trafficking, individuals fleeing violence perpetrated by non-State actors, the displacement of individuals internally and within transit countries, as well as the interface between international law and select domestic asylum systems.

courses.title: International Organizations
courses.desc: This course provides an introduction to the field, focusing on the interaction between international law and politics in international organizations. It begins by briefly reviewing theories of global governance and international institutions, from the perspective of both international law and international relations. It then provides an overview of the United Nations system, the European Union and other regional organizations. We then turn to a number of cross-cutting legal and institutional issues, including law-making, interpretation of the law, and the role of the executive head of an international organization. The bulk of the course is devoted to the substantive work of international organizations in peace and security, human rights, humanitarian affairs, development and the environment. The course concludes with several sessions on reform, focusing on the legitimacy of the existing institutional architecture and new models of global governance.

courses.title: International Environmental Law and Diplomacy
courses.desc: International environmental challenges rank among the most serious threats to peace, security, and sustainable development. This course examines how the international community is responding, focusing on the major international treaties and diplomatic initiatives of today. The course surveys global action on climate change, biodiversity loss, terrestrial and ocean conservation, ozone depletion, air and marine pollution, plastics, and hazardous chemicals. The course also examines cross-cutting themes, including the structure and patterns in environmental geopolitics, law and diplomacy, the role of foreign aid and private capital, links between trade and environmental policy, and emerging ideas relating to environmental justice. Thematic discussions are often explored in the context of the climate crisis, the most active and high-profile area of environmental diplomacy. The course includes a simulated international negotiating session that is timed to preview the outcomes of the annual global climate summit, offering students a chance to compare their solutions to those in the real world. The course is hybrid, with in-person discussions lead by the professor and virtual meetings featuring outstanding guest lecturers (environmental diplomats, legal experts, and advocates) from around the world.

courses.title: International Investment Law
courses.desc: This course offers an advanced introduction to the law of foreign investment, one of the most dynamic and yet contested areas of international law. It provides an overview of domestic and international law mechanisms for the protection of foreign capital, as well as the emerging network of soft law instruments relevant for foreign investment. The focal point of the course lies in the law of investment treaties. Students will become familiar with the notions of “investment” and “investor”, substantive standards of investment protection (e.g. the guarantee of a “fair and equitable treatment” and protection against expropriation), and legal devices striking a balance between the interests of foreign investors and the public interest (e.g. environmental and national security exceptions). The course draws particular attention to the settlement of investment disputes. It addresses key concepts of investor-State arbitration, such as jurisdiction of investment tribunals, admissibility of claims, applicable law, stages of the proceedings, and recognition and enforcement of arbitral awards. The final part of the course is devoted to the movements of reform and change in international investment law. Students will engage in ongoing debates about the future of international investment law and discuss competing reform agendas from both the global south and the global north.

courses.title: International Law and Humanitarian Assistance
courses.desc: This course provides the basic introduction to international law and the international legal system as a foundation for understanding the international regulation of humanitarian assistance. It is aimed at developing an understanding of the overall structure and processes of public international law and of the political contexts within which international law operates. It will examine foundational concepts and frameworks, including the nature and structure of the international legal system, sources of international law, the law of treaties, and international legal personhood (with a focus on states). It will then provide an overview of three substantive areas of international law – the jus ad bellum (the rules regulating recourse to the use of armed force), the jus in bello (the law of armed conflict, aka international humanitarian law), and international human rights law.

courses.title: Comparative Constitutional Law
courses.desc: This course explores topics—from constitutional design to fundamental rights—arising in the comparative study of constitutional law globally in a variety of systems, including new and older constitutional democracies, as well as autocratic regimes. Course readings will go beyond the field’s dominant focus on North American and European constitutional systems to also include jurisdictions from the Global South. Class sessions are a mixture of lecture, discussion, student presentations, and debates.

courses.title: Black World Literature
courses.desc: (Cross-listed w/ENG 20 and AFR 22) Fiction, poetry, and drama written principally in English by black writers from Africa, the Caribbean, and South America. Relation of modern black writing to African folk literature, classical Greek drama, European existentialism, and other contexts. Attention to specific geographical areas illustrating the transition from traditional tribal values and forms of expression to the attempted accommodations to colonialism and industrialism. All works are read in English.

courses.title: Ancient Egypt - Civ of The Nile & Near East
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as HIST 76, CLS 26, and ARCH 26) Survey of roughly 4,000 years of ancient Egyptian and Near Eastern civilization spanning c. 3,200 BCE to 651 CE. Analysis of the interrelations between art, architecture, history, and ideology, as preserved in material culture, inscriptions, and literary texts: pyramids, temples, tombs, settlements and cities, exceptional masterpieces and artifacts of daily life. Multiple excursions into religion, diplomacy, hieroglyphic writing, and artistic technique. Examination of the internal and external relations of Egypt in the context of a world system that included the kingdoms and empires of the Near East and the Mediterranean: from the Sumerians, Assyrians, Hittites, and Babylonians, to the Achaemenid Persian Empire, Alexander the Great, and the Imperium Romanum. Includes a field trip to the collections of the Museum of Fine Arts.

Auden, with particular focus on the role of poetry during times of cultural upheaval and uncertainty. Examination of the relationship between poetic form, historical context, and personal experience, including questions of ethnicity and sexuality. No prior knowledge of poetry required.

courses.title: Law and Rights in the Ancient World
courses.desc: (Cross-listed w/ HIST 16, HIST 119, CLS 73 & CLS 173) Introduction to the complex and intersecting practices of law and conceptions of personal rights in the ancient world from the organization of states in the Near East to the end of antiquity: c. 3,200 BCE to 800 CE; exploration of the role of social ideology and religion in recursively shaping how the Egyptians, Babylonians, Greeks, Romans, Chinese and others negotiated the formulation and practice of law and concepts of social rights: status, morality, social duty, religion, gender, and civic/personal identity. Extensive and intensive examination of primary evidence and secondary scholarship involving the close reading of ancient texts and material culture to investigate the role of law and rights in the ancient world: civil law, customary law, contract law, statutory law and decrees, constitutions, criminal process, treaties, oratory, and legal training. No prerequisite.

courses.title: Art of the Moving Image
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as FMS 1 & TPS 20) Exploration of cinema's basic aesthetic characteristics: its stylistic features, such as editing, cinematography, and sound, as well as its major narrative and non-narrative forms: mainstream and avant-garde, fiction and non-fiction, narrative and non-narrative, black-and-white and color, silent and sound. Discussion of the extent to which cinema's aesthetic features are shared by television, as well as what is artistically distinctive about television. Theoretical concepts relevant to moving image art, principally genre, authorship, and character identification.

courses.title: Global History of Cinema
courses.desc: (Cross-listed w/FMS 2) History of cinema beginning with the emergence of the technologies for making and exhibiting films around 1894 and the major genres of early cinema (1895-1904); the development of "classical" narrative film in the US in the 1900s and 1910s; the creation of alternatives to classical cinematic storytelling in the 1920s in France, Germany, the Soviet Union and elsewhere; the rise of documentary and experimental film; and the coming of synchronized sound in the late 1920s. European responses to the increasing political turmoil in the lead-up to WWII in the 1930s; Japanese popular traditions of filmmaking, the impact of WWII on film history; the emergence of Italian Neo-Realism and "modernist" art cinema in the late 1940s and 1950s; the New Waves of the late 1950s; and political modernist, post-colonial, feminist and other radical forms of filmmaking that arose in response to the political crises of the 1960s. Survey of world cinema since the 1970s, focusing on the changes that have occurred in mainstream Hollywood filmmaking and the work of filmmakers in Hong Kong and other non-western countries.

courses.title: Introduction to Media Culture and Theory
courses.desc: (Cross-listed with TPS 22 and FMS 101) Qualitative media studies, its history, intellectual development, and theoretical milestones. Introduction to study of popular media culture. Covers major areas of study, theoretical principles, methodologies, and debates that have shaped popular media studies. Theoretical approaches to issues and case studies (including representation, labor and authorship, contemporary media convergence, fandom and participatory culture, media globalization, reality television, game studies, industry research and more). Students acquire knowledge of the major theories that define the field and contemporary application of these theories in critical engagements with media texts and practices.

courses.title: Introduction to Literary and Cultural Studies
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ILCS 70) An introduction to the major critical and theoretical approaches for the study of literatures and cultures, especially of foreign cultures. Issues studied include: How do we analyze cultural productions, whether our own or those of other societies? What do we learn in comparing texts from different cultures with each other? What is the value of literature, and how do we define it? How do cultural productions allow us to understand social issues, and to what extent does it contribute to social change? How can we be critical yet ethical producers and consumers of literature and other cultural productions in an world that is increasingly global?

courses.title: Television in the Age of Change
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as FMS 165 & TPS 121) Examines how new technologies and shifting viewing habits are transforming television; how storytelling is changing in light of TV’s industrial and technological evolution and our global, networked, media environment; and how contemporary viewing habits are reshaping our theories of audiences, styles, and viewing pleasures. Focuses on story creation, changing genres, programming conventions and global trends, shifting technologies, social media, TV fans, and streaming content—and how all these influence television narratives and our media culture.

courses.title: Classical Mythology
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CLS 75) Exploration of the world of Greco-Roman mythology and its intersections with art, ideology, and ritual. Examination of the stories of the gods and heroes as cognitive tools for interrogating the essential questions of being human: justice and morality, fate and identity, humor and heroism, suffering and triumph – the meaning of life. Focus on how ancient myth has remained a powerful source of inspiration for millennia, informing the art and narratives of the Renaissance to the present.

Readings from Baudrillard, Benjamin, Butler, Derrida, Foucault, Haraway, Lacan, and ¿i¿ek , along with films by Cameron, Gilliam, Polanski, Scott, the Wachowski brothers, and Welles.

courses.desc: This is a survey based on lectures, texts, problem-solving and small group tutorials. courses.title: Elementary Italian I
courses.desc: Development of basic language skills. Introduction to Italian culture and fundamental grammar structures with emphasis on speaking, listening comprehension, and short writing assignments. Conducted in Italian.

courses.title: Intermediate Italian I
courses.desc:
Continued study of grammar and syntax with emphasis on more advanced structural principles. More extensive readings on cultural, social, and literary topics and the viewing of an epic film in episodes will form the basis for class discussions and activities. Students are required to register for a recitation section that consists of a weekly 40-minute conversation group. Conducted in Italian. 
Recommendations: Italian 002 or consent.

courses.title: Italian Language through Culture I
courses.desc:
Improve written and oral expression in Italian through the study of contemporary Italian culture and society. Specific topics of current interest (immigration, youth and women's voices, and the national character) will also be studied through films, narrative, and the integral reading of a novel. Emphasis on expanding vocabulary, reviewing advanced grammatical structures, improving and refining analytical, interpretive, and presentational skills. Class discussions, oral presentations, writing assignments, three tests, and a final paper. Conducted in Italian. 
Recommendations: Italian 0004 or equivalent, or consent.

courses.title: Interwoven Threads of Italian Cultural Narratives
courses.desc: Italy’s cultural transformation from the 18th century to the present, examining how cultural works reflect and respond to key historical and societal changes. Topics may include the effects of social resistance, national unification, migration, and the evolving representation of gender and nature. Analyze and contextualize ideas by engaging diverse cultural expressions. Interdisciplinary approach provides a deeper understanding of Italy’s modern identity, encouraging critical thinking and effective communication. In Italian. Prerequisites: ITAL 21, ITAL 22, or instructor permission.

courses.title: Dante's Inferno
courses.desc: An intensive study of Dante's Inferno, read in English translation with facing Italian text.

courses.title: Italian Foodways: Culinary & Cultural (R)Evolution
courses.desc: historical, cultural, and social overview of foodways in Italy. National culinary identity and its effects on food production, preparation, consumption, and exportation. Cultural and economic significance of regional specialties officially protected by the European Union. Health benefits and social practices related to the Mediterranean diet and to nutrition in the Italian “blue zones.” Traditional production techniques, current food systems, and their place in the environment during the era of climate change. Sustainable practices and food security initiatives; social justice; immigration and food evolution; physical and mental health. Readings, podcasts, and movies. Taught in English. No prerequisites.

courses.title: Special Topics - Japanese Animism/Environment
courses.desc: Courses on selected themes and authors. Conducted in English. Please see departmental website for specific details: http://ase.tufts.edu/grall/japanese/.

sections.attrs: BFA-Humanities|BFA-Language/Culture|East Asian Cult/Lang-Diasporas|East Asian Cult/Lang-Reg Orign|LA-Distribution-Humanities|SoE-HASS|SoE-HASS-Humanities|World Civilization Requirement
sections.note:
This course combines film, poetry and fantasy literature to journey into one of the most age-old and important issues in Japanese culture: How should humans relate to the natural world? Japanese culture has answered this question in a myriad of creative ways. The great Zen poet Matsuo Basho’s most famous poem depicts, from a subtly human perspective, a non-human setting brought to life by “the sound of the water.” In modern times what westerners refer to as “Green Shinto” attempts to construct a positive, even activist, engagement with nature, based on ancient indigenous beliefs. 
The course examines the role animism and the environment have played across Japanese culture and history, beginning with an exploration of Shinto and Japan’s other main religion, Buddhism, in relation to these issues. We will start with medieval Zen poetry but the bulk of the course will concentrate on the 20th and 21st century, starting with a look at the prewar writer Miyazawa Kenji’s poetry and fantasy, analyzing how Miyazawa connects literature with science in visions such as his concept of the “blue illuminations” of molecular energy. Moving on to post war films, we will look at Imamura Taihei’s The Ballad of Narayama, with its searing portrait of cycles of life and death in a mountain village, and Shinkai Makoto’s elegiac treatment of natural disaster and trauma, Your Name. Works from Studio Ghibli will include Nausicaa of the Valley of the Wind, Princess Mononoke, Ponyo and Pompoko and we will discuss the role of animation in defamiliarizing the natural environment.

courses.title: Special Topics - Genji and Heian Female Culture
courses.desc: Courses on selected themes and authors. Conducted in English. Please see departmental website for specific details: http://ase.tufts.edu/grall/japanese/.

sections.attrs: BFA-Humanities|BFA-Language/Culture|East Asian Cult/Lang-Diasporas|East Asian Cult/Lang-Reg Orign|LA-Distribution-Humanities|SoE-HASS|SoE-HASS-Humanities|World Civilization Requirement
sections.note: This course examines the 10th century masterpiece The Tale of Genji, the world’s first psychological novel and the first major novel ever written by a woman. Although over a thousand years old, Genji is in some ways shockingly contemporary, dealing with the problematic power dynamics between the sexes and even suggesting queer readings in a narrative that mixes powerful realism and stunning supernatural fantasy. The first part of the course involves a close reading of excerpts from the text in the context of the glittering world of the Heian court of Japan, where the novel is set. The final part of the semester we will look at the evolving response to Genji, from its initial appearance to 21st century iterations such as movies and manga. Issues and themes to be examined include gender dynamics, abjection, female resistance, women and the supernatural, reception theory, queer theory, spatial poetics and the role of the romance and aesthetics.

courses.title: Imagining The Holocaust On Stage And Screen
courses.desc: (Cross-listed w/FMS 45, TPS 25, & TPS 125) Plays and films dealing with the Holocaust, From Nazi-era propaganda to contemporary reflections on genocide. Special emphasis on the ethics of Holocaust represented and the responsibilities of artists (and audiences) who engage the Holocaust story. Texts include such plays as Camp Comedy, Ghetto, Kindertransport, Good, Bent, Who Will Carry the World?, and Annulla, as well as critical and theoretical readings. Triumph of the Will, Night and Fog, The Architecture of Doom, Partisans of Vilna, The Boat is Full, My Mother's Courage, Schindler's List, Life is Beautiful and Shoah are among the feature films and documentaries considered. (Graduate Students should register for TPS 125).

courses.title: Religious, Philosophical Roots of Modern World 1
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as MDVL 71, CVS 53, PHIL 29, CLS 29 and REL 29) Major religious and philosophical thinkers and concepts that played roles in the emergence of the modern world: Plato and Aristotle; Jewish, Christian, and Muslim scripture and theologians who merged their religions with the Greek tradition; the Ptolemaic universe and the Great Chain of Being. Medieval Jews, Christians, and Muslims saw themselves as having a privileged and objective place in a divinely-created and -ordered cosmos that was young, small, and centered on the earth.

sections.note:

courses.desc: (Cross-listed as REL 18 and HEB 70) Judaism as a diverse textual tradition and lived religion, with a focus on beliefs, ethics, and rituals. sections.note: This course surveys Jewish history from the Late Second Temple period to the mid-twentieth century. It begins with the emergence of rabbinic Judaism and Jewish life under Christian and Muslim rule, then examines the transformative ruptures of modernity, including political emancipation, religious reform, and nationalism, culminating in the Holocaust and the establishment of the State of Israel. Through close analysis of primary sources, students will learn how the modern Jewish world developed out of its premodern foundations.

courses.title: Introduction to Jewish Mysticism
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as REL 182 and HEB 172) Overview of the intellectual history of Kabbalah and Jewish Mysticism. courses.title: Special Topics - Modern Israel: Politics & Soc
courses.desc: For advanced and graduate students.Please see departmental website for specific details.

sections.note: This course examines Israeli politics, government, and society since the establishment of the state in 1948 to contemporary developments. The aims of the course are to provide students with a broad understanding of the Israeli state and society, situating these in comparative perspectives. Following an introduction to the Israeli case, the course is divided into three broad sections: Part 1: Israeli institutions, the government, and the economy, explores the development of the Israeli democracy; Part 2: Israeli social fabric and cleavages, focuses on societal levels, including majority-minority dynamics, secular-religious divides, and other social developments; Part 3: Wars, security, and the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, focuses on the different conflicts Israel has been engaged in, culminating in the current Israel- Hamas War. Throughout the course students are encouraged to consider what are some of the unique characteristics of the Israeli case as well as what are more common and comparable features. Students are also encouraged to take an active interest in ongoing developments in Israel through the international established media and social media, considering the ways in which many of the current challenges facing the Israeli state and society have their roots in historic processes and developments.

courses.title: Special Topics - Terrorism & Political Violence in the Middle East
courses.desc: For advanced and graduate students.Please see departmental website for specific details.

sections.note:
This course examines the multidimensional facets of political violence and terrorism. Its aims are to challenge conventional thoughts about such radical mobilization, exposing students to the multiple definitions, historical progression, and political and sociological developments of terrorism throughout the past centuries. Drawing on a range of historic and current examples from the Middle East, we will tackle a variety of questions on the subject, including: What are the differences between political violence, guerilla warfare, terrorism, and international warfare, and why do such distinctions matter? Are there differences between religious and non-religious terrorism and political violence? What are the historic developments that led to the rise of religious terrorism at the end of the 20th century, and is it still on the rise? Who are the major terror groups that have operated in the Middle East during the past decades, and which have been more successful in advancing their cause? 
The course is divided into three sections. The first focuses on definitions of terrorism, exploring how terror groups operate and taking students through a historical rundown of modern terrorism over the 20th and 21st centuries. The second focuses on theories explaining groups’ and individuals’ use of terrorism and political violence, emphasizing where different theories agree and where they come to drastically different conclusions. The third section covers a range of select case studies of different groups using such tactics, analyzing the internationalization processes of terrorism and comparing ideological worldviews, violent mobilization, and respective successes and failures. By the conclusion of the course, students will have a broad-based understanding of how terrorism and violent mobilization have influenced various political processes throughout the 20th and 21st centuries, gaining the tools to analyze such mobilization as it continues to unfold.
