courses.title: Leadership, Advocacy & Ethics in Occupational Therapy
courses.desc: Leadership theories relative to occupational therapy practice and administration, including change process. Advocacy models will be discussed at the individual, systems, and populations levels. The AOTA Code of Ethics will be addressed through case studies. Complete CITI training. Scholarship within the field of occupational therapy will also be highlighted. Synchronous (75%); asynchronous (25%)

courses.title: Occupational Justice: Diversity Equity Inclusion
courses.desc: Concepts of occupational justice include the understanding that peoples' occupations occur within multiple contexts, including social environments. Practitioners work with clients for whom barriers of social injustice, including ableism, impact their ability to perform their wanted and needed occupations. Discussion of and reflection on social issues, intersections of identities & disability, and impact to the occupational therapy evaluation process; intervention choices; and advocacy for persons, systems, and populations.

courses.title: Doctoral Continuation Part Time
courses.desc: Part-time. Please see departmental website for specific details.

courses.title: Doctoral Continuation Full Time
courses.desc: Full-time. Please see departmental website for specific details.

courses.title: Internal Medicine III
courses.desc: This course will focus on diseases of the gastrointestinal, renal, and rheumatologic systems. The pathophysiology, presentation, diagnosis, treatment, and prevention of diseases involving these topics will be discussed.

courses.title: OB/GYN
courses.desc: This course covers the spectrum of reproduction, conception, prenatal care, labor and delivery, and postnatal care. Students will learn the evaluation and management of core OB/GYN health care relating to the reproductive tract, including important aspects of history taking, physical examination, laboratory and imaging assessment of obstetric and/or gynecological patients, application of current concepts in management of diseases and pathologies, family planning, screening, and early detection of cancer and other diseases. The process of delivery and complications of delivery will also be discussed.

courses.title: Evidence-Based Medicine
courses.desc: This course introduces students to the knowledge, skills, and abilities necessary to be informed practitioners of evidence-based medicine to include generating clinical questions, conducting literature searches, and appraising and applying medical literature to clinical scenarios. Additionally, students will be introduced to common study designs and statistical analyses, as well as biases commonly encountered in the medical literature. This course will serve as the foundation for completion of their clinical year capstone project.

courses.title: Principles of Neuroscience
courses.desc: This course emphasizes the importance of the medical interview and the neurological examination to make neurologic diagnoses. During this course, physical examination skills learned thus far will be reinforced, with particular emphasis on the neurological examination. The signs, symptoms, and pathophysiology of neurologic diseases commonly encountered in primary care, internal medicine, and emergency medicine will be reviewed. Appropriate use and interpretation of diagnostic testing, including radiographic imaging and laboratories, will be explained.

instructors: Jennifer Carew Patoulidis, Megan Elizabeth Lee Thoren

courses.title: Pediatrics
courses.desc: This course provides the foundation of knowledge in pediatric health and organ-specific issues related to this patient population. Normal child growth and development and its aberration, as well as the importance of childhood immunizations, will be discussed. Additionally, the recognition of common childhood diseases of each organ system will be emphasized, as will diagnosis and management of common childhood diseases. In this course, emphasis is placed on addressing pediatric respiratory, cardiovascular, renal, and gastrointestinal illnesses and emergencies, as well as infectious diseases, cancer/hematologic disorders, pediatric ENT and ophthalmology, and endocrinology. Pertinent concepts related to child abuse/neglect, ADHD, and autism spectrum disorder will be covered as well.

courses.title: Orthopedics
courses.desc: This course will cover the diagnosis and management of common orthopedic conditions and orthopedic emergencies. The course will emphasize anatomy, physiology, incidence, presentation, physical exam findings, laboratory data, diagnostic imaging findings, treatment, and prevention of a wide selection of orthopedic conditions. There will be some discussion of surgical management options of various orthopedic conditions throughout the course. The effect of some systemic illnesses and genetic syndromes on the musculoskeletal system will also be covered in this course.

courses.title: Clinical Reasoning Workshop
courses.desc: This workshop-based course will focus on the development and application of clinical reasoning skills, including differential diagnosis, diagnostic work-up, and patient-centered management plan development. Students will engage with clinical cases each week through a combination of small-group work and classroom discussions. Weekly assignments will ensure preparation for sessions and reflection of skill development. The knowledge, skills, and abilities developed in this course will prepare students to transition from the classroom to the clinical learning environment.

courses.title: Principles of Critical Care Medicine
courses.desc: This course will introduce students to hemodynamic derangements in multiorgan system failure patients, including shock, trauma, cardiac arrest, acid-base and electrolyte management, and nutritional support. Other topics covered include COVID-19 pneumonia, ventilator management, invasive procedures, and diagnostic methods used in ICU care.

courses.title: Geriatrics
courses.desc: This course will introduce students to the process of aging as it affects the human body and mind. Atypical presentations of common acute and chronic diseases as they are seen in older populations will be addressed, as will the challenges of managing various and concomitant disease states. Pharmacologic therapy in older patients, Alzheimer's disease, dementia, patient compliance issues, and end-of-life care will be discussed as well.

courses.title: Introduction to Interprofessional Practice
courses.desc: This course prepares students to collaborate with members of other health professions in future practice in an effort to achieve optimal patient outcomes. Students will be provided with instruction on the roles and responsibilities of various members of the healthcare team, including their unique skills and expertise and what constitutes an appropriate referral. At the end of this course, learners will engage in an interprofessional educational activity working with healthcare students from a different discipline to analyze a complex patient case, incorporating their different perspectives while working collaboratively to develop a comprehensive treatment plan to improve patient outcomes.

courses.title: Primary Care III
courses.desc: This course is a continuation of Primary Care Medicine I and II and offers first year Physician Assistant students in-depth training in a wide variety of clinically related subjects, including common oral health conditions, urologic conditions, and special topics in medicine not covered elsewhere in the curriculum. The pathophysiology, clinical presentation, diagnosis, treatment, and prevention of diseases involving common oral health and urologic conditions topics will be covered. Special topics in medicine presented in this course include chronic pain management, opioid use disorder, health maintenance, smoking cessation, metabolic health, telemedicine, shared decision making, and motivational interviewing. Clinical case discussions/workshops and a simulated patient experience will be utilized to build the students’ patient care and critical thinking skills.

courses.title: Procedures Workshops
courses.desc: This course for Physician Assistant students focuses on common bedside procedures performed in clinical practice. Procedures taught range from simple laceration repair and phlebotomy to invasive procedures such as lumbar puncture and endotracheal intubation. Using peer practicums (venipuncture) and simulation models for more invasive procedures, key concepts and techniques will be taught.

courses.title: Capstone Project
courses.desc: Capstone is a year-long course designed to create a clinically relevant, scholarly activity in a mentored environment. The project serves as the culminating experience for graduate education in Physician Assistant studies and must be completed prior to the awarding of the MMS degree.

courses.title: Preparation for Clinical Practice
courses.desc: The Preparation for Clinical Practice seminar is a multi-faceted course that encompasses callback days and inter-professional activities during the clinical year. In addition, it will include formative assessments in the fall semester of didactic year and throughout the clinical year. The culmination is a summative assessment (End of Curriculum Examination and OSCE) to include evaluation of foundational medical knowledge, history taking, physical examination, diagnosis, management of a patient complaint, and patient education.

courses.title: Emergency Medicine Core Rotation
courses.desc: The Emergency Medicine Supervised Clinical Practical Experience (SCPE) exposes students to a broad range of experiences and patient populations in the emergency room for acutely ill patients. Students will hone their skills in triage, learning to recognize and manage patients that need immediate care. They will learn to prioritize care for conditions which are less urgent. Students will be responsible for taking medical histories and performing physical examinations on acute as well as emergent patients and presenting these to the medical preceptor. When appropriate, students will perform necessary diagnostic and therapeutic measures.

courses.title: Family Medicine Core Rotation
courses.desc: The Family Medicine Supervised Clinical Practical Experience (SCPE) exposes students to a broad range of experiences and patient populations that emphasize the patient as an individual and family member. Students are involved in the initial and ongoing assessment of patients in all age groups as well as management of individuals with new and established diagnoses. Emphasis is placed on evaluation, management, health promotion, and preventative medicine. Students are expected to be involved in the care of acute, chronic, and preventative visits.

courses.title: Inpatient Internal Medicine Core Rotation
courses.desc: The Inpatient Internal Medicine Supervised Clinical Practical Experience (SCPE) offers students an opportunity to become familiar with the assessment and management of varied medical problems that result in admission to the hospital. Students will attend medical rounds, perform diagnostic procedures, present case write-ups, record progress notes, and assist with discharge planning. It emphasizes the skills of collecting, assessing, and presenting patient data; ordering appropriate laboratory and diagnostic studies; counseling patients about therapeutic procedures; and helping to coordinate the contributions of other health professionals involved in management of the patient.

courses.title: Surgery Core Rotation
courses.desc: The Surgery Supervised Clinical Practical Experience (SCPE) exposes students to varied surgical patient care responsibilities with emphasis on general surgery, though students may have some exposure to surgical specialties and subspecialties. Students assist in surgical patients' preoperative initial assessment, which includes obtaining accurate medical histories and performing physical examinations. They also participate in preoperative management, including patient education and procedures necessary to prepare patients for surgery. Students assist surgeons in the operating room and have an opportunity to become familiar with operating room procedures and equipment. Students are also involved in patients' postoperative evaluation and management.

courses.title: Behavioral Medicine Core Rotation
courses.desc: The Behavioral Medicine Supervised Clinical Practical Experience (SCPE) is designed to provide an understanding of the behavioral components of health, disease, and disability. Through exposure to patients presenting with a broad spectrum of psychiatric disorders, students will develop history taking and mental status examination skills, classification skills utilizing DSM IV TR criteria, and be exposed to and evaluate different treatment modalities for varying presentations. The student will enhance their ability to recognize and categorize psychiatric disturbances and techniques of early intervention and psychiatric referral. Students are expected to be involved in the care of acute and chronic visits.

courses.title: Pediatrics Core Rotation
courses.desc: The Pediatrics Supervised Clinical Practical Experience (SCPE) is designed to develop the students' familiarity with pediatric medicine. The rotation will emphasize caring for a child from birth through adolescence. Students are provided opportunities to take medical histories and perform pediatric physical examinations. The focus will be on diagnosing and managing common childhood illnesses and evaluation of growth and development. Students will work on developing skills to counsel families about immunizations, child visits, growth and development parameters, common psychosocial problems, nutrition, and accident and poisoning prevention.

courses.title: OB/GYN Core Rotation
courses.desc: The OB/GYN Supervised Clinical Practical Experience (SCPE) allows students to participate in all aspects of OB/GYN care, including acute, preventive, chronic, and emergent situations. Students will be exposed to prenatal, labor and delivery, and postpartum care. Also, students will care for women across the lifespan, including menarche, infertility, menstrual conditions, benign and malignant gynecologic conditions, menopause, and postmenopausal situations.

courses.title: Orthopedic Core Rotation
courses.desc: The Orthopedic Supervised Clinical Practical Experience (SCPE) offers students an opportunity to care for injured and infirm patients in a variety of settings including, rehabilitation centers, and convalescent facilities, and exposes the student to issues of caring for patients with sub-acute but in many cases, multiple problems complicated by advanced age, post-acute event recovery issues, and complex social and economic problems commonly seen in this population. Students will also receive exposure to common musculoskeletal injuries from a broad range of etiologies.

courses.title: Elective Rotation
courses.desc: This Elective Supervised Clinical Practical Experience (SCPE) is designed to provide the student with the knowledge and skills in an area of interest. Students will gain an understanding of the variety of problems encountered in a medical or surgical sub-specialty discipline. The understanding of the varied medical and/or surgical sub-specialty problems is accomplished through history taking, physical exam, interpretation of diagnostic testing, and the development of a plan for each presenting problem including pharmacologic and non-pharmacologic management. In addition to gaining clinical skills specific to the specialty of the rotation, the student will also continue to develop skills in medical problem solving and patient management. Elective rotation sites are chosen based on practice characteristics that are important for the PA student within this rotation. These may include practice location, patient populations, and availability of specific experiences and procedures.

courses.title: Ambulatory Care/Outpatient Selective Rotation
courses.desc: The Ambulatory Care/Outpatient Supervised Clinical Practical Experience (SCPE) offers students the ability to spend additional time in an outpatient medical clinic and is meant to compliment the family medicine rotation. Students are involved in the initial and ongoing assessment of patients as well as management of individuals with established diagnoses. Students may see patients in venues that include hospital ambulatory care clinics, private offices, family medicine practices, clinics, and urgent care settings. As a selective, students may be placed in general medicine ambulatory rotations or a more specialized ambulatory care clinic.

courses.title: Inpatient Medicine Selective Rotation
courses.desc: During this Inpatient Medicine Supervised Clinical Practical Experience (SCPE), students will be exposed to patients presenting with acute and chronic illness requiring admission to the hospital setting. Students will elicit and record medical histories, perform physical examinations, and be involved in the management of the admitted patient. This SCPE is meant to complement the inpatient internal medicine core rotation by offering students additional time learning how to care for admitted patients. As a selective, students may be placed in a general inpatient medicine rotation or a more specialized in-patient experience.

courses.title: Introduction to Painting
courses.desc: Introduces practical information about the fundamentals of painting: shape, tone, edge, composition, color, line, perspective, and substance. Develops ability to describe visual world in multiple modes; provides grounding necessary to take more advanced painting courses. Demonstrations of materials and techniques, slide presentations, discussions, assignments, work periods, group and individual critiques. Majority of time spent in a studio/work mode. Course grounded in representation; recommended previous life drawing class or its equivalent, or concurrent with Introduction to Oil Painting. Introductory course open to all levels.

courses.title: Introduction Observational Painting
courses.desc: Development and articulation of a skilled and inventive approach to painting in preparation for intermediate and advanced level work. Basic skills in observational painting and how observation can build ecological and environmental knowledge as content for artwork. Ecology, along with traditional examinations of still life and self-portraiture as the subject matter for developing skills in value, color, and pictorial space. Exploration of dynamics of composition and investigation of the many painterly properties of oil paint through the lens of New Materialism and Vibrant Matter. Slide presentations, demos, discussions and visits to the MFA to extend painting abilities and knowledge of historical, ecological, and contemporary art based on observation. Recommendation: Any course in drawing.

courses.title: Intermediate Studio Seminar
courses.desc:
Bridge between project-based courses and independent work of Senior Thesis. Develop a strong and committed studio-based practice. Experience the challenges and rewards of sustaining a body of work from inception to exhibition. Depending upon access, studio space provided to support developing Applicants must be self-motivated and willing to spend substantial time working out of class. Applicants to this course must be in their second or third year and enrolled at least half-time studio throughout Fall and Spring semesters. Prerequisites include at least one introductory and one intermediate level course, or demonstrated equivalent through portfolio and statement. Faculty permission required.
Non-SMFA students will receive a letter grade.

courses.title: The Contemporary Landscape
courses.desc: (Cross-listed with PAIM 0080) Examines our relationship to the landscape and its histories. In considering both the geophysical origins and the cultural overlay of human presence, often created over millennia, the landscape reflects a living synthesis of people and place. Painting, Drawing, Land Art and other exercises offer ways to analyze not only the unique places we inhabit, but also their context in relation to ourselves. Projects are inspired by social and political themes and human perception of landscape to express our contemporary world via realism, metaphor and abstraction. One introductory painting course, such as PAI 003, PAI 10, PAI 21, PAIM 52, PAIM 54, or PAIM 93, is recommended to take this intermediate level course. Non-SMFA students will receive a letter grade.

courses.title: Bilder
courses.desc:
Develop paintings from a variety of source materials including methods for image generation (collage - digital and physical, drawing, image banking), and translation to canvas or similar surface. Demonstrations include revisions using Procreate, transferring images through printing and tracing, experimentation with different substrates, and extended techniques in oil and acrylic painting. Open to representation, abstraction, and combinations thereof. Students develop a theme throughout their work in this class, while maintaining an open and experimental attitude. Students learn extensive new information on materials and techniques, as well as an independent body of work.
Non-SMFA students and MAT Art Education students will receive a letter grade.

courses.title: Material Meaning
courses.desc:
Designed for intermediate and advanced students interested in exploring strategies for generating ideas and investigating methods of execution with a particular focus on materials and their relationship to content. Investigate the benefits of working in series in order to examine multiple conceptual and technical processes through assigned project. Discussion of both traditional and non-conventional materials, seeking alternative processes and materials that are appropriate to individual visions. Examination of historical and contemporary practices. Students encouraged to consider the nature of their work with regard to the contemporary context. Students must have completed at least 1 SMFA painting class or have relevant experience.

courses.title: Flora and Fauna

A broad range of media and methods discussed and used. Regular critiques and discussions help to support student’s projects. Designed for Intermediate level students. One previous introductory painting or drawing course recommended.

courses.title: Color and Critical Inquiry
courses.desc: Focus on the visual and aesthetic interactions of color in painting, the science of color perception, cultural contexts and metaphysical nature of color perception. This course offers a three-pronged approach to the study of color. 1. We will concentrate on fundamental properties of color and the dynamics of color interaction on two-dimensional surfaces. 2. Through projects/readings/slide talks, we will trace the roots of color use and color theories through the history of artistic practices. 3. We will explore the phenomenology of color as evidenced by its pivotal role in the evolution of biology, language, and culture. Prerequisite: PAI 03, PAI 06 or PAI 10, or by permission of the instructor. For intermediate and advanced level students.

Material demonstrations, slide lectures, readings and critiques to supplement working-in-class time. Intended for Intermediate Level Painting students with experience rendering in oil and/or acrylic paints. Non-SMFA students and MAT Art Education students will receive a letter grade.

Work observationally from models in class, as well as abstracting from photography, and using own source material. Explore the pluralistic state of contemporary figuration through readings, critical viewings. Best suited to students with previous instruction in painting or figure drawing.

Classes consist of demonstrations, discussion, painting exercises that build upon one another over the semester. Students gain comfort and familiarity with the language of painting by reading about and responding to contemporary painting/painters, and critiquing/discussing each other’s work. Open to all levels.

They learn new painting techniques, and use multiple perceptions and methods (drawing, photography, video, and digital image manipulation) to develop images. Demonstrations, one-on-one instruction, and generous easel time. Develop and express personal vision by reinterpreting realism. Previous painting experience helpful. Open to all levels.

courses.desc: This introductory-level course offers a broad perspective on epidemiological terminology, concepts, and methods. By the end of this course, students will be able to apply epidemiological methods to the breadth of settings and situations in public health practice.

courses.title: Principles of Biostatistics
courses.desc: This course provides an introduction to the basic principles and applications of statistics as they are applied to problems in clinical and public health settings. Topics include the description and presentation of data, random variables and distributions, descriptive statistics, introduction to probability, estimation, elements of hypothesis testing, one- and two-sample tests, ANOVA (including repeated-measures), non-parametric tests, and an introduction to linear and logistic regression. Lectures, problem sets, and computer output are used to develop these and additional concepts.

sections.req: HIA 0227 and PH 0205 are equivalent courses. Students may not register for more than one of these courses.

courses.title: Foundations of Public Health Practice
courses.desc: Public health is fundamentally about people, including the experiences, values, and perspectives that shape how health, illness, and community are understood. This required foundational course serves as the starting point for MPH students to explore public health practice and their role within it. Students engage with real-world challenges related to healthcare delivery, policy, environment and climate, and structural inequities, while developing skills in critical thinking, evidence-informed decision-making, and communication. Through applied activities and guided reflection, students examine tradeoffs, constraints, and the impact of public health decisions on individuals and communities. The course emphasizes belonging, helping students consider how they will contribute to public health in ways that are thoughtful, responsible, and grounded in advancing health equity.

courses.title: Law in Public Health
courses.desc: This course explores the complex and evolving legal environment surrounding public health and health care delivery systems. Issues include those related to tobacco-related injuries and Medicaid litigation, personal injury liability for toxic substance exposure, end-of-life decision making, medical malpractice, and insurance company regulation and liability. In analysis of these topics, the interrelationship of the levels and branches of government will be noted. Also, the course incorporates basic descriptions of financing mechanisms and providers in the US health care system.

courses.title: Survey Research Methods
courses.desc: This course uses real-world examples to introduce students to basic survey methodology. Students are introduced to the vast array of large government-sponsored survey activities. Students learn to apply the fundamentals of good survey design and how to create their own survey using Qualtrics software. Topics include formulating research questions and measurement objectives, sampling, validity measures, linking instruments to conceptual frameworks, principles of item construction and scale development, modes of survey administration, survey operations, and coding approaches.

courses.title: Infectious Disease Epidemiology
courses.desc: This course is designed to introduce you to key concepts in infectious disease epidemiology, including the methodological issues associated with control, surveillance, and research of infectious diseases. While a detailed presentation of the epidemiology of every infectious disease is well beyond the scope of this course, we will consider the epidemiology of several important diseases over the course of the semester.

sections.req: Course has a prerequisite of PH 0201 Principles of Epidemiology or an equivalent course. Contact the program for equivalent course approval.

courses.title: Introduction to Global Health and Development
courses.desc: This course addresses global health disparities. Students will compare various healthcare systems with the help of lectures, discussions, and country studies. The objective of the course is to identify the root causes of health disparities among and within nations related to primary healthcare, gender, ethnicity, and microhabitat issues. The course reviews important healthcare milestones and challenges and addresses emerging trends that have impacts on global health. Demographic trends will be used as a tool to quantify those disparities and progresses. Health governance will be addressed extensively, linking healthcare to the roles of international organizations, non-governmental organizations (those for profit and not for profit), and governments.

courses.title: Intermediate Epidemiology
courses.desc: This course in intermediate epidemiologic methods reinforces the concepts and methods taught in PH 0201, with in-depth instruction in issues of study design, assessing threats to study validity including confounding and selection bias, and analyzing data with standard regression models. The course emphasizes hands-on learning and includes a combination of discussions of methodologic papers and a required laboratory component where students will learn to apply the concepts learned in class to real-world problems.

sections.req: Course has prerequisites of PH 0201 Principles of Epidemiology and PH 0205 Principles of Biostatistics or equivalent courses. Contact the program for equivalent course approval.

courses.title: GIS for Public Health
courses.desc: In public health, place matters. Place is a close reflection of the social and economic deprivation and environmental exposures that can result in significant health disparities that are manifest in health outcomes, including morbidity and mortality. While uses of geographic information systems (GIS) and spatial epidemiology have increased steeply and steadily within the public health sciences during the past two decades, they are rapidly evolving. In health disparities, nutrition, disease prevention, and health services research, this is particularly evident. More than an estimated 80% of health issues have a spatial component; however, only a small fraction of research studies include a focus on the geography of health and spatial associations of putative exposures, access to care, and health outcomes. This course will provide students with the basic skills needed to obtain, analyze, and decipher spatial data in a GIS, using a variety of examples from public health, nutrition, urban development, and the US Census Bureau.

sections.req: HIA 0219 and PH 0262 are equivalent courses. Students may not register for more than one of these courses.

courses.title: Social Marketing
courses.desc: Students will develop an understanding of social marketing and how this approach can be used to influence behavior and social change. The course provides practice in positioning complex public health issues, identifying and analyzing audiences, creating targeted communication, identifying appropriate communication channels, translating research into creative concepts, and evaluating social marketing interventions. Students will apply these skills in designing a social marketing plan that addresses a public health topic. As part of this course, students will gain an understanding of the benefits of moving beyond promotion to designing marketing-based interventions aimed at facilitating behavior change.

courses.title: US Healthcare: Systems Thinking for Reform
courses.desc: This course provides an overview of the context, stakeholders, and function of healthcare systems. It covers a large amount of information about how health care in the U.S. functions so that, by the end of the course, students can apply what they know to evaluate options and contribute to conversations about policy solutions. Since policy information is constantly changing, students will also learn how to continue updating their knowledge on these topics throughout their careers. Students interested in careers in the health care system, government, or consulting will find this course invaluable.

Since policy information is constantly changing, students will also learn how to continue updating their knowledge on these topics throughout their careers. Students interested in careers in the health care system, government, or consulting will find this course invaluable.

courses.title: Qualitative Methods and Data Analysis
courses.desc: This course is an introductory course to begin, but not develop full mastery in, various relevant qualitative methods relevant for public health. The course emphasizes practical skills of qualitative research design, data collection (i.e., interviewing, focus group facilitation, participant observations, photonovella/photovoice, etc.), and analysis. The course introduces students to paradigms of qualitative research and inquiry, selected data collection, management, and analysis methods for qualitative research in public health, and standards for reporting qualitative findings. Students will learn about methods for analyzing qualitative data manually but will be exposed to the NVivo software platform.

courses.title: Qualitative Methods and Data Analysis

The course emphasizes practical skills of qualitative research design, data collection (i.e., interviewing, focus group facilitation, participant observations, photonovella/photovoice, etc.), and analysis. The course introduces students to paradigms of qualitative research and inquiry, selected data collection, management, and analysis methods for qualitative research in public health, and standards for reporting qualitative findings. Students will learn about methods for analyzing qualitative data manually but will be exposed to the NVivo software platform.

courses.title: Clinical Epidemiology
courses.desc: This course is designed to offer an overview of clinical epidemiology concepts at the introductory level. Clinical decision making requires background knowledge in three important areas of epidemiology: risk estimation, diagnosis, and intervention. Recorded lectures and slide-based asynchronous work is supplemented by reading chapters in a textbook. During the in-person classes, ongoing participation and a group presentation are the basis of assessment. The course includes individual assessments as well as group work. Each week covers a chapter in the textbook. Students will bring examples from the published literature for discussion in class.

courses.title: Minority Women's Reproductive Health
courses.desc: This course focuses on the critical evaluation of key research and issues surrounding minority women's reproductive health. The course content is strategically designed to highlight and examine historical factors shaping the well-being of minority women. Students will engage with historical perspectives to better comprehend the roots of existing health disparities and their lasting impacts on minority women's reproductive health. Emphasizing racial and ethnic disparities, the course delves into the intricate intersectionality of race, ethnicity, gender, and socioeconomic status, providing a comprehensive exploration of the factors influencing reproductive health outcomes for minority women in the United States.

courses.title: Project Management
courses.desc: This skills-focused course provides students with a foundation in project management principles and practices relevant to public health and healthcare. Grounded in the frameworks used by the Project Management Institute and aligned with the PMP certification domains, this course emphasizes practical tools and real-world application. Each session introduces a new public health or healthcare scenario to explore essential project management skills - including scope development, scheduling, risk mitigation, and communication planning - while students simultaneously work in teams to build a complete project plan for a healthcare or public health initiative. Through hands-on exercises, applied tools, and collaborative deliverables, students will leave the course with marketable skills and portfolio-ready artifacts they can use in future roles. The course also serves as an on-ramp to early career PMP certification by introducing key concepts, vocabulary, and tools used in professional project management practice.

courses.title: Consulting Skills for Healthcare and Public Health
courses.desc: This skills-focused course introduces students to the core tools and approaches used by consultants working in healthcare and public health settings. The course is grounded in a real-world consulting model, where students respond to a Request for Proposals and develop a structured, client-ready solution over the course of the semester. Each session focuses on a key consulting skill (e.g., problem framing, stakeholder analysis, work planning, budgeting, data synthesis, recommendation development, and executive communication) applied to a single, evolving case. Students learn how to move from an ambiguous problem to a clear set of actionable recommendations, while working within realistic constraints such as limited data, competing stakeholder priorities, and organizational complexity.

courses.title: Skills and Tools for Engaged Practice II (STEP II)
courses.desc: Skills and Tools for Engaged Practice (STEP) II is the second of a three-course sequence designed for students completing the MPH degree. This course enables students to progress through their MPH training experience while acquiring knowledge, skills, and perspectives essential for addressing critical public health challenges. This course includes didactic sessions on budgeting, management, leadership, and working with professionals from other professions and sectors. Students will review resources from career services and work in small groups with the instructor to refine their course plan, complete their proposal for the Applied Practice Experience (APE) and plan for the culminating Integrative Learning Experience (ILE), and update their Individualized Development Plans (IDP).

courses.title: Skills and Tools for Engaged Practice III (STEP III)
courses.desc: Skills and Tools for Engaged Practice (STEP) III is the final course of a three-course sequence designed for students completing the MPH degree. In this course, students will submit and present their Applied Practice Experience (APE) deliverables, obtain support for completing their Integrative Learning Experience (ILE), and continue to develop skills for their public health career. Students will have the opportunity to participate in a variety of workshops and modules to advance their knowledge, skills, and perspectives across an array of public health topics.

courses.title: Applied Practice Experience (APE) and Integrative Learning Experience (ILE) Planning
courses.desc: Students will review resources from career services and work in small groups with the instructor to complete their proposals for the Applied Practice Experience (APE) and the culminating Integrative Learning Experience (ILE). CITI Ethics certification and information about Tufts Global APE opportunities are also covered in this course.

courses.title: Applied Practice Experience (APE) Implementation
courses.desc: APE Implementation is the second course of a three-course sequence designed for students completing the MPH degree. In this course, students will submit and present their Applied Practice Experience (APE) deliverables and continue to develop skills for their public health career.

sections.req: PH 0321 APE & ILE Planning is a prerequisite for this course.

courses.title: Introduction To Linguistics
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as PSY 64 and LING 15.) How humans encode language in their brains, so that they can produce and understand an unlimited variety of utterances in context. Language and other forms of communication; how children acquire language; biological basis of language; the structure of language -- phonology (sound structure), syntax (grammatical structure), and semantics (meaning).

sections.note: Estimated Textbook Cost = $65

courses.title: An Introduction to Civic Studies: Theories for a Better World
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed as CVS 20 and PS 20) Exploration of contrasting conceptions of active citizenship with roots in philosophy and practical experimentation. Course aims better to understand how people engage with their communities and develop strategies for building a better world. Emphasis on the perspective of individuals and small groups: what we should do to create, nourish, and sustain good communities. Consideration of values (ethics), facts (empirical evidence), and strategies. Readings from historical and contemporary sources. 
No prerequisites.

courses.title: Introduction To Ethics
courses.desc: (Cross-listed with CVS 14) An introduction to moral judgment--and the reasoning it is based on--by a detailed study of current issues such as abortion, vegetarianism, and responsibility for war crimes, and the application to such problems of ethical theories, such as egoism, utilitarianism, and the doctrine of rights.

courses.title: Religious, Philosophical Roots of Modern World 1
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as MDVL 71, REL 29, CVS 53, CLS 29 and JS 29) Major religious and philosophical thinkers and concepts that played roles in the emergence of the modern world: Plato and Aristotle; Jewish, Christian, and Muslim scripture and theologians who merged their religions with the Greek tradition; the Ptolemaic universe and the Great Chain of Being. Medieval Jews, Christians, and Muslims saw themselves as having a privileged and objective place in a divinely-created and -ordered cosmos that was young, small, and centered on the earth.

sections.note:
High demand course. Instructor permission required. Please contact Yonatan Brafman at yonatan.brafman@tufts.edu to register.

10 seats reserved for CAP advising

courses.title: Logic
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as LING 33). An introduction to fundamental concepts of modern formal logic, including sentence logic, quantification theory, and identity. Emphasis on the application of formal methods to reasoning in philosophy, mathematics, and everyday affairs.

courses.title: Western Political Thought I
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CLS 41, CVS 18, and PS 41.) Central concepts of ancient, medieval, and early modern political thought. Ideas of Thucydides, Aristophanes, Plato, and Aristotle during the rise and fall of Athens. Subsequent transformations of political philosophy related to the decline of the Roman empire and the origins and development of Christian political doctrine, and the new political outlook of those who challenge the hegemony of Christianity. Analysis of how premodern political thought helped structure future political debate.

courses.title: War and Terrorism
courses.desc: (Cross-Listed as CVS 17). Examination of possible justifications of the use of violence and of moral constraints on the conduct of war. Topics include whether combatants bear moral responsibility for fighting, whether terrorism is always wrong, and how are we to understand pacifism as an alternative to violence. Commonly held assumptions about war and terrorism will be scrutinized. Readings from Walzer, Fanon, Clausewitz, Gandhi, Che Guevara, and Mao.

sections.note: 10 seats reserved for CAP advising

courses.title: Restorative Justice
courses.desc: Theory and practice of restorative justice, in which community members work to resolve criminal cases through community-based processes of mediation, accountability, and repair. Examination of existing models in the United States and abroad that address criminal wrongdoing without punishment. Possible visits from practitioners. Readings from moral and political philosophy, social science, and legal scholarship.

Juxtaposes and compares classic philosophical texts and contemporary feminist approaches to issues in ethics, epistemology, and metaphysics. Lower level of dual level course.

Kojeve, Hegel, Sartre, Paul Schrader, Bresson, and Ozu.

courses.desc: A philosophical examination of highly theoretical issues in normative ethics: what makes something right or wrong, good or evil, just or unjust; the role of moral principles in ethics; the methodology of moral inquiry; consequentialism; utilitarianism; Kantian deontology; pluralistic deontology; virtue theory; impartialism versus partialism; particularism versus generalism.

courses.title: Islamic Philosophy
courses.desc: (Cross-listed w/ CLS 154) Key problems and figures in Islamic philosophy. The rise of theological controversies in early Islam. The Arabic philosophical tradition between Neo-Platonism and Aristotelianism: Kindi (d. 870), Farabi (d. 950), and Avicenna (d. 1037). Al-Ghazali’s (d.1111) Incoherence of the Philosophers and the response by Averroes (d.1198); the powerful influence of philosophy on later Islamic theology; the anti-Aristotelian, Platonist philosophy of illumination of Suhrawardi (d. 1191), and the mystical monism of Ibn Arabi (d.1240). Developments of philosophy in Safavid Persia, the Ottoman Empire, and Mughal India until the 17th century. No prior knowledge of Islam is required. All readings in English translation. Prerequisites: one philosophy course or permission of instructor.

sections.note: Class Notes: No prior knowledge of Islam is required. All readings in English translation.

courses.title: Still Life Photography
courses.desc: Still Life photography as a practice that draws from the histories of painting, sculpture, photography, and video, incorporating a variety of natural or manufactured materials and objects, including small tableaux, doll houses, and miniature documentations from the outside world to documentation of the dead. courses.title: Image, Narrative, Psychoanalysis
courses.desc:
Intermediate to advanced level course, open to students of any discipline, explores relationship of image-making to storytelling and our unconscious mind. Focus is on image-making exercises, free association, weekly readings, and creation of mid term and final project. The unconscious, as understood Psychoanalysis, houses memories and feelings that are hidden from our conscious, yet art making can reveal what is hidden from us. Our dreams are a direct link to our unconscious, made of fragmented images telling non-linear narratives consisting of symbols. How can we come to better understand our unconscious mind, to make more unique art with a personal voice? Parallels between the narratives we create in our art to the messages in our dreams, our memories and internalized experiences are explored. The nature of the material requires preparedness for introspection and maturity. 
Non-SMFA students will receive a letter grade.

courses.title: Photo 1: Film & Darkroom

Focus on the tradition of photography, making pictures with a 35mm camera, film development and the craft of darkroom printing. Weekly demonstrations/ assignments develop the necessary techniques to produce quality negatives and prints. Assignments challenge students to learn to see photographically. courses.desc: Explores the archive as an artistic process and tool. Conceptual methods of thinking about archive as a time-based approach to copying, documenting, printing, and collecting. Hosted by the Center for Expanding Viewpoints in Higher Education (CEVIHE), this weekly series invites Tufts students to explore politics and culture by reading controversial books and articles, engaging with faculty discussants and guest speakers, and discussing sensitive political, economic, and social issues with depth, humility, and courage. Each week, participants will encounter sophisticated arguments associated with a diversity of ideological, religious, and cultural worldviews. Lunch will be provided, and seats are limited. Students do not need to sign up for course credit to attend, but enrolled students will have guaranteed seats. The series is open to students from all disciplines and majors who are intellectually curious and want to deepen their understanding of contentious and consequential public affairs and policy issues. The series is also open to faculty and staff attendees.

courses.title: Workshop in Political Science - Individualism and Nonconformity in Film
courses.desc: Please see departmental website for detailed course descriptions.

sections.note:
Class dates: 9/17, 10/15, 11/5, and 12/3

Hosted by the Center for Expanding Viewpoints in Higher Education (CEVIHE) in collaboration with the Film and Media Studies Program (FMS), this four-part film series invites Tufts students to examine the themes of individualism and nonconformity through screenings of landmark films drawn from a range of historical periods, political contexts, and cinematic traditions. Each session features a full-length film paired with faculty framing and guided discussion, allowing participants to analyze how individuals navigate the tension between personal conscience and collective pressure, and how political and social institutions respond to dissent. The series asks participants to think critically about moral independence, civic responsibility, and the costs and consequences of resisting conformity. Popcorn and pizza will be served. Students do not need to sign up for course credit to attend, but enrolled students will have guaranteed seats. The series is open to students from all disciplines and majors who are interested in exploring contested ideas, competing loyalties, and acts of principled resistance that shape public life. Faculty and staff are also welcome to join

courses.desc: Please see departmental website for detailed course descriptions.

sections.note: Hosted by the Center for Expanding Viewpoints in Higher Education (CEVIHE), this weekly Edge Fellowship seminar examines the habits of mind, character traits, and practical skills necessary for open inquiry and engagement across ideological, religious, and cultural differences. Through structured conversations, brief readings, reflective exercises, skill-building activities, discussions with guest facilitators, and camaraderie, fellows will practice close reading, evidence-based argumentation, media and digital literacy, generous listening, public speaking, and ethical reasoning. They will also learn to recognize cognitive biases and social pressures that distort judgment and undermine meaningful discourse. The seminar will strengthen the Edge Fellows as an intellectual cohort and prepare them to sustain and lead flourishing communities at Tufts University and beyond.

courses.title: Workshop in Political Science - Revolution and the Problem of Political Order
courses.desc: Please see departmental website for detailed course descriptions.

sections.note:
Wednesdays: 9/16, 9/23, 9/30, 10/7, 10/14, 10/21, 10/28, 11/4, 11/18, 12/2, 12/9

Hosted by the Center for Expanding Viewpoints in Higher Education (CEVIHE), this weekly reading group examines the political ideas and moral dilemmas of the French Revolution, from its opening in 1789 through the fall of Maximilien Robespierre in 1794. Through close reading of revolutionary texts and later interpretations, participants will consider how commitments to liberty, equality, popular sovereignty, and republican government came into tension with demands for order, religious authority, political representation, and revolutionary violence. The group will ask what makes revolutionary action legitimate; whether regicide and political violence can ever be justified; who should count as a citizen; and how a new constitutional order can establish authority after the overthrow of a monarchy. The principal texts will be writings by Robespierre and Alexis de Tocqueville, supplemented by excerpts from Louis Blanc, Antoine Saint-Just, Thomas Paine, Edmund Burke, Joseph de Maistre, and others. The group will be facilitated by Shani Agarwal Hood, CEVIHE Program Manager, and Riley Roche, A26, with guest facilitators including Professors Peter Levine and Elizabeth Foster. Students who are not registered for credit may also participate, subject to space, but should contact CEVIHE for access to readings and course materials. The group is open to students from all disciplines and majors interested in revolution, political thought, and the enduring tensions among freedom, equality, and authority.

courses.title: Workshop in Political Science - Christianity and Public Life
courses.desc: Please see departmental website for detailed course descriptions.

sections.note:
How do Christians understand the role of faith in shaping their social and political life? Since the turn of the 20th century, Christian authors have aimed to develop a principled theological response to the res novae or “new things” of the modern age – liberalism, pluralism, mass democracy, capitalism, and industrialization. In this reading group, we will explore a series of texts that are shaping the church’s public engagement with our own present political ideas, cultural movements, and social issues. In addition to exploring how Christians have grappled with the rise of modern liberalism, pluralism, and capitalism, we’ll explore prominent contemporary approaches to poverty and welfare, abortion and human life, the arts, the environment, and the rise of digital society.

Class Dates: 9/14, 9/21, 9/28, 10/5, 10/19, 10/26, 11/2, 11/9, 11/16, and 11/23

courses.title: An Introduction to Civic Studies: Theories for a Better World
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed as CVS 20 and PHIL 20) Exploration of contrasting conceptions of active citizenship with roots in philosophy and practical experimentation. Course aims better to understand how people engage with their communities and develop strategies for building a better world. Emphasis on the perspective of individuals and small groups: what we should do to create, nourish, and sustain good communities. Consideration of values (ethics), facts (empirical evidence), and strategies. Readings from historical and contemporary sources. 
No prerequisites.

courses.title: Western Political Thought I
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CLS 41, CVS 18, and PHIL 41.) Central concepts of ancient, medieval, and early modern political thought. Ideas of Thucydides, Aristophanes, Plato, and Aristotle during the rise and fall of Athens. Subsequent transformations of political philosophy related to the decline of the Roman empire and the origins and development of Christian political doctrine, and the new political outlook of those who challenged the hegemony of Christianity. Analysis of how premodern political thought helped structure future political debate.

courses.title: Introduction To International Relations
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CVS 61) Examination of several conceptual designs intended to make order out of the essential anarchy in international relations, from a theoretical assessment of the nation-state and the nature of national power to an exploration of behavior among nation-states, including the ultimate problem of war and peace and an appraisal of the factors that give an age its particular characteristics.

courses.title: Fieldwork In Politics
courses.desc: Internship placements with such employers as legislators, campaigns, news media, lobbies, law firms, and administrative agencies. Twelve to fifteen hours of work per week. Written assignments, with supporting readings, on organizational structure, goals and strategies, and occupational socialization.

sections.note: The class will meet three times during the semester.

courses.title: Political Science Research Methods
courses.desc: (Cross-listed w/ CVS 148). The study of quantitative methods for investigating political issues and policy controversies. Focuses on collecting, analyzing, and presenting data. Emphasizes hands-on training that provides useful skills for academic and professional settings. Topics covered include: measurement, hypothesis development, survey design, experiments, content analysis, significance tests, correlation, and regression. No prior statistics background necessary. Prerequisites: PS 11, 21, 41, 42, or 61. A methodologically focused course.

sections.req: Completion of any Political Science Foundation Course: PS 11, 12, 41, 42, or 61 or Political Science first year tutorials: PS 2, 3 or 4, or CVS 20

courses.title: The American Congress
courses.desc: Examines the United States’ Congress: congressional elections, representation, legislative organization, the legislative process, and inter-branch relationships. Recommendations: PS 0011

courses.title: US Elections: Rules, Strategies, and Outcomes
courses.desc: Election laws and political campaigns in the United States. Focusing on how rules, including the US Constitution, public policies, and party norms, affect the ways that strategic campaigns pursue voters. Topics may include the Constitution; parties; nominations/primaries; money in politics; redistricting; voting rights; term limits; competitiveness; electoral college; access and suppression; data and targeting; and messaging.

courses.title: Topics in American Politics - Imagining Law and Order in US
courses.desc: Please see departmental website for detailed course descriptions.

sections.note: Examination of both the development of state coercive institutions in the United States and the production of ideas about those institutions. Course begins with the Pinkerton private security agency and traces its influence on both policing practices and construction of myths and tropes in American popular culture. Other critical junctures include prohibition and gangsterism, the rise of the modern FBI, and the tough on crime movement that led to mass incarceration and police militarization. Sources include primary works by Allen Pinkerton, J. Edgar Hoover, and Jack Webb, as well as Hollywood films and television programs. The final section of the course considers to what extent the phenomenon of “copaganda” exists following recent changes in the criminal justice system and public attitudes toward law and order.

courses.title: Topics in American Politics - Intro to Federal & State Constitutional Law
courses.desc: Please see departmental website for detailed course descriptions.

sections.note:
This course will introduce U.S. constitutional law, state constitutional law, and the varying approaches that the U.S. and state supreme courts have taken on important issues. First we will examine the authorities from which the U.S. Supreme Court and state supreme courts derive their powers, as well as how state supreme courts differ from the U.S. Supreme Court. Next, we will introduce to various issues and examine how the U.S. Supreme Court and state supreme courts have taken different approaches, even when interpreting provisions that might, at first glance, seem to be nearly identical. The goals of this course will be: (1) to educate students about federal and state constitutional law, and (2) to help students understand how to reason about the law, stake out their own views, and defend them.
First year students can register with instructor permission.

courses.desc:
Survey of the domestic politics of the People's Republic of China. The development of Communist Party power through the political campaigns of the 1950s and 1960s. The political, cultural, economic, and social challenges faced by post-Mao reformers. Brief consideration of foreign policy.
Recommendations: Sophomore standing or permission of instructor.

courses.title: Modern Ukraine: Identity, Democracy, Society
courses.desc: Analysis of political developments in contemporary Ukraine, using major theories and concepts in comparative politics. Issues such as nation- and state-building, democratization and post-socialist market reforms, memory politics, mass mobilization, and war as a driver of political and social change since 2014. Focus on post-1991 Ukraine, with attention to earlier periods of imperial and Soviet rule, especially in the 20th century. Ukraine’s domestic politics and society, historical and contemporary relations with Russia, causes and consequences of the Russo-Ukrainian war, and Ukraine’s enduring significance for European and global order.

courses.title: Comparative Politics Of The Middle East
courses.desc:
Survey of the political development of the Arab states, Israel, Turkey, and Iran since the fall of the Ottoman Empire in World War I. Focus on the various factors that have helped shape the emergence of political institutions in those countries: history, economics, culture, religion, and foreign intervention. Prospects for future change (socioeconomic development, political liberalization, war and peace) in the Middle East.
Recommendations: Sophomore standing or permission of instructor.

courses.title: Topics In Comparative Politics - Work & Family Policy in Comp.
courses.desc: Please see departmental website for specific details.

sections.note: Work and family policies around the globe differ substantially. Some countries, such as Sweden, have robust paid parental leave policies, child subsidies, and subsidized or public child care, all of which are viewed as important public provisions promoting gender equality and assuring that all adults can take paid employment and still have children. Some countries at the opposite end of the spectrum, such as the US, have none of those, treating work and family issues as individuals’ personal problems to be solved at the household level and thereby making combining work and family very challenging. Communist countries had yet other ways of conceptualizing how to support working families at a time when all adults were required to work. What explains these differences among countries? How did they come to be over the course of the 20th century? How were policies shaped by politics, ideas about gender, and local culture? What might the future hold for these policies?

courses.title: Topics In Comparative Politics - Modern Israel: Politics & Society
courses.desc: Please see departmental website for specific details.

sections.note: This course examines Israeli politics, government, and society since the establishment of the state in 1948 to contemporary developments. The aims of the course are to provide students with a broad understanding of the Israeli state and society, situating these in comparative perspectives. Following an introduction to the Israeli case, the course is divided into three broad sections: Part 1: Israeli institutions, the government, and the economy, explores the development of the Israeli democracy; Part 2: Israeli social fabric and cleavages, focuses on societal levels, including majority-minority dynamics, secular-religious divides, and other social developments; Part 3: Wars, security, and the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, focuses on the different conflicts Israel has been engaged in, culminating in the current Israel- Hamas War. Throughout the course students are encouraged to consider what are some of the unique characteristics of the Israeli case as well as what are more common and comparable features. Students are also encouraged to take an active interest in ongoing developments in Israel through the international established media and social media, considering the ways in which many of the current challenges facing the Israeli state and society have their roots in historic processes and developments.

courses.title: Topics In Comparative Politics - Terrorism & Political Violence
courses.desc: Please see departmental website for specific details.

sections.note:
This course examines the multidimensional facets of political violence and terrorism. Its aims are to challenge conventional thoughts about such radical mobilization, exposing students to the multiple definitions, historical progression, and political and sociological developments of terrorism throughout the past centuries. Drawing on a range of historic and current examples from around the world, we will tackle a variety of questions on the subject, including: What are the differences between political violence, guerilla warfare, terrorism, and international warfare, and why do such distinctions matter? Are there differences between religious and non-religious terrorism and political violence? What are the historic developments that led to the rise of religious terrorism at the end of the 20th century, and is it still on the rise? Who are the major terror groups that have operated around the world throughout the past decades, and which have been more successful in advancing their cause? 
The course is divided into three sections. The first focuses on definitions of terrorism, exploring how terror groups operate and taking students through a historical rundown of modern terrorism over the 20th and 21st centuries. The second focuses on theories explaining groups’ and individuals’ use of terrorism and political violence, emphasizing where different theories agree and where they come to drastically different conclusions. The third section covers a range of select case studies of different groups using such tactics, analyzing the internationalization processes of terrorism and comparing ideological worldviews, violent mobilization, and respective successes and failures. By the conclusion of the course, students will have a broad-based understanding of how terrorism and violent mobilization have influenced various political processes throughout the 20th and 21st centuries, gaining the tools to analyze such mobilization as it continues to unfold.

courses.title: Shakespeare's Rome
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed as CLS 145). Study of Shakespeare’s Rape of Lucrece, Coriolanus, Julius Caesar, and Antony and Cleopatra in light of his classical sources, Plutarch and Livy. The reasons for Rome’s greatness and the causes of its decline; ancient Rome as a model of civic participation; the demands of Roman virtue; the role of women in a martial regime; the place of philosophy in the city; and the effect of the regime on the character of individuals. Examination of the question whether Shakespeare diverges from his classical sources to come to an independent judgment of Rome.
Recommendations: PS 41, PS 42, CLS 32, or CLS 38

courses.title: The Meaning Of America
courses.desc:
Examination of American political thought, concentrating on the founding debate, the development of Lincoln's thought and the Civil War, and Alexis de Tocqueville’s Democracy in America. Topics include the Puritan origins of America, the meaning of and the relationship between our founding documents, the challenges posed by the Anti-Federalists, the defense of the large republic in The Federalist, the role of religion in American life, the problems presented by slavery, the proper role of a democratic statesman, and Tocqueville's hopes and worries about liberal democratic society and government (especially its American variant)..
Recommendations: One of the following: PS 41, 42, or permission of instructor.

courses.title: Topics In Political Thought - Politics and Generative AI
courses.desc: Please see departmental website for specific details.

sections.note: This is a class about the politics and ethics of Generative AI. The first part of the course will examine the problems that arise when we apply AI models. We will ask what it might mean for AI outputs to be fair and how this fairness might be achieved. The second part of the course will consider the broader social effects of AI as it exists today. We will ask who benefits (and who does not benefit) from its remaking of the world, how the proliferation of chatbots reshapes our politics and economies, and what happens when we give these models control of our decisions and voices. Course will be taught by Samuel Stevens (https://www.sfhstevens.com/).

courses.desc:

Recommendations: Sophomore standing or permission of instructor.

courses.desc: Examination of the causes and consequences of nuclear weapons proliferation for international politics since 1945. Topics include the dynamics of nuclear proliferation; nonproliferation and counterproliferations strategies; nuclear strategy and deterrence; and future of strategic arms control. Prerequisite: PS 0061 and junior or senior standing.

courses.desc: Systematic survey of the field of psychology, covering important general principles in the topics of psychological development, sensory processes, perception, motivation, emotion, learning, thinking, intelligence, aptitudes, social problems, and personality.

courses.title: Psychopathology
courses.desc: An introduction to the scientific study of major psychological and behavioral syndromes – including psychotic, mood, anxiety, personality, and substance use disorders – with an emphasis on assessment, symptoms, prevalence, possible causes, and treatment approaches.

courses.title: Social Psychology
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CVS 35) How situations and the people around us influence our thoughts, feelings, and behavior. Aggression, attitudes, attraction, attribution, conformity, group processes, helping behavior, non-verbal behavior, self-knowledge, social cognition, social influence, and stereotypes and prejudice. Applications of social psychological concepts to topics such as health, intergroup relations, and law.

courses.title: Emotion
courses.desc: Introduction to theory and research on the nature of emotion and its regulation. Topics include defining and measuring emotion and related constructs; theories of emotion elicitation, expression, and regulation; perspectives on the function of emotions; discrete emotions such as joy, surprise, fear, anger, sadness, and disgust; emotion across cultural, developmental, and clinical contexts; the neural, endocrine, and autonomic concomitants of emotion. Course assignments typically include readings, exams, and class exercises.

courses.title: Physiological Psychology
courses.desc: The biological basis of behavior. Basic functioning of the nervous system; physiological basis of hunger, thirst, sex, aggression, sleep, sensory and motor systems, learning and memory. Lectures and demonstrations. Students cannot receive credit for both PSY 25 and PSY 103. Biopsychology majors, who completed PSY 25 before declaring the major, should speak with an advisor about substituting another course for the PSY 103 major requirement

courses.title: Animal Learning
courses.desc: A survey and analysis of the principles of learning, memory, and cognition in animals. Emphasis on the adaptive nature of learning and the importance of theoretical and methodological issues in the experimental analysis of cognition. Topics include evolution of learning, basic processes in conditioning, stimulus control, attention, time and space orientation, awareness, and the role of feedback and reward.

courses.title: Perception
courses.desc: Processes that transform physical energy (e.g., light, sound, heat) into psychological experiences (e.g., seeing objects, hearing music, feeling warmth). Emphasis on visual perception; topics such as speech perception and active touch will also be covered. Special issues include development of perceptual abilities, perception in animals, pathologies of perception, and perception's role in art.

courses.title: Cognitive Psychology
courses.desc: Introduction to human mental processes. Topics include attention, perception, problem solving, pattern recognition, imagery, memory retention, language comprehension, and knowledge acquisition as fundamental processes of cognition.

courses.title: Statistics For Behavioral Science

Statistical methods for the treatment of data in the behavioral sciences. Descriptive and inferential methods. Use of statistical software to explore conceptual issues and analyze data. One laboratory period in addition to lectures. 
Prerequisites: PSY 1 and a declared major in Psychology, Biopsychology, Clinical Psychology, Cognitive & Brain Science, Engineering Psychology, or Human Factors Psychology.

sections.note:
You will work in groups on a semester-long project of your choice (within ethical and logistical bounds) in which you conduct a largely quantitative study, collect and analyze your own data set, and present your findings verbally and in writing.

PSY 32 has an optional textbook that can be rented or purchased if you would like to use it as additional resources: please obtain the 10th edition if you do so. The ebook is available on reserve at Tisch Library.

Enrollment in the lecture section of PSY 32 is tied to lab enrollment: you have to enroll successfully in a lab to secure a spot in the course as a whole. If you're waitlisted for a lab, you will be waitlisted for lecture too. For more on the PSY 32 waitlist, see our departmental FAQ page (full link: https://as.tufts.edu/psychology/resources/faqs-undergraduates).
 
In general, I do not go above course capacity because course instruction is intense for both students and the teaching team. Student projects in PSY 32 are heavily scaffolded throughout the semester and require close advising and guidance from the teaching team. The more students we admit beyond the cap, the less capacity we have to give you timely feedback and support. If you cannot enroll in PSY 32 this semester, you may monitor SIS to see if a spot opens up, but if that also does not work, please wait for a future semester to do so. We on the PSY 32 teaching team seek your understanding and will also protect our capacity to advise you and your cohort when it comes time for you to enroll in the course.

courses.desc: (Cross-listed as PHIL 15 and LING 15.) How humans encode language in their brains, so that they can produce and understand an unlimited variety of utterances in context. Language and other forms of communication; how children acquire language; biological basis of language; the structure of language -- phonology (sound structure), syntax (grammatical structure), and semantics (meaning).

courses.title: Psychiatric Medications in Children
courses.desc: Seminar addressing the diagnosis and treatment of mental illness in children. The number of children diagnosed with serious mental illness such as bipolar disorder is on the rise; treatment of these illnesses includes mood stabilizers, antipsychotics, stimulants, antidepressants and some therapy. Questions considered include: Do these drugs affect the developing brain? Do these drugs permanently affect the brain? Are these drugs even effective in children?

courses.title: Social Identity, Stigma and Coping
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as PSY 215) People who are targeted by stereotypes and prejudice experience the world in unique ways. Investigation of the psychological consequences of stereotypes for victims and examination of how targets of prejudice actively cope with being members of devalued social groups. Examination of short- and long-term outcomes for people who possess devalued social identities, including the development of strategies to protect well-being in the face of discrimination. Discussion of the situational and interpersonal factors that facilitate versus undermine victims’ efforts to speak out about discrimination. Emphasis on empirical research and on teaching students how to interpret and critique research in social psychology.

sections.note:
When Octavia Butler published Parable of the Sower in 1993, she predicted the future. How did we get to this climate crisis? How do we make sense of its intersectional nature? How might we survive it and ensure that our world does too? This course explores the contributions and limitations of psychology as a framework and tool to tackle climate injustice. We will read classic and contemporary psychological research that examines the role of human decision-making, emotion, prior knowledge, and biases in creating, exacerbating, and addressing climate injustice. We will also examine complementary perspectives, frameworks, and tools that address the climate crisis, including but not limited to: Indigenous science, social movement studies, speculative fiction, and community organizing. The course uses a co-creative approach to content curation, learning, and teaching—you will actively choose course materials, come up with discussion prompts and learning activities, as well as design some key assessments for the course. courses.title: Human Communication
courses.desc:
Our elaborate system for communicating with each other is one of the primary
reasons for the evolutionary success of our species. No other animal can
communicate complex meanings as flexibly and efficiently as humans can. We are in fact so good at it that we are usually not even aware how advanced our
communication system is, and how much cognitive scaffolding it requires. Even
though human communication is severely underrepresented as a topic in Cognitive
Psychology, it is in fact one of the crown jewels of human cognition. This course is
aimed at providing a summary of how our communication system works from a
cognitive-psychological perspective, and giving a comprehensive overview of what
we do and don’t know about it.

sections.note: This course critically engages the political, economic, and social histories of the contemporary criminal legal system. Together, we will historicize and theorize the advent of the US prison in a genealogy of surveillance, captivity, and punishment constitutive of racial slavery. Thematics including abolition, resistance and revolt, state repression, borders, gendered violence, and Black radicalism will be at the heart of the coursework. sections.note: This course broadly considers Atlantic slavery through its multiple geographies, temporalities, and institutions of emergence. Through an engagement with canonical and contemporary historiographic texts of slavery that consider themes and problematics like political economy, gendering, and intellectual history, students will encounter a range of perspectives on Atlantic Slavery, not as an historical event of the ‘past,’ but as a condition of possibility for our modern world. Using primary archival sources to supplement vital secondary literature, the course offers access to resources that are held in hard-to-access libraries and archives to prompt curiosity regarding the nature of historiographic evidence, the predicament of experience, and the complexity of ‘official records.
