courses.title: Special Topics - Queer Nightlife
courses.desc: Mid-level courses open to undergraduate students. Please see departmental website for detailed course descriptions.

sections.note:
FULL COURSE TITLE: Queer Nightlife: Pleasure, Politics, Place

This class takes up a variety of nightlife spaces and contexts in which queer and trans people perform their pleasures and politics. Queer nightlife has been the center or political action. We have witnessed state sanctioned raids on Compton’s Cafeteria in San Francisco in 1966, Stonewall in NYC in 1969, the White Party in Bombay in 1999, the Queen Boat in Cairo in 2001, amongst many others. Additionally, in the wake of the massacre at Pulse Nightclub in Orlando in 2016, scholars have connected overlapping projects of imperialism that made queer life so precarious at Pulse. From these key moments have erupted important moments of activism that shifted common understandings of queer and trans life; nightlife has been a politically salient ground for shaping queer and trans cultures. In this class, we explore how and why queer nightlife become so threatening to the state, and the ways that nightlife offers a place of refuge from the mundane violence of everyday life. The class explores ball, drag, BDSM, disco, and rent party cultures, amongst many other forms of queer nightlife, and will include visits to local nightlife venues and class guests working in various nightlife worlds.

courses.title: Special Topics - Iran: Modern Lit. & Culture
courses.desc: Mid-level courses open to undergraduate students. Please see departmental website for detailed course descriptions.

sections.note: This course presents an introduction to the study of the literary and visual cultures of modern Iran (from the 19th century to the present day). Through engaging with a wide range of literary, visual, and cinematic texts, the course charts a path exploring the role of cultural expression as an arena of political and social resistance—not only to variety of forms of domestic authority (political tyranny, patriarchy, religious theocracy) but also to the influence and hegemony of colonial and imperialist forces. The course begins with the early literary and visual cultural innovations that fed into the revolutionary forces of the 1906 Constitutional Revolution, then explores the rise of nationalist and anti colonialist ideals expressed in literary and visual arts in the mid-20th century, to the variety of voices that came together in the 1979 revolution, and ends with more contemporary expressions of cultural resistance such as the Women Life Freedom movement and the 2026 uprising. Alongside the reading and viewing of primary texts—short stories, poems, novels, works of visual art, cinema—we will read secondary works of cultural and social theory that address how societies foster cultures of resistance to authoritarianism and repression. In particular. we will look to theorists and critics from Iran to provide frameworks for the study and analysis of the primary texts in the course.

courses.desc: Upper-level special topics course offered by RCD faculty members drawing on their current research. See current listings at https://as.tufts.edu/rcd/.

sections.note:
7 seats reserved for CAP advising 

W.E.B. Du Bois and the Problem of the Color Line 

In 1903, W.E.B. Du Bois wrote that "the problem of the twentieth century is the color line." By that time, Du Bois had already published multiple works examining the lived experiences and political struggles of Black people in the United States. He continued to write on these topics for the nearly sixty years. This course examines the interdisciplinary scholarship of W.E.B. Du Bois. Reading across his sociological, historical, and literary works, we will study how he employed multiple research methods and genres of writing to explore how Black people in the United States understood, experienced, and sought to redress "the color line." Readings will include fiction and non-fiction books, essays, poems, and newspaper articles written by Du Bois.

courses.title: Special Topics Research Seminar - Asian/Black American Anti-Colonial Struggle
courses.desc: Upper-level special topics course offered by RCD faculty members drawing on their current research. See current listings at https://as.tufts.edu/rcd/.

sections.note:
Full Title: Serve the People: Asian/Black American Anti-Colonial Struggle

In the structure of American racial hierarchies, a durable legacy of colonialism, Asian Americans and African Americans have long been pitted against one another—in education, labor, social standing, political objectives, and, always, in their perceived relation to whiteness. Yet, for at least a century, strong Black and Asian/American inter-influences and alliances have existed in political movements, intellectual thought, and cultural productions: from Ho Chi Minh’s anti-lynching writings; Paul Robeson’s and W.E.B. Du Bois’ visits to China; the 1955 Bandung Conference; through to the influence of Maoist thought on the Black Panthers; Black Power and Yellow Power movements; Bruce Lee as global masculine (non-white) icon; coalitions against the Vietnam War; and up to current alliances in various anti-racist and anti-imperialist endeavors (George Floyd, Gaza), Black and Asian/Asian diasporic peoples have refused Western colonial strategies of divide-and-conquer and have repeatedly challenged white supremacy and racial capitalism through acts of political solidarity and ideas and movements whose praxis was (and is) rooted in making concrete material change “for the people,” in this country and abroad. We will examine political and theoretical writings, literature, film, and music by Du Bois, Hughes, Richard Wright, Ho Chi Minh, Mao Tse-tung, Martin Luther King, Malcolm X, Bruce Lee, Huey Newton, Fred Hampton, George Jackson, Yuri Kochiyama, Fred Ho, Grace Lee Boggs, and Jackie Wang, among others.

Attention to the expression and contestation of Hinduism in colonial, postcolonial and diasporic contexts. Critical reflection on Hindu beliefs, social structures, popular customs, and rituals.

courses.title: Introduction to Judaism
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as JS 34 and HEB 70) Judaism as a diverse textual tradition and lived religion, with a focus on beliefs, ethics, and rituals. Contemporary Jewish communities from a global perspective; Hebrew Bible; rabbinic literature; medieval and modern theology and mysticism; social forms, law, and practice

courses.title: Introduction To The Talmud
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as JS 87 and HEB 61) Selected passages from the Talmud and rabbinic literature, Mishna, Gemara, Commentaries. Relevance to contemporary moral and ethical issues. All texts in English. If taken at the 100-level: Extra assignments and class meetings in Hebrew.

courses.title: Religious, Philosophical Roots of Modern World 1
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as MDVL 71, CVS 53, PHIL 29, CLS 29 and JS 29) Major religious and philosophical thinkers and concepts that played roles in the emergence of the modern world: Plato and Aristotle; Jewish, Christian, and Muslim scripture and theologians who merged their religions with the Greek tradition; the Ptolemaic universe and the Great Chain of Being. Medieval Jews, Christians, and Muslims saw themselves as having a privileged and objective place in a divinely-created and -ordered cosmos that was young, small, and centered on the earth.

sections.note:
High demand course. Instructor permission required. Please contact Yonatan Brafman at yonatan.brafman@tufts.edu to register.

10 seats reserved for CAP advising

courses.title: Law, Religion, and International Relations
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed with CVS 24) Relations between religion and the state seen through the lens of law and the day to day function of the judiciary in the US, Egypt, and China. Ways that religions provide the justification and structural foundation for the exercise of political and legal power within and between states as well as ways that religions respond to legal constraints enacted by governments. Focus on the repercussions of “Freedom of Religion” both historically and internationally and the role of secularism in fostering distinctly modern forms of religiosity and
“fundamentalisms.” First Amendment case-law in the United States; issues of sovereignty, law, and the state in Egypt and China.

courses.title: A Global History of Christianity to the Middle Ages
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as HIST 9 and MDVL 72). Development of Christianity as a world movement from antiquity through the medieval period. Study of key figures, events, and issues that helped shape Christian traditions in a variety of cultural, social and historical contexts.

sections.note: 10 seats reserved for CAP advising

courses.title: Readings in the Study of Religion
courses.desc: The academic study of religion through scholarly-theoretical texts, lectures, and films. Topics include theory of ritual and myth, history of the field of religion, anthropology, political philosophy, and current events that intersect with the study of religion. Prerequisite: Must have taken at least one class in the Religion Department at Tufts.

sections.note: 1-credit reading group. We will meet five times over the course of the semester, to read and discuss contemporary scholarship in the study of religion. This Fall, we will be looking at Kwame Anthony Appiah’s Captive Gods: Religion and the Rise of Social Science. Specific dates TBD.

courses.title: Theory And Method In The Study Of Religion
courses.desc:
Seminar on selected theories and methods in religious studies; may include anthropological, sociological, psychological, philosophical, text-critical, economic, feminist, and Marxist perspectives. Required for Religion majors and minors.
Recommendations: At least two other Religion courses or permission of instructor.

courses.title: Special Topics - Jewish History: Med. to Modern
courses.desc: Please see departmental website for detailed information.

sections.note: This course surveys Jewish history from the Late Second Temple period to the mid-twentieth century. It begins with the emergence of rabbinic Judaism and Jewish life under Christian and Muslim rule, then examines the transformative ruptures of modernity, including political emancipation, religious reform, and nationalism, culminating in the Holocaust and the establishment of the State of Israel. Through close analysis of primary sources, students will learn how the modern Jewish world developed out of its premodern foundations.

courses.title: Religion and Film
courses.desc: (Cross-listed w/ FMS 118) Analysis of religion and religious issues through their portrayal in contemporary film. Focus on approaches to film taken by scholars of religion, including mythological, theological and cultural studies, with consideration of film theory. Genres include drama, comedy, animation and science fiction.

courses.title: Religion and Colonialism in South Asia
courses.desc: Seminar on religious change in South Asia from the rise of British colonial rule to the partition of British India. Special emphasis on 19th-century Hindu, Muslim, and Sikh movements, the colonial construction of religious categories, competing modes of reformist and customary religion, and debates over the meaning of history, community, and gender.

courses.title: Islamic Spirituality: the Sufi Tradition
courses.desc: Seminar examining Islam's mystical tradition, including introduction to medieval and modern Sufi practice, and Sufi cosmology and metaphysics. Also examines Western studies and understandings of Sufism and mysticism more broadly.

courses.title: Introduction to Jewish Mysticism
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as JS 172 and HEB 172) Overview of the intellectual history of Kabbalah and Jewish Mysticism. Introduction to mystical ideas and doctrines from Biblical texts to contemporary sources, also within a wider, non-Jewish context. Inherent tensions within the mystical enterprise and the conflict between mysticism and rationalism. Reflects on uses and limits of mysticism in shaping contemporary religious experience.

courses.title: Book Of Genesis And Its Interpreters
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as HEB 132, JS 132 and ILVS 132) A detailed study of the biblical Book of Genesis in its ancient Near Eastern setting, with special attention to the role the Book of Genesis played in postbiblical Jewish tradition, as well as in Christian, Gnostic, and Islamic traditions and in the lives of many cultures, ancient, medieval, and modern.

courses.title: Special Topics - Slavery&Tufts: Archival Rsrch
courses.desc: Please see departmental website for detailed information.

sections.note: Since its founding in 1853, Tufts University has been a center of progressive education with deep ties to Universalist and anti-slavery traditions. Yet, this history has obscured the university's ties to the Atlantic slave trade, to colonial exploitation, and to the African American and Afro-Native communities in Medford and Boston. Tufts' Slavery, Colonialism, and their Legacies Project explores this complex history, as part of a recent wave of universities reckoning with their slave-owning past. This class, co-taught by scholars spearheading the project, provides students an opportunity to study Tufts' historic ties to slavery and colonialism through archival research and intense engagement with the SCL research team.

courses.title: Elementary Russian
courses.desc: Introduction to basic communication skills in Russian. Emphasis on speaking and listening. Fundamentals of Russian grammar, including the main parts of speech, verb conjugation, and basic sentence structure. Students learn to talk about friends and family, studies and interests, and daily schedules. Introduction to Russian culture through songs, poems, and brief readings. Online audio and video materials. Students may not earn credit for RUS 01 if RUS 01/2 has already been taken.

courses.title: Intermediate Russian
courses.desc: Further development of speaking, listening, reading, and writing skills. Students learn to express their opinions in a more sophisticated manner on such topics as work, study, and interests, Russian culture, and cultural difference. Mastery of more advanced grammar topics, including complex sentences, case usage, and verbal aspect. Online audio and video materials and authentic Russian texts. Recommended: Russian 2 or placement exam and permission of instructor.

courses.title: Composition And Conversation
courses.desc: Readings of unsimplified texts, fiction (classics and contemporary literature) and non-fiction (newspapers and magazines), feature films and documentaries. Expanding stylistic ability through composition and discussion. Grammar review and some advanced grammar concepts. Recommended: Russian 4 or placement exam and permission of instructor.

courses.title: Russian Literature & Revolution: 1880-1930
courses.desc: Russian literature in a period of political, social and cultural upheaval. Focus on how literature encouraged and critiqued ideas of revolution and the character of the revolutionary. Attention to political currents, avant-garde movements and their interconnection plus the dynamic response in the 1920s to the Bolshevik revolution. Readings include Tolstoy, Chekhov, Bely, Zamyatin, Bulgakov, Mayakovsky, Kollontai as well as political manifestoes and essays. Alternate years. (May be taken at 100 level with consent).

courses.desc: Advanced concepts in grammar and stylistics through reading, composition, and discussion of 19th- 21st century Russian short stories, contemporary periodicals, films and TV programming. courses.title: Today’s Russia: Society and Culture
courses.desc:
Language course for advanced students of Russian, including native/near-native speakers, focusing on society and culture in contemporary Russia. Topics include the revival of the culture industry and its role in the creation of a resurgent Russia and a new 21st century, post-soviet, Russian national identity and society. Course materials include literature, film, music, TV, pop culture and pulp fiction, and the internet. Work includes essays, oral reports and an independent research project. All work and materials in Russian.
Recommendations: RUS 122 or placement exam and permission of instructor.

courses.desc: Introduction to a wide range of digital fabrication toolsets, basic software, and hardware to learn to use digital fabrication in projects to meet 3D design challenges. Vector-based file creation in Adobe Illustrator, foundational tools of digital fabrication such as laser and vinyl cutters, and 3D modeling in programs such as Blender. courses.title: Drawing for Sculpture
courses.desc: Two-dimensional drawings for three-dimensional thinking. Examines the ways in which drawings can help in sculpture problem solving. Focus on making technical drawings to bring sculptures to scale. Demonstrations via the wood and welding shops facilitate understanding of how to execute forms from plans. Wood shop certification is included. Open to all levels.

courses.title: Body as Site
courses.desc: Intermediate sculpture and performance studio-seminar investigates the body as a primary site for material extension, prosthetic inquiry, and environmental immersion. Readings and historical research inform the design and fabrication of objects that challenge the boundaries between the physical form, wearable sculpture, and surrounding architecture. Focus on structural planning, material transformation, and the political implications of objects that activate the body in space. Critical inquiry and studio practice to explore the body as a location for the circulation of power and identity. No prior experience necessary.

courses.title: Kinetic Sculpture
courses.desc: Intermediate sculpture studio course that investigates movement as a structural, mechanical, and conceptual dimension of sculpture. Design and fabrication of projects that activate form in time and space through mechanical systems, motors, gravity, or responsive elements. Focus on structural planning, fabrication precision, material durability, and iterative prototyping. Readings and lectures situate kinetic practice within contemporary art and technological experimentation. Prior experience in fabrication studios or at least one previous sculpture course recommended. Prerequisites: 3D Foundations or equivalent, or instructor consent.

courses.title: Craft Theory Studio Seminar
courses.desc: Advanced studio-seminar examining historical and contemporary craft movements through critical theory, material culture studies, and interdisciplinary discourse. Craft’s evolving relationship to fine art, design, labor, gender, race, nationalism, and global production systems. Through sustained research, writing, discussion, and studio production, independent projects synthesize theoretical inquiry with material practice. Foundational and contemporary texts in craft theory, materiality, and critical studies to analyze how objects circulate within aesthetic, political, and social frameworks. Research-driven studio projects accompanied by written and verbal articulation of their conceptual frameworks. Prerequisites: Junior standing or above, and at least one prior course in SCP, MTL, FIB, or CER; or instructor consent.

courses.title: Ephemeral Objects
courses.desc: Intermediate-level course explores the material and theoretical aspects of ephemerality in sculpture and installation. Each week introduces a different theme for discussion and responsive work, such as material entropy, site-specificity, modular construction, immateriality, sustainability, performativity, ideas as objects and the ‘unmonumental’. Employs a wide range of material and media and consists of projects, critiques, readings, discussions, field trips and introduction to the work of contemporary artists in the field. Requires a basic understanding of sculptural materials and fabrication techniques; students must have taken 3D Foundations or obtain permission of instructor. Open to any media. Examines foundational woodworking processes through hands-on studio practice using both hand tools and machines. Introduces wood properties, material behavior, and basic fabrication strategies, including measuring, cutting, joinery, shaping, and surface treatment. Technical demonstrations and workshops support the development of safe tool use, structural thinking, and material literacy. Through a series of guided exercises and studio projects, students create objects of their own design using additive and subtractive processes. Lectures, discussions, and occasional field trips provide additional context for contemporary woodworking practices.

Address recent strategies and examine the shift of socially engaged artists from studio to situation or participatory actions. Non-SMFA students and MAT Art Education students will receive a letter grade.

courses.title: Post Baccalaureate Seminar
courses.desc: The Seminar is a mandatory core component of the curriculum for post-baccalaureate students, who take it both fall and spring semesters. Content is determined by the needs of the class and changes from fall to spring. The seminar includes professional presentations, student presentations, directed group discussions and writing projects, critiques of work, and visits to museums, galleries, collections, and other sites. We discuss the work and ideas of class members in the context of broad issues such as the role and purpose of art making, the practice of art as a career, and the perspectives currently under discussion in art criticism and theory. Emphasis is on group collaboration and peer support for individual artistic development. To keep discussion groups small, faculty lead separate seminar sections. (These groups occasionally hold meetings together.) Be ready to talk at the first class about your ideas and needs in your artwork, school, and prospective career, so that we can plan the semester's content.

courses.title: Post Baccalaureate Consultations
courses.desc: Individual critique sessions promote and foster abundant work and rapid progress by helping you deepen an understanding of your art, creative process, and work methods through focused critical feedback at regular intervals. Students meet individually with the instructor several times during the semester for critiques, to present works in progress, and to discuss emerging issues of individual interest. These consultations support and complement the work in the Post-Baccalaureate Seminar. Post-baccalaureate students are expected to actively seek individual critiques and consultation from their assigned faculty advisors and from faculty members teaching studio courses in which they are working.

courses.title: Directed Study - Drawing & Painting
courses.desc: One-on-one meetings with faculty and group meetings over the course of the semester to critique work, assess progress, and develop mentorship. Critique sessions promote and foster abundant work and rapid progress, deepening understanding of the creative process and work methods. Prior to 1st meeting, student must present a statement of intent, quantifying expected output, topics of interest and goals. At the end of the semester students summarize their work via an all class critique that includes a developed artists statement. Upper classmen and advanced students (MFA, Post-Baccalaureate, Diploma or Third and Fourth year BFA Students). Faculty permission required.

sections.req: MFA, Post-Baccalaureate, Diploma or Third and Fourth year BFA Students

courses.title: Grad Group Critique
courses.desc: This course is designed to build and develop the verbal and written articulation critique skills among the first and second year graduate students in a group setting facilitated by a faculty member. Critique is an essential skill for students to develop. Graduate Group Critique is a forum in which the capability of each student to identify and articulate the concerns, issues and motivations that form the basis of their research and practice expands. Through focusing on the ability to articulate the concerns investigated and addressed through each individual student’s art work, in whichever form that may take, this course assists students in both preparing for their review boards and preparing for the defense of their thesis. All first and second year Master of Fine Arts students are required to take this course each semester.

instructors: Boyang Hou, Kanthy Peng, Kate Conlon, Molly Caitlin Morin

courses.title: Graduate Professional Practices
courses.desc: For graduate students working in any art discipline. Links individual student practice to strategies of negotiating the art world after the MFA. Topics may include teaching jobs, residencies, grants, and professional opportunities in the arts across a diverse range of fields. Covers exhibitions, working with galleries, documenting work, and the many ways to build a healthy sustainable career as a creative practitioner. Write about work, present, participate in discussions, and hold one-on-one and group critiques.

courses.title: Intro. to Sociology: The Scientific Study of Society
courses.desc: Introduction to the systematic and scientific study of human social behavior. Topics include how history and social structure shape individuals’ daily interactions and experiences in the world, how individuals co-create social categories and cultural meanings together through interaction, and how human behavior varies across large and small groups. How societies maintain social control, set up stratification systems based on class, race, and gender, and regulate daily life through institutions such as families, schools, politics, and labor markets.

sections.note: One recitation required
Students enrolled in SOC 01 MUST take one recitation A or B

courses.title: Asian Americans in Contemporary Society
courses.desc: Sociological analysis of race, ethnicity, racism, immigration, and collective struggles of Asian Americans, frequently overlooked and implicitly posed as a group of people unscathed by discrimination. Negotiation of intra-group identities and mutual resistance, historically and today, to mistreatment through structural and micro-level approaches.

courses.title: Families, Romance & Intimacy
courses.desc: Understanding the contemporary American family, defined broadly as those with whom one shares resources and values and to whom one has a long-term commitment. Topics include historical and cross-cultural variations, dating and romantic love, cohabitation and marriage, parenting, family roles of men and women, divorce and family stability, and the future of the family.

courses.title: Smartphones, Social Judgment, and the Self
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as STS 21) Smartphone use as a socially meaningful and emotionally charged practice. Examination of the social meanings attached to phone use and how those meanings shape evaluations of the self and others. Topics include everyday judgments about screen time; emotions such as guilt, anxiety, and moral concern associated with smartphone use; and the influence of cultural norms and social expectations on lived experiences of connection, distraction, and attention. Readings, discussion, and real-world observation to analyze how smartphones function as sites of social regulation, identity formation, and moral evaluation in contemporary society. Students who have previously taken this course as SOC 94-MM1 are not eligible.

sections.note: 7 seats reserved for CAP advising

courses.title: Gender and Society
courses.desc: (Cross-listed w/WGSS 40 and CVS 30) Examination of gender and its prevalence in social life. Topics include the relationships between gender, sex and power relations; and how perceptions of gender change over time and help shape life opportunities and outcomes, and gender functions as a social construction. Consideration of gender expression through configurations of femininity and masculinity, and co-construction with race, sexuality, social class, ability, nation, and other lines of difference. Case studies may include the nature vs. nurture debate; gender and institutions, including families, schools, and religion; how gender shapes the nation state; masculinity; and feminist politics.

courses.title: Sociology of Drugs in America
courses.desc: Examination of the use, misuse, and regulation of drugs in the United States. Analysis of both legal medications and illicit “street” drugs, with attention to contemporary debates and dilemmas surrounding drug use, including the opioid crisis, emerging weight loss medications, and vaccines. Social, medical, and policy perspectives on drugs and their effects on individuals, communities, and society.

courses.title: Globalization And Social Change
courses.desc: Review of progress and social problems associated with the development of globalization. Alternative interpretations of the core features of the world system. Exploration of specific issues including distribution of economic and political power, role of multinational businesses, movement of peoples, cultural flows, intersection of global and local, the negative features of globalization, global cities, "anti-global" social movements, and different models for reform.

courses.title: Sociology of Latinxs
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as LAS 72) Overview of the diverse social, economic, political, and cultural histories of individuals who are now commonly identified as "Hispanics/Latinos/Latinxs/Latines" in the United States. Exposure to the political and historical development of the Hispanic/Latino panethnic category and group in the late 20th century, including tension between its racialized and immigration histories. Attention to the range of variables (such as nationality, nativity, citizenship and legal status, generation, cohort of arrival, social class, skin tone, race/ethnicity, gender, sexuality, religion) that create diversity within the group. Analysis of Latinxs' experiences across key social institutions - particularly schools, neighborhoods, the labor market, media, the immigration and criminal justice systems, and the American racial hierarchy.

courses.title: Deviance and Conformity
courses.desc: Foundational theories and methods in the study of deviance. Social construction of deviant categories. Role of social power and social order. Consequences of the deviant label and deviance of the powerful. Development of deviant identity and stigma management. Efforts to contest and transform deviant categories.

courses.title: Special Topics - Intro to Carceral Studies
courses.desc: Please see department website for detailed information.

sections.note: This course critically engages the political, economic, and social histories of the contemporary criminal legal system. Together, we will historicize and theorize the advent of the US prison in a genealogy of surveillance, captivity, and punishment constitutive of racial slavery. Thematics including abolition, resistance and revolt, state repression, borders, gendered violence, and Black radicalism will be at the heart of the coursework. Students can expect to gain a better understanding of the key terms of the developing disciplines of Carceral Studies and Prison Studies using primary and secondary source material, film, poetry, and other new media.

This two-credit course examines the cultural, organizational, political, and racial dynamics of contemporary policing in the United States; processes of expanding and resisting police power; events leading up to and following the 2020 uprising. This course runs for eight weeks."

courses.title: Internship
courses.desc:
Opportunity for students to apply a body of sociological knowledge in a practical setting, including community-based, profit or nonprofit, governmental, or other sites. Individual faculty sponsor internships in their areas of expertise. Students must have an on-site supervisor, and complete a piece of meaningful scholarly work related to the internship area.Please see departmental website for specific details.
Recommendations: SOC 1 or 10, plus one additional course in sociology related to internship area. To be arranged by individual members of the department.

courses.title: Research Design and Interpretation
courses.desc: Introduction to common empirical research methods to understand and explain social phenomena. Crafting of sociological questions and designing research to answer them. Methods include surveys, experiments, ethnographic methods, in-depth interviewing, material-based research, and focus groups; addresses the strengths, limitations, and complexities of each approach. Application of methodology through interpretation and critical assessment of existing research to become skilled consumers of sociological research.

courses.title: Quantitative Research Methods
courses.desc:
Data analysis and statistics for the social sciences. Sampling, describing data, and logic of inference, especially with surveys. Introduction to microcomputer tools for analysis and graphic display. Answering research questions through individual or group projects.
Recommendations: One introductory social science course.

courses.title: Sociological Theory
courses.desc: (Cross-listed with CVS 112) Examination of major theoretical traditions and their critical challenges in sociology. Explores diverse frameworks that address systems of power and oppression (e.g., racism, misogyny, capitalism, colonialism, adultism, and their intersections). Sociological discussions focusing on modernity, evolution of society, community and division, domination; approaches to highlighting past and contemporary social divisions and imagining social visions for alternative futures.

sections.req: Requires the completion of at least one Sociology course.Sociology Majors and Minors only

courses.title: Political Repression & Resistance
courses.desc: Forms of political repression and resistance; particular attention to current events in the US and across the world. Ways that state and non-state armed actors (organized crime, guerrilla fighters, etc.) try to control populations, as well as the strategies that different groups use to resist this control. Theories and concepts on repression, violence, and resistance.

courses.desc: Social organization of selected institutions and/or analysis of current issues. Please see Department website for detailed information.

sections.note:
Prerequisite: one or more of the following: SOC 100, SOC 101, SOC 102, or comparable methods training from another department

Engaging students in studying current social issues using quantitative and qualitative methods. In this 1-SHU course, students will examine how communities, institutions, and political and economic actors respond to contemporary problems such as climate change and environmental inequality, emphasizing the social forces that explain policy change and inaction. Lab members will collaboratively develop research projects for dissemination through multiple channels, including peer-reviewed journals, public-facing print and web media, conference presentations, podcasts, and the lab's blog. 
Prerequisite: one or more of the following: SOC 100, SOC 101, SOC 102, or comparable methods training from another department

courses.title: Selected Topics In Sociology - W.E.B Du Bois
courses.desc: Social organization of selected institutions and/or analysis of current issues. Please see Department website for detailed information.

sections.note:
7 seats reserved for CAP advising 

W.E.B. Du Bois and the Problem of the Color Line 

In 1903, W.E.B. Du Bois wrote that "the problem of the twentieth century is the color line." By that time, Du Bois had already published multiple works examining the lived experiences and political struggles of Black people in the United States. He continued to write on these topics for the nearly sixty years. This course examines the interdisciplinary scholarship of W.E.B. Du Bois. Reading across his sociological, historical, and literary works, we will study how he employed multiple research methods and genres of writing to explore how Black people in the United States understood, experienced, and sought to redress "the color line." Readings will include fiction and non-fiction books, essays, poems, and newspaper articles written by Du Bois.

courses.title: Seminar: Intimate Violence
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CVS 160) Examines intimate violence as a product of and contributor to broader structures of inequality. Focuses on causes, forms, and costs of abuse committed in the context of intimate relationships in the US and globally. Considers the influence of the media, economics, segregation, politics, gender, race, nationality, and history on intimate violence. Prerequisites: Junior standing and declared major in sociology or permission of instructor.

courses.title: Seminar: Body, Culture & Society
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as WGSS 181) How the body influences our understanding of the social world, the ways we interact with others, and self-perception. Examination of the body as a product of complex social arrangements and processes. Topics may include how bodies are regulated by social forces; how individuals use bodily knowledge to understand the social world; and whether a “right” body exists. Prerequisites: Two sociology courses or instructor permission.

courses.title: Seminar: US Meritocracy: Myth or Reality?
courses.desc: Sociological exploration of meritocracy, a system in which individuals are rewarded for their merits. Topics include how selection systems distinguish applicants, how ideas about merit have changed over time, and beliefs about equal opportunity. Consideration of access and inclusion, especially related to race and class, in systems of meritocracy. Prerequisites: Junior standing or instructor permission. Recommendations: Two sociology courses.

sections.note: This Spanish course examines the complex landscape of identity and social issues in the Spanish-speaking world through a diverse selection of films, short stories, novels, poems, articles, and songs. This class takes an interdisciplinary approach to the study of Puerto Rico. While students continue to review grammar and practice oral and aural skills, they study the history, literature, and culture of Puerto Rico and Puerto Ricans on the island and on the mainland. They debate the possible political destinies of Puerto Rico and discuss the lasting effects of Hurricane María, the debt of 72 billion dollars, the corruption in the administration of various former governors, and the resistance of Bad Bunny and other Puerto Rican activists. Students view films, sample Puerto Rican cuisine, and visit one of the major Puerto Rican neighborhoods of Boston: Villa Victoria. Required weekly recitation session. Conducted in Spanish. courses.title: Diversidad: Identity & Dissent in Modern Spain
courses.desc: Exploration of cultural productions that shaped the history of Modern Spain from the 18th century to the present. Interdisciplinary approach to literary texts, films, songs, and visual works to examine Spain's diverse identities. Key questions include whether Spain can be considered a modern country and how modernity is reflected in its contemporary literary and cultural productions; whether religion remains a defining characteristic of modern Spain; and what non-canonical works reveal about equality and freedom in the country. Topics and literary movements may include the Enlightenment, Romanticism, Realism, Modernism, Generations of ‘98 & ‘27, immigration, and nationalism. Development of critical skills by analyzing diverse cultural forms to understand their historical significance and contemporary relevance. Not for senior majors or students returning from programs abroad. Prerequisite: SPN 22, SPN 23, or instructor permission.

courses.title: Latin America: Cultural Perspectives
courses.desc: Exploration of the cultural productions that have shaped key moments in the histories of Latin America and the Caribbean, from the early 20th century to the present. Interdisciplinary approach to literary texts, films, songs, and visual works to unpack the complexity of Latin American cultures and their ongoing transformations. Key questions include how identities are constructed and how they relate to literature, film, and the dynamics of cultural production and in what ways artistic movements and popular culture engage with these identities. Topics may include modernity, the Latin American literary boom, authoritarianism, the climate crisis, and indigeneity. Development of critical skills in analyzing diverse cultural forms to understand their historical significance and contemporary relevance. Not for senior majors or students returning from programs abroad. Prerequisite: SPN 22, SPN 23, or instructor permission.

courses.title: Convivencia: Identity and Dissent in Early Modern Spain
courses.desc: Interdisciplinary study of cultural expression in Spain between the 11th and 17th centuries, a period of coexistence and intense exchange between Christians, Muslims, and Jews that culminated in the creation of a unified, monocultural Spain. Focus on key literary texts and corresponding cultural materials, like art, music, historical documents, to examine the beliefs underpinning major social and artistic developments of the era. Topics such as national identity, gender, religion as devotion and suppression, and models of love and beauty may be interwoven with an exploration of how the Catholic Kings’ concept of empire influenced the myth of Convivencia. Understanding of contemporary cultural forms and society by recognizing their origin in Spain’s past. Not for senior majors or students returning from programs abroad. Prerequisite: SPN 22, SPN 23, or instructor permission.

sections.req: Spanish 22, Spanish 23, or consent of the instructor

courses.title: Latin America: Colonial (Dis)encounters
courses.desc:
Cultural, social, and political transformations from pre-Hispanic civilizations to the late 19th Century. Focus on colonial and post-colonial materials to explore how colonial legacies continue to shape our contemporary world. Topics may include indigenous worldviews, (often violent) encounters between European and Native American cultures, the imposition and adaptation of colonial structures, slavery and its
legacies, evangelization and syncretism, and literature's role in shaping and challenging colonial ideologies. Analysis of historical objects, connecting them to contemporary issues, to understand the ongoing relevance of colonial histories in modern societies. Development of cultural literacy skills by analyzing diverse forms to appreciate their historical significance and interconnectedness. Not for senior majors or students returning from programs abroad. Prerequisite: SPN 22, SPN 23, or instructor permission.

sections.req: Spanish 22, Spanish 23, or consent of the instructor

courses.title: Spanish Labyrinth
courses.desc: Exploration of the historical, cultural and ethnic richness and complexity of the land we know as Spain. Focus on the cultural heterogeneity, the workings of Spain’s imperialist traditions, and the transcultural forces of globalization in contemporary Spain. No prerequisites.

courses.title: Special Topics - Latinx History: Race Migration

courses.title: Advanced Composition And Conversation I - Adv Spanish Composition & Conv
courses.desc: Examines dynamics of power through an interdisciplinary approach that includes perspectives from philosophy, psychology, sociology, sociolinguistics, history, and politics. Explores a variety of literary genres (poetry, drama, and prose), other forms of art (film, photography, comics, music, etc.) and non-fiction texts (essays and news reports). Advances written and oral expression in Spanish, with focus on the development of fluency through informal live and online conversations with classmates and Spanish native speakers, oral presentations and active group discussions (mesas redondas). Reflects on grammar and vocabulary as needed for material analysis and course projects. Studies colloquial and dialectal expressions to amplify knowledge and use of colloquial Spanish. In Spanish. Prerequisites: SPN 22, SPN 23, or instructor permission.

sections.req: Spanish 22, Spanish 23, or consent of the instructor

courses.title: Medical Spanish
courses.desc: Overview of the practice of medical interpretation in Spanish. Building skills in communication, ethics, and medical vocabulary, while exploring cultural and advocacy questions. Opportunity to practice interpretation in a simulated medical setting. Class discussions include role-play, cultural readings, vocabulary expansion, videos, and film. Conducted in Spanish.

courses.title: Creative Writing In Spanish
courses.desc: Composition skills for writing short stories, poetry, and creative essays in Spanish. Analysis of a selection of essays, short stories, and poems from contemporary Latin American literature to learn how some authors mastered their craft. Workshop-based. Conducted in Spanish. Recommendations: Two courses above Spanish 22 or consent of the instructor.

courses.title: Don Quijote
courses.desc: A careful reading of both books of Don Quijote (1605 and 1615) as expressions of the Renaissance and Baroque visions of man and his destiny. Conducted in Spanish. Recommended: Two 30-level Spanish courses or consent of the instructor.

sections.note:
A close reading of books I and II of Cervantes's masterpiece, a work that satirizes and celebrates the most popular literary genres and models of the Spanish Golden Age. A novel that celebrates the spirit of adventure, friendship, play-acting and storytelling, the Quijote draws both its protagonists and its readers into a variety of fictional worlds. Its composition reflects the exuberance of the Renaissance and the disillusionment of the Counter Reformation, a duality that defines the rise and decline of the Spanish empire during this remarkable period of artistic achievement. Readings will focus on the innovative ways in which Cervantes explores existing theories of literature while anticipating future critical theories and reading strategies for generations to come. 
Prerequisite: Spanish 30 or 32, 31 or 33, or consent from professor.

courses.title: Spanish Language Varieties
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as LING 0145) Exploration of the social and linguistic variability within and across diverse Spanish-speaking regions, with a focus on pronunciation and phonetic principles. For students proficient in Spanish. Overview of how factors like socioeconomic status, gender, age, multilingualism, and geography influence how Spanish speakers use the language. Distinguishing characteristics among dialects and the processes behind their development, including the impact that pronunciation has on the formation of regional identities and stereotypes while enhancing linguistic skills and cultural awareness. Recommendations: Two courses above SPN 22 or instructor permission; Spanish heritage speakers: one course above SPN 23 or instructor permission. In Spanish.

courses.title: Spanish In The Community
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed as LST 146 and CVS 186) Application of academic study of Spanish language and Hispanic cultures to volunteer work in bilingual situations with organizations that serve Latino communities. Focus on the history, literature, and politics of Puerto Ricans on the island and the mainland and the experiences of Salvadorans and Mexicans in their native countries and in the United States. Minimum of four hours of volunteer work per week. In Spanish. Prerequisite: At least two courses above SPN 0022 or consent. Native Spanish-speakers require
consent of the instructor.

courses.title: Health in the Spanish-Speaking World
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CH 124 & LAS 148) Examination of the determinants of health in Latin American countries and among Latino communities in the United States. Focus on disease, drugs, maternal and child health, nutrition, poverty, and health. Texts include scholarly articles, narrative, poetry, and film. Conducted in Spanish. Recommendations: Two courses above Spanish 22 or consent of the instructor.

courses.title: Borges and the Encyclopedia of the World
courses.desc: (Cross-listed with LAS 153) Introduction to the literary world of Jorge Luis Borges, one of the major authors of 20th-century literature in any language. Close attention to Borges’s philosophical interests as well as the ways his literature engages with a wide range of cultures and traditions, like Jewish mysticism, the classical world, Islam or Buddhism, and Argentinian culture and history. Readings include Borges's major stories, essays, lectures, and conversations. Conducted in Spanish. Recommendations: Two 30-level Spanish courses or consent of the instructor.

courses.title: Women and Film in Latin America
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as FMS 127) Critical study of the representation of women in Latin American cinema. Beginning with Mexico's edad de oro (1930-1940) to the present, an exploration of the positioning of a gendered spectator, the role of melodrama, as well as issues of race and class in the construction of women's identity through film. Includes a variety of films, primarily from Argentina, Brazil, Cuba, Mexico and Peru. Conducted in Spanish. Recommended: Two 30-level Spanish courses or consent of the instructor.

courses.title: STS Lunch Seminar
courses.desc: Attendance at weekly speaker series featuring presentations from Science, Technology, and Society experts from academia, industry, and other organizations. Written reflections on each presentation. Detailed information about speakers can be found on the STS website. Talks are open to the public.

courses.title: STS Reading Lab - Classification
courses.desc: Reading- and discussion-only course, intended to complement courses outside the STS curriculum. Discussion of readings from a list organized around rotating topics of interest. Topics vary by semester and may include energy, life, information, classification, power, and models. See STS website or SIS detail view for semester-specific information. Course but not topics may be repeated for credit.

courses.title: Smartphones, Social Judgment, and the Self
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as SOC 21) Smartphone use as a socially meaningful and emotionally charged practice. Examination of the social meanings attached to phone use and how those meanings shape evaluations of the self and others. Topics include everyday judgments about screen time; emotions such as guilt, anxiety, and moral concern associated with smartphone use; and the influence of cultural norms and social expectations on lived experiences of connection, distraction, and attention. Readings, discussion, and real-world observation to analyze how smartphones function as sites of social regulation, identity formation, and moral evaluation in contemporary society. Students who have previously taken this course as SOC 94-MM1 are not eligible.

courses.title: Introduction to the Anthropology of Science and Technology
courses.desc: (Cross listed w/ ANTH 32) An anthropological approach to the social and cultural studies of science and technology. Asks how and whether sociocultural forces shape the content of science, how to define “technology,” and how science and technology impact culture and society. Covers anthropological methods and research findings on topics such as algorithms, genetics, theoretical physics, classification, cyborgs, facts, infrastructure, and magic.

courses.title: AI in Motion: Ethics & Impact in Media Industries
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CVS 13 & FMS 36) Examination of the transformative role of artificial intelligence (AI) in digital media industries, with a particular focus on cinema and television. Engagement with theoretical and empirical literature and discussion of the history and current ethical debates surrounding AI, including AI’s impact upon contemporary media practices. Hands-on experience with cutting-edge AI tools for text, sound, image, and motion picture generation. Development of skills in critically analyzing and creatively engaging with the future of AI in media.

courses.title: The Energy Transition
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed as UEP 133, CEE 101, ME 174, and ENV 161) Consideration of engineering concepts relevant to the global transition from fossil fuels to renewable sources of energy. Interface between policy and technology in the energy sector and its relevance to decision making. Offshore wind energy is used as an example to illustrate the convergence of
technology, infrastructure, policy, and markets that is necessary to achieve a just and equitable energy transition. Course is open to juniors, seniors, and graduate students from across the university.

sections.req: Junior, Senior, or Graduate students only

courses.title: Development Of Knowledge And Reasoning In The Science Curriculum
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ED 111) Through interviews of students and readings from science education research, participants develop multiple perspectives on the development of scientific knowledge and reasoning, consider current teaching practices in middle and secondary school science, and design their own instructional plans.

courses.title: Mathematics Learning Environment
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ED 112) Explores models of learning, reasoning, and understanding in mathematics through readings from education and cognitive science research, practical experience, and experimental interviews in the context of secondary, postsecondary, middle, and elementary curriculum.

courses.title: Philosophy Of Biology
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed w/PHIL 118) Conceptual foundations of evolutionary biology and ecology. Focus on specific theoretical controversies including fitness, natural selection explanations, macroevolution, biological functions, genetics, inheritance and levels of selection.
Recommendations: Two courses in Philosophy or Biology or consent.

sections.req: 2 courses in BIO or PHIL or philosophy graduate student

courses.title: Development Of Knowledge & Reasoning In Engineering
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ED 119) Exploration of topics of engineering and engineering education considering both historical and emerging perspectives. Design of instructional plans and example lessons to teach specific engineering and design concepts to K-12 students.

courses.title: Epistemology
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed as PHIL 131) An investigation of fundamental issues and problems concerning the nature and scope of human knowledge: belief, truth, evidence; skepticism and certainty; perception; intuition; and the a priori.
Recommendation: PHIL 2 and 33, or permission of instructor.

courses.title: Medical Anthropology
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed w/ANTH 0148). Cultural models of illness, health, deviance, and normality. Institutions of medicine and healing in non-Western contexts and in the contemporary U.S. Using a critical medical anthropological approach, special topics (such as AIDS, madness, and gender-related concerns) will be explored.
Recommendations: Sophomore standing

courses.title: How to Pay Attention
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ANTH 189 and FMS 109) Collective investigation of attention as a sociocultural phenomenon. Reading-, writing-, and discussion-intensive seminar, supplemented by experimental exercises in and out of class. Topics include information overload, distraction, boredom, enchantment, expertise, social media, attention economies and ecologies, attention deficits and surpluses, and ideologies of attention in politics, education, and ethnographic fieldwork. Recommendations: Junior standing and one sociocultural anthropology course, or permission of instructor.

courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ENT 141, AMER 141, and CVS 187) Learn how to address systemic social and environmental problems and generate financial returns. Choose a problem based on your why. Form a diverse team and interview stakeholders. Harness AI for marketing and product development. Execute a pilot project with real users. Create and present a pitch deck. Interact with impact entrepreneurs and investors. Emerge as a more confident leader with valuable career skills, a broader network, and maybe even an impact venture.

courses.title: Leadership in Action

Development and application of leadership skills across a range of contexts including startups, corporations, and nonprofits and across different stages of a business. Frameworks to navigate conflict and leadership challenges. Development of inclusive teams. Strategies for developing self-awareness and leading with authenticity. Alignment of actions with goals and intentions. Connection of life experience and strengths to leadership approach.

courses.title: Mastering Money: Developing Financial Literacy

courses.title: Introduction Theatre, Dance, & Performance Studies
courses.desc: Interdisciplinary foundations of analysis and critique in theatre, dance, and performance studies. How embodied practice shapes social, political, and cultural environments both in formal performance and in everyday life. How performance shapes and constructs social hierarchies, such as race, gender, and sexuality, as well as how artists create alternative social scripts. Historicizes theatre, playwriting, and choreographic practices to identify how performances have evolved over time and influence what we see today.

courses.title: Foundations of Performance and Production
courses.desc: Creative process and the collaborative aspects of production and theatre-making. Exploration of all areas of theatre including practical projects as designers, directors, stage managers, dramaturgs, technicians, and actors, culminating in final presentations/performances.

courses.title: Modern And Postmodern Theatre
courses.desc: This discussion-based course examines dramatic literature and its theatrical performance from the explosion of "-isms" at the beginning of the twentieth century, through the innovations heralding the beginning of the twenty-first. Modern societies and ways of thinking have undergone radical transformations during this period, as have dramatic and theatrical expression. We will journey through this era of change through the close examination of approximately twenty plays, related critcal readings, films of plays, class presentations, and lively discussions.

courses.title: Latinx Theatre and Film
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as LST 51) Introduction to Latinx theatre, film, and performance as a potent creative and political force in the United States. Representative works by Latinx playwrights, performance artists, and filmmakers will be discussed in light of issues such as labor and immigration, gender and sexuality, generation gaps in Latinx culture, hybridized identities, interculturalism, and the United States' relationship with Latin American nations.

courses.title: Art of the Moving Image
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ILVS 51 & FMS 1) Exploration of cinema's basic aesthetic characteristics: its stylistic features, such as editing, cinematography, and sound, as well as its major narrative and non-narrative forms: mainstream and avant-garde, fiction and non-fiction, narrative and non-narrative, black-and-white and color, silent and sound. Discussion of the extent to which cinema's aesthetic features are shared by television, as well as what is artistically distinctive about television. Theoretical concepts relevant to moving image art, principally genre, authorship, and character identification.

sections.note: First-years, sophomores, or juniors - seniors with permissions. Mandatory twice weekly recitation (film screening).

courses.title: Introduction to Media Culture and Theory
courses.desc: (Cross-listed with FMS 101 & ILVS 54) Qualitative media studies, its history, intellectual development, and theoretical milestones. Introduction to study of popular media culture. Covers major areas of study, theoretical principles, methodologies, and debates that have shaped popular media studies. Theoretical approaches to issues and case studies (including representation, labor and authorship, contemporary media convergence, fandom and participatory culture, media globalization, reality television, game studies, industry research and more). Students acquire knowledge of the major theories that define the field and contemporary application of these theories in critical engagements with media texts and practices.

courses.title: Imagining The Holocaust On Stage And Screen
courses.desc: (Cross-listed w/FMS 45, JS 25, HIST 39 & TPS 125) Plays and films dealing with the Holocaust, From Nazi-era propaganda to contemporary reflections on genocide. Special emphasis on the ethics of Holocaust represented and the responsibilities of artists (and audiences) who engage the Holocaust story. Texts include such plays as Camp Comedy, Ghetto, Kindertransport, Good, Bent, Who Will Carry the World?, and Annulla, as well as critical and theoretical readings. Triumph of the Will, Night and Fog, The Architecture of Doom, Partisans of Vilna, The Boat is Full, My Mother's Courage, Schindler's List, Life is Beautiful and Shoah are among the feature films and documentaries considered. (Graduate Students should register for TPS 125).

courses.title: Greek & Roman Tragedy - Greek Tragedy, Trojan War
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as CLS 155.) For advanced undergraduates and graduate students, in-depth study in conjunction with TPS 28. (Also offered as lower-level).

sections.req:
Only one credit of CLS 55, 155, TPS 53, 153 allowed.
Students may only receive one credit from CLS 55,155, TPS 53, 153.

courses.title: Introduction To Acting
courses.desc: A basic course in acting aimed at enhancing self-confidence, oral expression, and creativity. Emphasis on concentration, motivation, and improvisation, and what it means to create a character and speak before an audience. Limit of eighteen students per section.

courses.title: Acting Realism and Naturalism
courses.desc: Use of Stanislavski’s terms — given circumstances, through-line, sense memory, creative imagination and ensemble acting — to analyze Arthur Miller’s play “A View from the Bridge.” Exercises (dramaturgy, radio play, documentary, and masked improv) bring the class deeply into the moment-to-moment world of the play. Focus on stage-worthy acting, how an actor thinks and honoring the body's expressive impulses. Individual coaching and skill set analysis through scene work. Prior acting experience in productions and/or acting classes recommended. No prerequisites.

courses.title: Musical Theatre Song Rep
courses.desc: Performance-based class on the songs of the musical theater tradition including repertoire selection, analysis of musical styles, and song preparation. Development of a wide-ranging and individualized repertoire of musical theater songs, selection and preparation of audition material, collaborating with an accompanist, and incorporating the singing voice into an effective dramatic presentation.

courses.title: Voice And Speech - The Art Of Confident Expression
courses.desc: A course in persuasive communication designed to empower students to speak with confidence and fluency in any situation. Explores the connection between sound and movement, breath and body, mindfulness and positive energy through physical and vocal exercises intended to maximize the full range of flexibility, variety and contrast in vocal expression. Focuses on such essential aspects of voice as pitch, pace, volume, inflection, and articulation, with special attention to the demands of public speaking.

courses.title: Public Speaking

courses.title: Special Topics - Queer Nightlife
courses.desc: This course explores special topics in theatre or film. For more about the specific listings offered each semester please see the department website at: http://dramadance.tufts.edu.

sections.note:
FULL COURSE TITLE: Queer Nightlife: Pleasure, Politics, Place

This class takes up a variety of nightlife spaces and contexts in which queer and trans people perform their pleasures and politics. Queer nightlife has been the center or political action. We have witnessed state sanctioned raids on Compton’s Cafeteria in San Francisco in 1966, Stonewall in NYC in 1969, the White Party in Bombay in 1999, the Queen Boat in Cairo in 2001, amongst many others. Additionally, in the wake of the massacre at Pulse Nightclub in Orlando in 2016, scholars have connected overlapping projects of imperialism that made queer life so precarious at Pulse. From these key moments have erupted important moments of activism that shifted common understandings of queer and trans life; nightlife has been a politically salient ground for shaping queer and trans cultures. In this class, we explore how and why queer nightlife become so threatening to the state, and the ways that nightlife offers a place of refuge from the mundane violence of everyday life. The class explores ball, drag, BDSM, disco, and rent party cultures, amongst many other forms of queer nightlife, and will include visits to local nightlife venues and class guests working in various nightlife worlds.

courses.title: Special Topics - Contemporary Comedy
courses.desc: This course explores special topics in theatre or film. For more about the specific listings offered each semester please see the department website at: http://dramadance.tufts.edu.

sections.note:
FULL COURSE TITLE: Contemporary Comedy: American Stand-up from Vaudeville to Today

This class looks at contemporary American comedy, primarily through jokes, sets, personae, and oral histories of American comedy from roughly 1950 to today. It views comedy through select historical context, including technologically-driven changes in media and economic relationships. Pioneering artists with vaudeville roots are introduced, the stand-up boom of the 1980s is presented as having shaped today's comedy business, and cultural moments concerning race and immigration are discussed via their representation in comedy. Some time is devoted to improv and sketch, but the core of the subject matter is stand-up, which we treat as a variety of theatrical monologue. Performance studies concepts including matrixed performance, social drama, and performativity are introduced through application to stand-up comedy. Theories of comedy by Freud, Bergson, and others are discussed.

Assignments include short in-class essays, multiple-choice quizzes, and an optional final assignment: perform your own original 3-minute stand-up set.

courses.title: Special Topics - Fashion & Clothes Histories
courses.desc: Please see departmental website for detailed information: http://dramadance.tufts.edu/

sections.note:
COURSE: Fashion Histories: Thinking With Clothes.

How can a study of clothing enrich an understanding of history? Why can producing, consuming, wearing, or displaying dress offer new insight to the past? 

This course will examine how historians use dress and fashion to interpret the past and will explore the theories, concepts, and questions that drive dress history and material culture studies. We will use a comprehensive definition of dress to include clothing, adornment, and embellishment. Clothing, makeup, earrings¿all of these can offer a useful lens into cultural, political, economic, and gender dynamics of a time and place. While this course focuses on the historical discipline, dress and fashion history is a highly interdisciplinary field. We will draw from fields beyond history including art history, anthropology, and museum studies. Examining the production, consumption, and display of dress, we will explore how clothing is integral to understanding personal and political identity. This course encourages us to see dress as a way to uncover perspectives and stories that otherwise may be obscured. What kinds of answers can dress and fashion offer about the past that written sources cannot? 

INSTRUCTOR: Margot Rashba (A18, G21) is a PhD candidate in History at Boston University. Her dissertation “Britishness on the Runway: Dress and Identity from Punk to the Present” explores Britishness and national identity in the collections of designers Vivienne Westwood, John Galliano, and Alexander McQueen from 1970 to 2015. Margot received both her BA and MA from Tufts University, with her Master’s in history and museum studies. She has worked in the museum and public history world for the past eight years in institutions including the Peabody Essex Museum and the Boston Symphony Orchestra Archives.

courses.title: Television in the Age of Change
courses.desc: (Cross listed as ILVS 72 & FMS 165) Examines how new technologies and shifting viewing habits are transforming television; how storytelling is changing in light of TV’s industrial and technological evolution and our global, networked, media environment; and how contemporary viewing habits are reshaping our theories of audiences, styles, and viewing pleasures. Focuses on story creation, changing genres, programming conventions and global trends, shifting technologies, social media, TV fans, and streaming content—and how all these influence television narratives and our media culture.

courses.title: Imagining The Holocaust On Stage And Screen
courses.desc:
(Cross-listed w/FMS 45 & TPS 25 and JS 25) Plays and films dealing with the Holocaust, From Nazi-era propaganda to contemporary reflections on genocide. Special emphasis on the ethics of Holocaust represented and the responsibilities of artists (and audiences) who engage the Holocaust story. Texts include such plays as Camp Comedy, Ghetto, Kindertransport, Good, Bent, Who Will Carry the World?, and Annulla, as well as critical and theoretical readings. Triumph of the Will, Night and Fog, The Architecture of Doom, Partisans of Vilna, The Boat is Full, My Mother's Courage, Schindler's List, Life is Beautiful and Shoah are among the feature films and documentaries considered.
Recommendations: Graduate Standing.

courses.title: Colonial Unknowing
courses.desc: This graduate level course is designed to consider the making and unmaking of colonial epistemologies, an active process scholars have referred to as colonial unknowing. Western discourse is underpinned by universalist assumptions on subject-object divides, particularly on fundamental topics like temporality, space, humanism, and nature. Focusing on an undisciplined approach to thinking and learning, we will consider knowledge relationally across decolonial, anti-imperialist and anti-colonial intellectual movements. We will analyze texts and artworks that capture the global and intersecting histories of racialization and colonization, and the active efforts to reject colonization’s overwhelming matrix of power. Our study of artistic interventions will allow us to accrue strategies and methods of challenging colonial extraction, including methods of refusal, illegibility and opacity. Key scholars include Sylvia Wynter, Anibal Quijano, Frantz Fanon, Tiffany King, Maria Lugones, and Leanne Betasamosake Simpson. Graduate level course open to advaned undergraduates with instructor permission. Open to graduate students through SMFA and Tufts (specifically Art History, English, and History).

courses.title: Feminist, Queer and Trans Performance
courses.desc: If gender and sexuality, as embodied social categories, significantly inform how we become legible, how and to what ends do performers use bodies and their environments to transform, question, obscure, and expand what we understand as human, or even a body? This class draws on critical race, disability, indigenous, and postcolonial scholars who ask how power, pleasure, and violence are distributed and accessed via the management of gender and sexuality. It pairs these critical texts with artistic works to examine how queer, trans, and feminist theories are made in the flesh.

courses.desc: This course will provide a review of the history of US housing policy in the 20th and 21st Centuries with a focus on understanding the systems and structures that created and reinforce our current settlement patterns characterized by racial, ethnic, and income sorting. courses.title: Drones for Data Collection, Mapping & Analysis
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ENV 121) Covers the foundations of Unoccupied Aircraft Systems (UAS, aka drones) for data collection; provides skills to manage, plan, and execute remote flight operations. Applications in many fields including ecology, environmental science, urban planning, agriculture, natural and cultural resources management, and emergency response. Legal aspects of flying UAS, including FAA requirements; collecting and processing imagery data for use in Geographic Information Systems (GIS); creating data for spatial analysis and remote sensing. Incorporates the use of Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) for field data collection.

courses.title: Negotiation, Mediation & Conflict Resolution
courses.desc: (Cross-listed with CVS 183). courses.title: The Energy Transition
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as STS 101, ME 174, CEE 101 & ENV 161) Consideration of engineering concepts relevant to the global transition from fossil fuels to renewable sources of energy. Interface between policy and technology in the energy sector and its relevance to decision making. Offshore wind energy is used as an example to illustrate the convergence of technology, infrastructure, policy, and markets that is necessary to achieve a just and equitable energy transition. Course is open to juniors, seniors, and graduate students from across the university.

sections.req: Junior, Senior, or Graduate students only

courses.title: The Gap Between Law and Justice
courses.desc: The class will look closely at the roles of some of the players in the justice system; the presence or absence of power; prosecutorial misconduct; the psychological impact of wrongful accusation and the relationship between law enforcement and the media. Together we will consider issues of race, class, gender and religion as we make connections between these issues, fundamental fairness, societal costs and freedom.

courses.title: Fundamentals of ESG & Impact Investing
courses.desc: Interest in sustainable and responsible investments is moving to center stage for retail investors, financial institutions, corporate boards, government agencies, NGOs and executive teams interested in minimizing harm or maximizing the opportunity to improve social and environmental outcomes through return-seeking investments. This course examines the history of Impact Investing, by introducing students to the functions of capital markets and the values embedded in those markets. The course will explore investment vehicles and the ways that a range of impact investments can be deployed across asset classes. The class uses this analysis to explore the false dichotomy between ESG and Impact. Throughout the course, the cohort will explore the key metrics needed to assess various forms of value. Students will learn key developments in the industry and the economic forces and ethical challenges driving the pressure for companies to operate more sustainably and responsibly. Starting with the assumption that impact investors seek prudent positive impact, students will also examine the ways that retail investors can shape that impact. The students will come away from the class with an informed, personal definition of impact investment and the fundamental understanding to consider ways that impact investment can serve the issues that matter to them.

courses.title: Impact Investing for Catalytic Impact: Filling Capital Gaps
courses.desc: (Cross-listed as ENV 188) This course explores the impact investing capital continuum from government agencies to ESG funds, banks, advisors, endowments, impact funds and individual investors and ways they can bridge traditional investment expectations with those required by an economy focused on positive impact. The course focuses on the role impact investors can play to fill ‘capital gaps’ to advance sustainability and equity, defined by the intersectional needs of social entrepreneurs and impact investors. By drilling down into the practical correlations between mission, cost structure and financial returns, the course explores opportunities and challenges for impact capital to advance a sustainable and equitable agenda. Students will gain insight into capital limits and matchmaking opportunities for different segments of capital providers, including philanthropy, ESG funds, regulated financial institutions, place-based funders and other potential sources of impact funds. Given the rapid emergence of the field, students will be exposed to an array of contemporary learning experiences including case studies, workshops, lecture, and guest speakers. Students will leave this course with the conceptual and practical framework required to deploy catalytic capital and to distinguish this segment of the impact investing space from aligned and complimentary strategies.
